airlaw_1.brief: ICAO Annex 6 requires Certificate of Registration, Airworthiness, ARC, Logbook, and crew papers on board for international flights.
airlaw_1.detailed: ICAO Annex 6 Part I Chapter 4 and EU Regulation 965/2012 require: Certificate of Registration, Certificate of Airworthiness, Airworthiness Review Certificate, Airplane Logbook, and crew licenses. EASA Form 1 is a part release certificate, not a flight document. The Technical Logbook is used for maintenance tracking but not mandatory for international flights.

airlaw_2.brief: A restricted area can be crossed with permission from the controlling authority, unlike prohibited areas.
airlaw_2.detailed: A restricted area (ICAO designation 'R') can be entered with permission from the controlling authority. Prohibited areas ('P') cannot be entered. Dangerous areas ('D') indicate potential hazards. No-fly zones are a military designation.

airlaw_3.brief: The AIP (Aeronautical Information Publication) contains detailed information about airspace restrictions.
airlaw_3.detailed: The AIP contains detailed airspace structure and restrictions. ICAO 1:500,000 charts show airspace visually. AICs provide general information. NOTAMs give temporary changes. The restriction type, hours, and conditions are published in the AIP ENR section.

airlaw_4.brief: Bilateral agreements are between two states, covering air services between their territories.
airlaw_4.detailed: A bilateral air services agreement (ASA) is a treaty between two states regulating commercial air transport. These agreements preceded the EU's single aviation market and are still used with non-EU countries.

airlaw_5.brief: Multilateral agreements involve more than two states, such as the Chicago Convention.
airlaw_5.detailed: Multilateral agreements involve multiple states. Examples: the Chicago Convention (1944) established ICAO, the EU Single European Sky, and the European Common Aviation Area (ECAA) agreement.

airlaw_6.brief: EASA regulations are directly applicable as EU law in all member states without needing national ratification.
airlaw_6.detailed: EASA is an EU agency. Its regulations (Part-FCL, Part-MED, Part-21, etc.) are adopted as European Commission regulations and are directly binding in all EU member states without national transposition.

airlaw_7.brief: EUROCONTROL provides ATC in the upper airspace over Northern Europe and central flow management (ATFM) across Europe.
airlaw_7.detailed: EUROCONTROL's objectives include: air traffic control in upper airspace over many Northern European states, and Air Traffic Flow Management (ATFM) via the Central Flow Management Unit (CFMU) in Brussels, which processes all IFR flight plans in Europe.

airlaw_8.brief: The Certificate of Airworthiness remains valid as long as the aircraft remains airworthy and the ARC is renewed.
airlaw_8.detailed: The Certificate of Airworthiness (CofA) has unlimited validity, provided the aircraft is maintained per its approved maintenance programme and the Airworthiness Review Certificate (ARC) is renewed periodically.

airlaw_9.brief: ARC stands for Airworthiness Review Certificate, which confirms the aircraft meets airworthiness standards.
airlaw_9.detailed: The Airworthiness Review Certificate (ARC) is issued after a satisfactory airworthiness review. For EASA aircraft, the ARC is valid for 1 year (for aircraft under 2730kg MTOM) or 3 years (with approved maintenance programme).

airlaw_10.brief: ICAO Annex 1 covers Personnel Licensing - standards for pilot and crew licensing worldwide.
airlaw_10.detailed: ICAO Annex 1 'Personnel Licensing' contains Standards and Recommended Practices (SARPs) for the licensing of flight crew, air traffic controllers, and aircraft maintenance personnel.

airlaw_11.brief: ICAO Annex 1 licenses are recognized by all ICAO contracting states, enabling international flight.
airlaw_11.detailed: Article 29 of the Chicago Convention requires pilots to carry a valid license. ICAO Annex 1 licenses are recognized by all 193 ICAO contracting states, subject to the state's acceptance of the license.

airlaw_12.brief: A PPL does not expire; it remains valid provided the holder maintains recency and medical fitness.
airlaw_12.detailed: Under Part-FCL, the PPL has unlimited validity. However, the holder must maintain: valid medical certificate, recency requirements (3 take-offs and landings in 90 days for day VFR, 90 days for night), and separate ratings (SEP, MEP, etc.) have their own validity periods.

airlaw_13.brief: EASA Part-FCL requires 5 hours night flight, including 3 hours dual instruction with 1 hour cross-country.
airlaw_13.detailed: EASA Part-FCL Appendix 7 requires: 5 hours night flight time total, including 3 hours dual instruction with a flight instructor including 1 hour cross-country, and 5 solo take-offs and full-stop landings.

airlaw_14.brief: For pilots aged 60+, Class 2 medical certificates are valid for 12 months (EASA Part-MED).
airlaw_14.detailed: EASA Part-MED: For Class 2 medical certificates, the validity is 60 months for ages 17-39, 24 months for ages 40-59, and 12 months from age 60 onwards.

airlaw_15.brief: If SEP recency requirements are not met, renewal requires a proficiency check with an examiner.
airlaw_15.detailed: Under Part-FCL.740, SEP revalidation requires 12 hours in 12 months. If not met, the rating must be renewed by a proficiency check with an examiner (with refresher training as determined by the ATO).

airlaw_16.brief: A PPL holder may act as PIC on non-commercial flights and receive compensation only as an instructor or for flights with MTOW ≤2000kg.
airlaw_16.detailed: Under EU Regulation 965/2012, a PPL holder may act as PIC on non-commercial flights with no compensation. Cost sharing is permitted. As a flight instructor (FI) with appropriate rating, compensation may be received. The 2000kg MTOW limit applies when receiving compensation.

airlaw_17.brief: BCMT = Before entering airspace C: Transponder Mandatory - a reminder to switch on transponder before entering Class C airspace.
airlaw_17.detailed: BCMT is a reminder phrase for entering Class C airspace: Before entering Class C airspace: switch on Transponder Mode C and squawk assigned code. It's a memory aid commonly used in training.

airlaw_18.brief: Before entering a TMZ, pilots must switch on and operate the transponder with Mode A/C or Mode S.
airlaw_18.detailed: In a Transponder Mandatory Zone (TMZ), all aircraft must carry and operate an SSR transponder with Mode A/C or Mode S. No specific clearance is needed, but compliance with SERA.6001 is mandatory.

airlaw_19.brief: SERA = Standardised European Rules of the Air, harmonizing air traffic rules across EASA member states.
airlaw_19.detailed: SERA (Standardised European Rules of the Air) is Implementing Regulation EU 923/2012, replacing the previous national rules of the air across all EASA member states for harmonized air traffic rules.

airlaw_20.brief: IFR = Instrument Flight Rules, governing flights conducted solely by reference to instruments.
airlaw_20.detailed: IFR (Instrument Flight Rules) are rules governing flight solely by reference to instruments in the cockpit, used in IMC or as required by airspace classification. Defined in SERA.5005.

airlaw_21.brief: A visual flight is conducted under Visual Flight Rules (VFR), not necessarily in VMC.
airlaw_21.detailed: SERA.2001 defines a visual flight as a flight conducted under Visual Flight Rules (VFR). The key distinction is the regulatory framework (VFR), not meteorological conditions.

airlaw_22.brief: IMC = Instrument Meteorological Conditions, where flight by visual reference is not possible.
airlaw_22.detailed: IMC (Instrument Meteorological Conditions) are conditions with visibility and cloud distance below VFR minima. Defined in SERA.3010 as meteorological conditions expressed in terms of visibility and distance from clouds.

airlaw_23.brief: Bad weather near an aerodrome is not a valid reason to fly below minimum safe altitudes.
airlaw_23.detailed: SERA.3101 allows deviations from minimum heights only for: take-off/landing, dropping objects, and approaches without landing. Bad weather is not a valid exception - pilots must divert or hold.

airlaw_24.brief: When two aircraft are on converging courses, both shall alter course to the right (SERA.3210).
airlaw_24.detailed: SERA.3210 right-of-way rules: When two aircraft are converging at approximately the same altitude, the aircraft that has the other on its right shall give way. Both aircraft must turn right.

airlaw_25.brief: The angle between aircraft determines the term: crossing (>70°) or passing (<70°).
airlaw_25.detailed: SERA.3206 defines crossing as converging with an angle >70°, passing as parallel or near-parallel tracks. Crossing requires the aircraft on the right to give way.

airlaw_26.brief: Minimum height above industrial sites handling flammables/explosives is 1000ft above the highest obstacle within 600m.
airlaw_26.detailed: SERA.3105 requires minimum height over congested areas of 1000ft above the highest obstacle within a 600m radius. For industrial sites handling hazardous materials, this same standard applies.

airlaw_27.brief: Priority order (lowest to highest): engine-driven, gliders, hang-gliders/paragliders, balloons.
airlaw_27.detailed: SERA.3210 establishes priority as: balloons, gliders, airships, hang-gliders/paragliders, engine-driven aircraft. The question asks for lowest priority first (reverse order).

airlaw_28.brief: When two engine-driven aircraft converge at the same altitude, both shall turn right.
airlaw_28.detailed: SERA.3210(a): When two aircraft are on converging courses, the aircraft that has the other on its right shall give way, and both shall avoid collision by turning right.

airlaw_29.brief: When taxiing towards each other, both aircraft shall turn to the right.
airlaw_29.detailed: SERA.3210(g): When two aircraft are taxiing on a collision course, each shall stop and give way. If approaching head-on, each shall alter course to the right.

airlaw_30.brief: In an RMZ, pilots must maintain radio watch and establish communication if possible.
airlaw_30.detailed: Radio Mandatory Zones (RMZ) require aircraft to maintain a continuous listening watch on the appropriate frequency and establish two-way communication if possible (SERA.6001).

airlaw_31.brief: Ceiling is the height of the base of the lowest cloud layer covering more than half the sky below 20000ft.
airlaw_31.detailed: SERA.2001 defines ceiling as the height above ground or water of the base of the lowest layer of clouds covering more than half the sky, below 20000ft.

airlaw_32.brief: VFR flight visibility in Class C airspace at and above FL100 is 8 km.
airlaw_32.detailed: SERA.5001 Table 1: VFR visibility minima in Class C, D, and E airspace at and above FL100 is 8 km.

airlaw_33.brief: In Class B airspace below FL100, VFR flight visibility minimum is 5000 m.
airlaw_33.detailed: SERA.5001 Table 1: VFR visibility minimum in Class B airspace is 5000 m below FL100 and 8000 m at/above FL100.

airlaw_34.brief: VFR cloud clearance in Class B: vertically 1500m, horizontally 300m.
airlaw_34.detailed: SERA.5001 Table 1: VFR cloud clearance in Class B: 1500m vertically, 300m horizontally from clouds.

airlaw_35.brief: In Class C airspace below FL100, VFR minimum flight visibility is 5000 m.
airlaw_35.detailed: SERA.5001 Table 1: VFR minimum flight visibility in Class C airspace below FL100 is 5000 m.

airlaw_36.brief: Special VFR requires the aircraft to remain clear of clouds and in sight of the surface.
airlaw_36.detailed: Special VFR (SERA.5010) requires: visual reference to the terrain, clear of clouds, ground visibility ≥1500m (for fixed-wing), and flight visibility ≥1500m.

airlaw_37.brief: The military interceptor is signaling 'Follow me' by rocking wings and turning left.
airlaw_37.detailed: ICAO Annex 2 Appendix 1, Section 1: Interceptor signals. Alternating ailerons followed by left turn = 'You have been intercepted, follow me'.

airlaw_38.brief: A sudden 90° heading change and pull-up means 'You may continue your flight'.
airlaw_38.detailed: ICAO Annex 2 Appendix 1: A sudden 90°+ heading change and pull-up without crossing the intercepted aircraft's path = 'You may continue your flight'.

airlaw_39.brief: Altimeters are switched from QNH to standard 1013.25 hPa when passing the transition altitude on climb.
airlaw_39.detailed: SERA.6005 and SERA.6015: The transition altitude is the altitude at which pilots change from QNH to standard pressure (1013.25 hPa) when climbing.

airlaw_40.brief: At Flight Level 80, the altimeter must be set to standard pressure 1013.25 hPa.
airlaw_40.detailed: At Flight Levels (FL), the altimeter must be set to 1013.25 hPa (standard pressure). FL80 = 8000ft on standard pressure setting.

airlaw_41.brief: The semi-circular rule assigns cruising levels based on magnetic track to reduce collision risk.
airlaw_41.detailed: SERA.4005: The semi-circular rule assigns VFR cruising levels based on magnetic track: odd FLs + 500ft for tracks 0-179°, even FLs + 500ft for tracks 180-359°.

airlaw_42.detailed: ICAO Annex 10: SSR codes: 7500 = unlawful interference, 7600 = communication failure, 7700 = emergency. 7600 disables Mode C reporting.

airlaw_43.brief: SSR transponder modes used in civil aviation are A (identity), C (altitude), and S (selective).
airlaw_43.detailed: SSR modes: Mode A = identity (4-digit code), Mode C = pressure altitude, Mode S = selective addressing with data link capability. Modes B and R are military.

airlaw_44.brief: Mode C and Mode S transponders automatically transmit pressure altitude information.
airlaw_44.detailed: Mode C and Mode S transponders both report pressure altitude automatically using a 15-bit Gillham code from the encoding altimeter or air data computer.

airlaw_45.brief: The IDENT button should only be pressed when specifically requested by ATC.
airlaw_45.detailed: The IDENT (Special Position Identification) pulse should only be pressed when ATC specifically requests 'Squawk IDENT' to identify the aircraft on radar.

airlaw_46.brief: ATC (Air Traffic Control) is primarily responsible for the safe conduct of flights.
airlaw_46.detailed: ATC provides separation (vertical, horizontal, and longitudinal) between IFR flights and, where required, between VFR flights. FIS provides information only, not separation.

airlaw_47.brief: In Class E airspace, VFR traffic receives no separation service from ATC.
airlaw_47.detailed: In Class E airspace, IFR flights receive ATC separation from other IFR flights. VFR flights receive no separation service but require ATC clearance.

airlaw_48.brief: FIS (Flight Information Service) is contacted via radio communication on appropriate frequencies.
airlaw_48.detailed: FIS (Flight Information Service) is provided via radio on specified frequencies. In many countries, FIS is available on 120.475-123.475 MHz or through designated sector frequencies.

airlaw_49.brief: A correct position report uses the format: callsign, position, time, altitude.
airlaw_49.detailed: SERA.8025 prescribes position report format: Aircraft identification, Position, Time, Flight Level/Altitude, Next position and ETA, followed by name of ATS unit.

airlaw_50.brief: The AIP General (GEN) section contains administrative information such as access rules, pilot requirements and licence specimens.
airlaw_50.detailed: AIREP (Aircraft Report) is a meteorological report from aircraft. The AIP GEN section contains: national regulations, ATS system, met services, SAR, fees, and charges.

airlaw_51.brief: A PIB (Pre-Flight Information Bulletin) presents current NOTAM information before flight.
airlaw_51.detailed: A PIB contains NOTAM information (not AIP, AIC, or ICAO) of operational significance, prepared before flight to alert the pilot to changes affecting the route.

airlaw_52.brief: The NOTAM validity is from B) 1305211200 to C) 1305211400, so it's valid until 14:00 UTC on 21/05/2013.
airlaw_52.detailed: NOTAM format: Series number/year, A) FIR, B) Start date-time, C) End date-time. A1024/13 starts at B) 13/05/21 12:00 and ends at C) 13/05/21 14:00 UTC.

airlaw_53.brief: Aerodrome elevation is defined as the highest point of the landing area.
airlaw_53.detailed: ICAO Annex 14 defines aerodrome elevation as the elevation of the highest point of the landing area (runway). This is used for altimeter setting calculations.

airlaw_54.brief: A runway is a rectangular area on a land aerodrome prepared for landing and take-off.
airlaw_54.detailed: ICAO Annex 14: A runway is a defined rectangular area on a land aerodrome prepared for the landing and take-off of aircraft. Heliports have different definitions.

airlaw_55.brief: Water patches on a runway means visible patches of standing water, creating slippery conditions.
airlaw_55.detailed: ICAO reporting: 'WATER PATCHES' = patches of standing water on the runway surface. This affects braking action, classified as medium/good when dry patches exist.

airlaw_56.brief: A SNOWTAM is a special series NOTAM reporting snow, ice, and standing water on movement areas.
airlaw_56.detailed: A SNOWTAM is a special series NOTAM (format given in ICAO Annex 15) reporting the presence of snow, ice, slush, or standing water on movement areas.

airlaw_57.brief: 'Damp' indicates a change of colour on the runway surface due to moisture, without standing water.
airlaw_57.detailed: 'DAMP' indicates the runway surface has changed colour due to moisture but there is no standing water. Braking action should be normal.

airlaw_58.brief: Flashing red light to an aircraft in flight means 'Airport unsafe, do not land'.
airlaw_58.detailed: ICAO Annex 2 Appendix 1: Flashing red light to aircraft in flight = 'Aerodrome unsafe, do not land'. This overrides any previous clearance.

airlaw_59.brief: Steady green light to an aircraft in flight means 'Cleared to land'.
airlaw_59.detailed: ICAO Annex 2 Appendix 1: Steady green light to aircraft in flight = 'Cleared to land'.

airlaw_60.brief: Flashing white light on ground = 'Return to starting point'.
airlaw_60.detailed: Aerodrome light signals: Flashing white = Return to starting point. Flashing red = Clear taxiway/runway. Steady red = Give way/Stop.

airlaw_61.brief: Flashing green light to an aircraft in flight means 'Return for landing'.
airlaw_61.detailed: ICAO Annex 2 Appendix 1: Flashing green light to aircraft in flight = 'Return for landing' (followed by steady green to land when appropriate).

airlaw_62.brief: A wind direction indicator (windsock) may be surrounded by a white circle for better visibility.
airlaw_62.detailed: ICAO Annex 14: A wind direction indicator should be visible from the air and may be marked by a white circle or other contrasting background for visibility.

airlaw_63.brief: Pilots confirm receipt of light signals by rocking wings during daytime.
airlaw_63.detailed: ICAO Annex 2 Appendix 1: Aircraft acknowledge light signals by: daytime - rocking wings, nighttime - flashing landing lights twice.

airlaw_64.brief: A landing direction indicator is shaped like a 'T' (tetrahedron).
airlaw_64.detailed: ICAO Annex 14: A landing direction indicator (tetrahedron or T) shows the direction of landing and take-off in use at a non-controlled aerodrome.

airlaw_65.brief: The signal square contains visual symbols indicating aerodrome conditions to overflying aircraft.
airlaw_65.detailed: ICAO Annex 2 Section 2.4: The signal square provides visual signals about aerodrome conditions to overflying aircraft, such as right-hand traffic patterns.

airlaw_66.brief: According to ICAO Annex 14, runway markings are white.
airlaw_66.detailed: ICAO Annex 14 Table 5-1 specifies white for all runway markings (designation, centerline, threshold, touchdown zone, side stripe markings).

airlaw_67.brief: Parallel runways are designated with suffixes 'L' (left) and 'R' (right).
airlaw_67.detailed: ICAO Annex 14: Parallel runways are designated by the same number with suffixes L (left), R (right), or C (center) when viewed from the approach direction.

airlaw_68.brief: Longitudinal stripes (touchdown zone markings) indicate the touchdown zone - don't touch down before them.
airlaw_68.detailed: ICAO Annex 14: Touchdown zone markings (longitudinal stripes) identify the touchdown zone for landing aircraft. Pilots should not touch down before these markings.

airlaw_69.brief: Runway edge lights are white, except on instrument runways where they may be yellow at the end.
airlaw_69.detailed: ICAO Annex 14: Runway edge lights are white (variable white on precision approach runways), last 600m section may have yellow edge lights.

airlaw_70.brief: DETRESFA = Distress Phase, the most serious emergency phase indicating grave danger.
airlaw_70.detailed: ICAO Annex 12: DETRESFA (Distress Phase) = Aircraft and occupants in grave and imminent danger requiring immediate assistance. Third and most serious emergency phase.

airlaw_71.brief: Search and rescue services are provided jointly by military and civil organizations.
airlaw_71.detailed: ICAO Annex 12 requires states to provide SAR services jointly by military and civil organizations coordinating through RCCs (Rescue Coordination Centres).

airlaw_72.brief: ALERFA (Alert Phase) is triggered when fuel exhaustion is suspected and no landing message received.
airlaw_72.detailed: ICAO Annex 12: ALERFA (Alert Phase) is declared when: fuel may be exhausted, aircraft has been cleared to land but not landed within 5 minutes, or information indicates aircraft safety is jeopardized.

airlaw_73.brief: INCERFA is triggered when an aircraft has not arrived within 30 minutes after ETA.
airlaw_73.detailed: ICAO emergency phases: INCERFA = 30 min past ETA without contact. ALERFA = fuel exhaustion concerns. DETRESFA = imminent danger requiring immediate assistance.

airlaw_74.brief: The ground signal 'X' means 'Unable to proceed'.
airlaw_74.detailed: ICAO Annex 12: Ground-air visual signal code: 'X' = 'Unable to proceed'. Created with fabric strips, snow trenches, or other visible means.

airlaw_75.brief: The ground signal 'V' means 'Need help' or 'Require assistance'.
airlaw_75.detailed: ICAO Annex 12: Ground-air visual signal code: 'V' = 'Require assistance' (or 'Need help'). The signal should be at least 2.5m x 0.5m.

airlaw_76.brief: In flight, a pilot confirms visual signals by rocking the wings.
airlaw_76.detailed: ICAO Annex 12: An aircraft acknowledges visual signals by rocking wings (daytime) or flashing lights (nighttime).

airlaw_77.brief: Accident investigation aims to identify causes and issue safety recommendations, not to apportion blame.
airlaw_77.detailed: ICAO Annex 13: The sole objective of accident investigation is prevention, not apportionment of blame or liability. The final report contains safety recommendations.

humanperf_1.brief: Human factors contribute to approximately 80% of aviation accidents, making human performance the leading causal factor.
humanperf_1.detailed: According to IATA and Boeing studies, approximately 80% of aviation accidents involve human factors as a primary or contributing cause. Technical failures account for about 15%, with environmental factors making up the remainder. The HUman Factors Analysis and Classification System (HFACS) provides a framework for analyzing these errors.

humanperf_2.brief: The SHELL model (Software, Hardware, Environment, Liveware) illustrates the interfaces between pilots and their operational environment.
humanperf_2.detailed: The SHELL model (developed by Elwyn Edwards and refined by Frank Hawkins) consists of: Software (procedures, checklists), Hardware (aircraft systems, controls), Environment (weather, ATC, terrain), Liveware (pilot, crew). The interfaces between these components are where human errors typically occur.

humanperf_3.brief: Reason's Swiss Cheese Model explains how multiple latent failures must align for an accident to occur, like holes in slices of cheese.
humanperf_3.detailed: James Reason's Swiss Cheese Model (1990) illustrates how defenses against accidents are like multiple slices of Swiss cheese. Latent conditions and active failures must align for an accident to occur. Each layer of defense has holes (weaknesses) that vary in size and position over time.

humanperf_4.brief: Flying skills are developed through deliberate practice and experience, not just natural ability or pharmaceuticals.
humanperf_4.detailed: Skill acquisition follows the Dreyfus model: novice → advanced beginner → competent → proficient → expert. This requires deliberate practice (Ericsson, 1993) with specific goals and feedback, not just repetition.

humanperf_5.brief: Mental rehearsal and visualization techniques benefit pilots at all experience levels, not just students or instructors.
humanperf_5.detailed: Mental practice activates the same neural pathways as physical practice (mental imagery). Studies show it improves performance in: emergency procedures, instrument scanning, and flight maneuvers. Effective at all experience levels (Feltz & Landers, 1983).

humanperf_6.brief: The percentage of oxygen in the atmosphere remains constant at 21% up to approximately 100,000 ft. It's the partial pressure that decreases with altitude.
humanperf_6.detailed: The percentage of oxygen in the atmosphere remains constant at 21% up to approximately 100 km (328,000 ft). At 6000 ft, the partial pressure of oxygen decreases to about 158 mmHg (from 160 at sea level), but the percentage remains 21%.

humanperf_7.brief: Henry's Law governs DCS: gases dissolve in liquids proportionally to partial pressure.
humanperf_7.detailed: Decompression sickness is governed by Henry's Law: the amount of gas dissolved in a liquid is proportional to its partial pressure. Rapid ascent causes nitrogen to come out of solution, forming bubbles.

humanperf_8.brief: Atmospheric pressure halves at approximately 18,000 ft (the 500 hPa level in ISA).
humanperf_8.detailed: In the International Standard Atmosphere (ISA), pressure decreases approximately 1 hPa per 27 ft. At 18,000 ft MSL, pressure is approximately 500 hPa (half of 1013.25 hPa).

humanperf_9.brief: Carbon monoxide from cigarette smoke binds to haemoglobin 200-300x more readily than oxygen, reducing oxygen-carrying capacity.
humanperf_9.detailed: CO binds to haemoglobin 200-300 times more strongly than oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin (COHb). Smokers typically have 5-15% COHb, reducing oxygen delivery. Even 5% COHb impairs night vision and cognitive function.

humanperf_10.brief: Redout occurs during negative g-forces (pushing over) when blood rushes to the head, causing a red-tinted vision.
humanperf_10.detailed: During negative g-forces (push-over), blood pools in the upper body and head. The high pressure in retinal capillaries causes a red-tinted visual field. This contrasts with 'grey-out' (positive g, blood pooling in lower body).

humanperf_11.brief: Pulse oximeters measure oxygen saturation but cannot detect hyperventilation (low CO2), which can cause symptoms similar to hypoxia.
humanperf_11.detailed: Pulse oximeters measure SpO2 via light absorption through tissue. They cannot detect PaCO2 levels. Hyperventilation reduces CO2 without affecting SpO2 significantly, so it remains undetected. The pilot may have normal SpO2 but be incapacitated by hypocapnia.

humanperf_12.brief: Cracked heat exchangers in cabin heating systems can leak engine exhaust containing carbon monoxide into the cockpit.
humanperf_12.detailed: Cabin heater systems in light aircraft often use a shroud around the exhaust manifold. Cracks or corrosion in the heat exchanger can allow exhaust gases containing CO to enter the cabin air supply. Regular inspection of the heater muff is critical.

humanperf_13.brief: Cyanosis is a symptom (blue discoloration), not something that is NOT a symptom. Hyperventilation symptoms: tingling, spasms, LOC.
humanperf_13.detailed: Hyperventilation symptoms: paraesthesia (tingling), carpopedal spasm (hand/foot cramps), visual disturbances, dizziness, and eventually loss of consciousness. Cyanosis (blue skin) is a sign of hypoxia, not hyperventilation.

humanperf_14.brief: Carbon monoxide poisoning causes anemic hypoxia by reducing the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity without reducing blood flow.
humanperf_14.detailed: Anemic hypoxia results from reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood. CO poisoning reduces available haemoglobin. Unlike hypoxic hypoxia (altitude), the PO2 in the blood is normal, but less oxygen is carried.

humanperf_15.brief: Erythrocytes (red blood cells) contain haemoglobin which transports oxygen from lungs to body tissues.
humanperf_15.detailed: Erythrocytes are biconcave discs containing haemoglobin. Each haemoglobin molecule can bind up to 4 oxygen molecules. The oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve shows this binding is cooperative - facilitating loading in lungs and unloading in tissues.

humanperf_16.brief: Thrombocytes (blood plates) are responsible for blood clotting, preventing excessive bleeding from injuries.
humanperf_16.detailed: Thrombocytes (platelets) are cell fragments produced in bone marrow. They aggregate at injury sites and release clotting factors. Normal count: 150,000-400,000/microliter. Low count increases bleeding risk - relevant for pilot medical certification.

humanperf_17.brief: Leukocytes (white blood cells) form the body's primary immune defense against infection and foreign substances.
humanperf_17.detailed: Leukocytes are part of the immune system: neutrophils (phagocytosis), lymphocytes (antibody production), monocytes (tissue cleanup), eosinophils (allergic response). High count indicates infection; low count may indicate immune deficiency.

humanperf_18.brief: Cyanosis (blue lips/fingernails) is a classic sign of hypoxia, indicating inadequate oxygen saturation.
humanperf_18.detailed: Cyanosis occurs when reduced haemoglobin exceeds 5g/dL in capillary blood. It's most visible in nail beds, lips, and mucous membranes. In aviation, it's a late sign of severe hypoxia requiring immediate action.

humanperf_19.brief: Vision is the first sense affected by hypoxia due to the retina's high oxygen demand.
humanperf_19.detailed: The retina consumes oxygen at a rate of ~10 mL O2/100g/min - one of the highest in the body. Rods (night vision) are more sensitive to hypoxia than cones (day/color vision). Night vision starts degrading from 4000-5000 ft cabin altitude.

humanperf_20.brief: The body typically starts reacting to decreasing atmospheric pressure from around 7000 ft due to reduced oxygen partial pressure.
humanperf_20.detailed: The physiological altitude zone: 0-5000 ft (indifferent zone), 5000-10000 ft (compensatory zone - increased ventilation/heart rate), 10,000-15,000 ft (disturbance zone - symptoms appear), above 15,000 ft (critical zone).

humanperf_21.brief: Early hypoxia symptoms include: impaired judgment, vision disorders, and cognitive difficulties - often described as 'drunk-like' behavior.
humanperf_21.detailed: Early hypoxia symptoms (often described as 'Euphoria' stage): impaired judgment (risk-taking), loss of self-criticism, overconfidence, vision disorders (tunnel/ blurred vision), and difficulty with mental tasks. These symptoms are insidious - the pilot is often unaware.

humanperf_22.brief: The respiratory center is most sensitive to CO2 levels, not O2. Rising CO2 triggers the urge to breathe.
humanperf_22.detailed: The primary respiratory center is in the medulla oblongata. Chemoreceptors (central and peripheral) are most sensitive to CO2 levels via pH changes. Rising CO2 (hypercapnia) strongly stimulates breathing. Peripheral chemoreceptors also respond to O2 below 60 mmHg.

humanperf_23.brief: Hypoxia is a condition where the body or a region is deprived of adequate oxygen supply.
humanperf_23.detailed: The four types of hypoxia: 1) Hypoxic (altitude) - low O2 partial pressure, 2) Anemic - reduced O2 capacity, 3) Stagnant (circulatory) - reduced blood flow, 4) Histotoxic - cells can't use O2 (e.g. alcohol, cyanide).

humanperf_24.brief: Time of Useful Consciousness (TUC) is the time available to perform tasks efficiently with inadequate oxygen before incapacitation.
humanperf_24.detailed: TUC varies with altitude: 18,000 ft = 20-30 min, 22,000 ft = 10 min, 25,000 ft = 3-6 min, 28,000 ft = 2.5-3 min, 30,000 ft = 1-2 min, 35,000 ft = 30-60 sec, 40,000 ft = 15-20 sec. Exercise halves TUC.

humanperf_25.brief: Smokers have higher COHb levels (5-15%), reducing oxygen capacity. They experience hypoxia symptoms at lower altitudes than non-smokers.
humanperf_25.detailed: Smokers abuse: COHb levels of 5-15% in smokers vs 0.5-1% in non-smokers. This is equivalent to losing 5000-7000 ft of physiological altitude. A smoker's effective 'physiological altitude' is about 8000 ft at sea level.

humanperf_26.brief: Haemoglobin has a 200-300x greater affinity for carbon monoxide than oxygen, making CO poisoning particularly dangerous.
humanperf_26.detailed: CO affinity for haemoglobin is ~240x that of O2. CO also shifts the O2 dissociation curve left, reducing O2 release to tissues. Half-life of COHb is ~4-6 hours breathing air, ~1 hour breathing 100% O2.

humanperf_27.brief: Hyperventilation symptoms (tingling, visual disturbances, dizziness) can mimic hypoxia and are triggered by stress/anxiety.
humanperf_27.detailed: Hyperventilation: rapid breathing reduces PaCO2, causing respiratory alkalosis (high blood pH). This constricts cerebral blood vessels and reduces O2 delivery to the brain. Symptoms: tingling, muscle spasms, visual disturbances, dizziness, LOC.

humanperf_28.brief: Rebreathing into a bag increases CO2 levels, counteracting the hypocapnia (low CO2) causing hyperventilation symptoms.
humanperf_28.detailed: Rebreathing into a paper bag increases inspired CO2, correcting hypocapnia. If symptoms don't resolve quickly, consider hypoxia as the cause. The Valsalva manoeuvre is for ear pressure, not hyperventilation.

humanperf_29.brief: The circulatory system distributes oxygenated blood and nutrients throughout the body via arteries, veins, and capillaries.
humanperf_29.detailed: The circulatory system: pulmonary circuit (heart-lungs for oxygenation) and systemic circuit (heart-body for O2 delivery). Heart rate, stroke volume, and peripheral resistance are affected by altitude, stress, and G-forces.

humanperf_30.brief: After blood donation, pilots should wait 24 hours before flying to allow plasma volume and haemoglobin levels to stabilize.
humanperf_30.detailed: After blood donation (typically 450-500 mL): plasma volume recovers in 24-48 hours. Red cell mass takes 4-6 weeks for full recovery. EASA Class 2 requires haemoglobin >13.5 g/dL (men) or >12 g/dL (women).

humanperf_31.brief: Swallowing, chewing, or the Valsalva manoeuvre opens the eustachian tubes, equalizing pressure across the eardrum.
humanperf_31.detailed: The Valsalva manoeuvre is performed by: closing mouth, pinching nose, and gently exhaling against the obstruction. This increases pharyngeal pressure, opening the eustachian tubes. Swallowing and yawning also help.

humanperf_32.brief: At 25,000 ft, TUC is approximately 3-6 minutes without supplemental oxygen. Physical effort reduces this time significantly.
humanperf_32.detailed: TUC at FL250 (25,000 ft / 7,620 m): 3-6 minutes at rest, 1-2 minutes with exercise. EASA ORO.GEN requires supplemental oxygen when cabin altitude exceeds 10,000 ft for more than 30 min, and immediately above 13,000 ft.

humanperf_33.brief: Fear, excitement, and stress trigger hyperventilation by increasing breathing rate beyond metabolic needs.
humanperf_33.detailed: Hyperventilation is often triggered by psychological factors: anxiety (about flying, weather, performance), stress (ATC communication, emergencies), excitement. It can create a feedback loop - symptoms cause more anxiety, worsening hyperventilation.

humanperf_34.brief: Adjusting cabin temperature and avoiding steep banks helps prevent vasovagal reactions in passengers.
humanperf_34.detailed: Passenger discomfort during flight: common causes are anxiety, motion sickness, hypoxia, hyperventilation. Treatment: reduce anxiety (reassurance), adjust air vents, shallow banks, level flight, and consider oxygen if above 10,000 ft.

humanperf_35.brief: A reflex is an involuntary, stereotypical response to a stimulus, such as the knee-jerk reflex or blinking.
humanperf_35.detailed: Reflexes are mediated by reflex arcs (sensory neuron → spinal cord → motor neuron), bypassing the brain for speed. Examples: patellar reflex, withdrawal from pain, pupillary light reflex. Relevant to aviation: vestibular-ocular reflex, startle response.

humanperf_36.brief: The human nervous system is divided into: central (brain/spine), peripheral (nerves), and autonomic (involuntary functions).
humanperf_36.detailed: Central NS: brain (cognition, control) + spinal cord (relay). Peripheral NS: cranial nerves (12 pairs) + spinal nerves (31 pairs). Autonomic NS: sympathetic (fight/flight) + parasympathetic (rest/digest).

humanperf_37.brief: Night vision starts diminishing from about 5000 ft due to reduced retinal oxygen supply affecting rod function.
humanperf_37.detailed: Night vision degrades due to: reduced retinal illumination at altitude, hypoxia affecting rod function, and decreased contrast sensitivity. The effect begins at 4000-5000 ft and is significant by 10,000 ft.

humanperf_38.brief: Laser attacks can cause temporary or permanent eye damage and disorient the pilot, endangering flight safety.
humanperf_38.detailed: Laser attacks can cause: temporary flash blindness, afterimages, glare (disruption), and permanent retinal damage. The beam can track the aircraft, making evasion difficult. Report to ATC and file a laser report.

humanperf_39.brief: Cones are retinal photoreceptors responsible for colour vision and high visual acuity in bright light.
humanperf_39.detailed: Three types of cones: S-cones (short wavelength - blue), M-cones (medium - green), L-cones (long - red). Color vision testing (Ishihara plates) is required for Class 1 medical. Deuteranopia (green deficiency) is the most common color blindness.

humanperf_40.brief: The retina is the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye containing rods and cones for phototransduction.
humanperf_40.detailed: The retina has ~120 million rods (scotopic vision - low light, monochrome) and ~6 million cones (photopic vision - bright light, color). The fovea (center of macula) has only cones for sharp vision.

humanperf_41.brief: Effective scanning uses short, regular eye movements covering 10° segments with 1-2 second dwells.
humanperf_41.detailed: Effective scanning technique (see and be seen): scan 10° segments for 1-2 seconds, overlapping each segment. Most effective method avoids 'empty field myopia' where eyes focus on nothing at 1-2m.

humanperf_42.brief: In poor visibility, eyes default to a resting focus of 1-2m (empty field myopia), reducing detection of distant traffic.
humanperf_42.detailed: Empty field myopia: in poor visibility or featureless sky, eyes default to a resting focus of 1-2m. This means distant aircraft may not be detected. Regular scanning and changing focus helps prevent this.

humanperf_43.brief: The eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx, enabling pressure equalization.
humanperf_43.detailed: The eustachian tube (auditory tube) connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx. Normally closed, it opens during swallowing/yawning to equalize pressure between the middle ear and ambient. Blockage causes 'aerotitis' (ear pain).

humanperf_44.brief: Swallowing and yawning help open the eustachian tubes, preventing ear pain during descent.
humanperf_44.detailed: During descent, ambient pressure increases. If the eustachian tube is blocked (congestion, cold), the middle ear pressure cannot equalize. The eardrum is pushed inward, causing pain (barotrauma). Prevention: decongestants, slow descent, frequent swallowing.

humanperf_45.brief: After a prolonged turn, stopping the turn creates a somatogyral illusion of turning the opposite way.
humanperf_45.detailed: The somatogyral illusion: the semicircular canals detect rotation via fluid movement. After a sustained turn, the fluid catches up. When the turn stops, fluid continues moving, creating an illusion of turning the opposite way.

humanperf_46.brief: Non-accelerated straight and level flight provides no sustained angular or linear accelerations to stimulate the vestibular system.
humanperf_46.detailed: Motion sickness requires motion (acceleration). Non-accelerated (constant velocity) straight and level flight provides no sustained vestibular stimulation. With eyes closed, you cannot tell you're moving.

humanperf_47.brief: Acceleration in level flight creates a somatogravic illusion of climbing.
humanperf_47.detailed: The otolith organs detect the backward force of acceleration, normally associated with nose-up pitch (takeoff). The brain misinterprets this as a climb.

humanperf_48.brief: Acceleration in level flight produces a sensation of pitching nose-up.
humanperf_48.detailed: Otolith organs detect linear acceleration. Acceleration displaces otoliths backward, interpreted as nose-up pitch without visual reference (somatogravic illusion).

humanperf_49.brief: Positive g-force sequence: visual disturbances (grey-out), tunnel vision, blackout, then unconsciousness if sustained.
humanperf_49.detailed: G-LOC (G-induced Loss Of Consciousness): +Gz forces cause blood to pool in lower body. Symptoms: grey-out (dimming vision - retinal ischemia), tunnel vision, blackout (complete vision loss but conscious), G-LOC (unconsciousness). Recovery takes 15-30 seconds.

humanperf_50.brief: The Coriolis illusion occurs when head movements during a prolonged turn stimulate multiple semicircular canals simultaneously.
humanperf_50.detailed: The Coriolis illusion: when turning, the semicircular canals detect rotation. If the pilot moves their head in a different plane (e.g., looking down at charts), the fluid in multiple canals is stimulated simultaneously, causing severe vertigo and disorientation.

humanperf_51.brief: An upsloping runway makes the pilot feel too high, leading to a too-low approach (below glide slope).
humanperf_51.detailed: Upslope runway illusion: the upward slope of the runway makes the aim point appear higher than it is. The pilot compensates by descending below the glide path, risking a short landing or undershoot.

humanperf_52.brief: Vertigo is most likely when moving the head during a turn, as it creates conflicting vestibular signals.
humanperf_52.detailed: Moving the head during a turn can cause the Coriolis illusion or simply disorient the vestibular system. The semicircular canals are designed to detect rotation in one plane only. Cross-coupled stimulation causes vertigo.

humanperf_53.brief: Grey-out is caused by positive g-forces reducing blood flow to the retina, causing temporary dimming of vision.
humanperf_53.detailed: Grey-out (visual dimming) occurs at approximately +4 to +5 Gz. Vision returns immediately when G-forces are reduced. The time between grey-out and blackout is only 1-2 seconds, and between blackout and LOC is 3-5 seconds.

humanperf_54.brief: Visual illusions result from the brain misinterpreting sensory information based on expectations and prior experience.
humanperf_54.detailed: Visual illusions result from the brain's attempt to interpret ambiguous sensory information using prior knowledge and expectations. Common aviation illusions: runway width, slope, terrain, atmospheric refraction, and autokinetic (light movement).

humanperf_55.brief: In instrument meteorological conditions or after spatial disorientation, instruments (eyesight/reading) are the most reliable source.
humanperf_55.detailed: The semicircular canals and otoliths are unreliable during sustained turns due to adaptation. 'Seat of the pants' sensations are misleading. Instruments provide the only reliable attitude and heading information.

humanperf_56.brief: An aircraft on a reciprocal course first appears stationary, then decreases in size - important for collision avoidance.
humanperf_56.detailed: The 'stationary' visual cue is the key to collision detection: an aircraft on a collision course shows no relative movement in the windshield, appearing to 'loom' (grow in size) rather than track across. Any movement means it will pass safely.

humanperf_57.brief: After completing a coordinated turn, the somatogyral illusion may make it feel like still turning in the original direction.
humanperf_57.detailed: The somatogyral illusion: after stopping a turn, the endolymph in the semicircular canals continues moving, creating the illusion of turning in the opposite direction. Closing eyes or looking inside the cockpit prevents visual correction.

humanperf_58.brief: With gastroenteritis, a pilot is unfit to fly due to dehydration, discomfort, and possible sudden incapacitation.
humanperf_58.detailed: Gastroenteritis symptoms (vomiting, diarrhea, fever) cause dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, and sudden incapacitation risk. EASA Part-MED requires pilots to be free from any condition that may cause sudden incapacitation.

humanperf_59.brief: The human circadian rhythm is approximately 25 hours, which is why jet lag causes misalignment with the 24-hour day.
humanperf_59.detailed: The circadian rhythm is generated by the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) in the hypothalamus. Without external cues, the cycle runs ~24.2-25 hours (free-running). Light exposure is the primary entraining agent via the retinohypothalamic tract.

humanperf_60.brief: Blood alcohol decreases at approximately 0.015% per hour. For 0.15% BAL, it takes about 10 hours to reach zero.
humanperf_60.detailed: BAL reduces at approximately 0.015-0.020 g/dL per hour via liver alcohol dehydrogenase. 0.15 BAL requires 8-10 hours to reach zero. EASA prohibits flying within 12 hours of alcohol consumption (or below 0.2 g/L blood alcohol).

humanperf_61.brief: Both prescription and OTC medications should be evaluated the same way - never assume OTC means safe for flying.
humanperf_61.detailed: EASA Part-MED requires that no psychoactive substances or medications that may affect flight safety be used. This includes prescription and OTC medications. The AME should be consulted for any regular medication.

humanperf_62.brief: Overweight/obesity is a major risk factor for Type 2 diabetes, which can affect medical certification.
humanperf_62.detailed: Diabetes risk factors: obesity (BMI >30), family history, age >45, sedentary lifestyle, hypertension. EASA Class 2: well-controlled diabetes (non-insulin dependent) is usually OK. Insulin-dependent diabetes is disqualifying for Class 1.

humanperf_63.brief: The medical certificate lists conditions requiring consultation with an AME before flying.
humanperf_63.detailed: The EASA Part-MED medical certificate includes information about conditions requiring AME notification. These are listed in Part-MED Annex IV (requirements for medical certificates) and include cardiovascular, neurological, psychiatric, and other conditions.

humanperf_64.brief: Preventive dental screening does not require AME consultation unless medication or anesthesia is involved.
humanperf_64.detailed: Routine dental checkups (screening) without sedation or major procedures don't affect fitness. However: extractions, implants, and procedures requiring local anesthesia may require a 24-48 hour no-fly period. Always consult AME after any dental surgery.

humanperf_65.brief: Vaccinations may cause delayed reactions (fever, fatigue) 24-48 hours later, affecting fitness to fly.
humanperf_65.detailed: Vaccination side effects typically appear 24-48 hours after administration: fever, fatigue, muscle aches, injection site pain. These can impair pilot performance. A general recommendation is to observe for 24-48 hours before flying.

humanperf_66.brief: Before flying after taking any pharmaceuticals, even prescription-free ones, an aeromedical examiner should be consulted to ensure flight safety.
humanperf_66.detailed: Prescription-free drugs can still have side effects (drowsiness, dizziness, reduced reaction time) that impair pilot performance. EASA regulations require pilots to consult an AME before flying after taking any medication. Even common drugs like antihistamines can cause unexpected impairment. The safest policy is: no medication without AME approval.

humanperf_67.brief: Leaking exhaust heat exchangers allow CO into the cabin - a particular risk in piston-engine aircraft.
humanperf_67.detailed: Cabin heat systems in small aircraft (Cessna, Piper) use a shroud around the exhaust muffler. Cracks allow engine exhaust to enter the cabin. CO detectors (electronic or spot) should be installed. Symptoms of CO poisoning: headache, nausea, confusion.

humanperf_68.brief: At 0.015-0.02% per hour reduction, a BAL of 0.15 takes approximately 8-10 hours to clear, so 12 hours is the minimum.
humanperf_68.detailed: BAL elimination rate: 0.015% per hour average. For 0.15% BAL: 0.15/0.015 = 10 hours to zero. EASA requires minimum 8 hours bottle-to-throttle (but recommends 12+). Many operators require 12 hours minima.

humanperf_69.brief: Altitude exacerbates alcohol effects by reducing oxygen partial pressure, compounding impairment.
humanperf_69.detailed: Altitude effects on alcohol: reduced oxygen partial pressure compounds alcohol's effects. The same BAL at 10,000 ft produces more impairment than at sea level. Hypoxia and alcohol are synergistic - impairment is greater than the sum of individual effects.

humanperf_70.brief: 550 kt closing speed over 5 km = 18 seconds to impact. Visual acquisition varies by aircraft conspicuity.
humanperf_70.detailed: Closing speed: 550 kt. At 5 km (2.7 NM) range: time = distance/speed. 2.7 NM / 550 kt = 0.0049 hr = 17.6 seconds. Each pilot has ~18 seconds to see, decide, and act. Heavier aircraft have longer collision courses due to slower response.

humanperf_71.brief: Perception is heavily influenced by experience and expectations, which is why pilots 'see what they expect to see'.
humanperf_71.detailed: Perception is not a passive process but an active interpretation of sensory input based on past experience. Pilots with experience in an area are more likely to detect and correctly interpret visual cues and traffic patterns.

humanperf_72.brief: A small-looking runway (narrower than expected) appears farther away, causing the pilot to fly too high on approach.
humanperf_72.detailed: Runway width illusion: if the runway is narrower than expected (e.g., 23m vs 45m), it appears farther away. The pilot may fly a higher approach (expecting to be farther back) and risk landing long or overshooting.

humanperf_73.brief: A downsloping runway creates the illusion of being too high, resulting in a too-shallow approach.
humanperf_73.detailed: Downsloping runway: the runway slopes away from the threshold. This makes the aim point appear low, creating the illusion of being too high. The pilot descends below the correct glide path, risking a short landing.

humanperf_74.brief: Aircraft on collision course remain stationary in the visual field and then grow rapidly - the basis of collision avoidance.
humanperf_74.detailed: The relative motion principle: an object on a collision course appears stationary in the windshield, growing in size. This was tragically demonstrated in the 1996 Charkhi Dadri collision. Any lateral movement means passing safely.

humanperf_75.brief: The perception-reaction time for collision avoidance is approximately 5-10 seconds, including decision and control input.
humanperf_75.detailed: The see-and-avoid process: visual detection (1-2 sec), recognition (1-2 sec), decision (1-2 sec), reaction (1-2 sec) = total 5-10 seconds. At 500 kt closing speed, 10 seconds covers 1.4 NM.

humanperf_76.brief: Downsloping terrain before the runway makes the approach appear too high, causing dangerously low approaches.
humanperf_76.detailed: Downsloping terrain before the runway: the terrain drops away before the threshold. The runway threshold appears low relative to the terrain, creating the illusion of being too high. The pilot descends too early, risking undershoot.

humanperf_77.brief: Short-term memory holds approximately 7±2 items for 10-20 seconds (Miller's Law).
humanperf_77.detailed: Miller's Law (1956): short-term (working) memory can hold 7±2 'chunks' of information for 10-20 seconds. Chunking (grouping information) increases capacity. For pilots: this means radio calls and checklists should be designed for this capacity.

humanperf_78.brief: Short-term memory stores information for approximately 10-20 seconds without rehearsal.
humanperf_78.detailed: Short-term memory: duration is 10-20 seconds without active rehearsal (repeating the information). Rehearsal can maintain it longer but requires attention. This is why ATC clearances should be read back immediately.

humanperf_79.brief: Even highly experienced pilots make mistakes. Training reduces but does not eliminate human error.
humanperf_79.detailed: The Dunning-Kruger effect: experienced pilots may overestimate their abilities and become complacent. The 'experience fallacy' assumes past success guarantees future safety. Error prevention requires continuous learning regardless of experience.

humanperf_80.brief: A latent error remains hidden in the system and only becomes apparent when combined with other factors.
humanperf_80.detailed: Latent errors (Reason, 1990): conditions that lie dormant in the system for extended periods, such as poor design, inadequate training, or flawed procedures. They differ from active errors (immediate effect) like mis-setting the altimeter.

humanperf_81.brief: Pilots often hide mistakes due to fear of punishment, which prevents organizational learning (just culture).
humanperf_81.detailed: Just Culture: an atmosphere of trust where people are encouraged to report safety information without fear of punishment. Without it, errors go unreported and the organization cannot learn, increasing risk of repeated accidents.

humanperf_82.brief: FORDEC: Facts, Options, Risks/Benefits, Decision, Execution, Check - a structured decision-making model.
humanperf_82.detailed: FORDEC: the six-step decision-making model recommended by EASA and IATA. Facts (gather info), Options (generate alternatives), Risks/Benefits (evaluate each), Decision (choose best), Execution (implement), Check (monitor outcome).

humanperf_83.brief: Critical decisions should follow standard operating procedures (SOPs) to reduce emotional decision-making under stress.
humanperf_83.detailed: The DECIDE model: Detect (change), Estimate (significance), Choose (safe outcome), Identify (actions), Do (implement), Evaluate (outcome). Standard procedures reduce cognitive load and emotional decision-making during emergencies.

humanperf_84.brief: CFIT: Controlled Flight Into Terrain - an airworthy aircraft under pilot control is flown into terrain, water, or obstacles.
humanperf_84.detailed: CFIT (Controlled Flight Into Terrain) was the leading cause of aviation fatalities for decades. Prevention: Enhanced GPWS (EGPWS), MSAW (Minimum Safe Altitude Warning), altitude awareness, and proper instrument scan.

humanperf_85.brief: Heinrich's Triangle (1:600 rule): 1 fatal accident for approximately 600 incidents in the accident pyramid.
humanperf_85.detailed: Heinrich's Triangle (1931): For every 1 fatal accident, there are ~29 minor injuries and ~300 near-misses. Modern aviation safety: the ratio is approximately 1 fatal accident per 600 reported incidents/occurrences.

humanperf_86.brief: Situational awareness is the continuous perception of elements in the environment and projection of future status.
humanperf_86.detailed: Endsley (1995) defines three levels of SA: Level 1 (perception - seeing elements), Level 2 (comprehension - understanding meaning), Level 3 (projection - predicting future status). Loss of SA is a major factor in aviation accidents.

humanperf_87.brief: Sitting too low reduces forward and oblique visibility, especially critical during approach and landing.
humanperf_87.detailed: Proper seat adjustment: ensure full rudder/brake travel without stretching, clear view of instruments, forward visibility over the nose. Sitting too low: reduced visibility, increased fatigue, possible spatial disorientation.

humanperf_88.brief: Standardized phraseology ensures clear communication regardless of language differences (ICAO Annex 10).
humanperf_88.detailed: ICAO Annex 10 Volume II (Aeronautical Telecommunications) establishes standard phraseology. Benefits: reduces ambiguity, bridges language differences, improves efficiency. 'Readback/hearback' and 'closed loop' communication are essential.

humanperf_89.brief: Most communication errors involve listening errors and misunderstandings, not radio failures.
humanperf_89.detailed: Communication errors (study by the FAA/NASA): 70% involve terminology/readback errors, 15% incorrect frequency, 10% call sign confusion, 5% message content errors. The 'closed loop' communication model helps prevent these.

humanperf_90.brief: Synergetic is a positive attitude. Hazardous attitudes: macho, impulsivity, invulnerability, resignation.
humanperf_90.detailed: Hazardous attitudes (FAA): Anti-authority ('Don't tell me'), Impulsivity ('Do something quickly'), Invulnerability ('It won't happen to me'), Macho ('I can do it'), Resignation ('What's the use'). Antidotes are specific counter-statements.

humanperf_91.brief: Group dynamics can lead to 'risky shift' - accepting higher risks as a group than as individuals.
humanperf_91.detailed: Groupthink (Janis, 1982): the tendency for groups to suppress dissent, seek consensus, and make poor decisions. Risky shift: groups make riskier decisions than individuals. Related: 'plan continuation bias' where groups persist with a flawed plan.

humanperf_92.brief: Risky shift is the tendency for groups to make riskier decisions than individuals would make alone.
humanperf_92.detailed: Risky shift (Stoner, 1961): group decisions are more extreme (riskier) than average individual decisions. In aviation: 'we've done this before', 'others are doing it', 'the group knows best'. Mitigation: encourage dissent, use CRM principles.

humanperf_93.brief: Macho ('I'll show them') and invulnerability ('It won't happen to me') are often linked hazardous attitudes.
humanperf_93.detailed: Macho attitude: 'I'll show them I can do it' - leads to continued VFR into IMC, exceeding personal limits. Invulnerability: 'It won't happen to me' - leads to inadequate planning, risk-taking. Combined: a dangerous overconfidence.

humanperf_94.brief: Confirmation bias leads us to see what we expect, potentially missing critical information.
humanperf_94.detailed: Confirmation bias: seeking evidence that confirms existing beliefs and ignoring contradictory evidence. In aviation: fixating on one instrument, misdiagnosing engine problems, or continuing a flawed approach despite warning signs.

humanperf_95.brief: The five hazardous attitudes: anti-authority, impulsivity, invulnerability, macho, and resignation.
humanperf_95.detailed: The FAA identified 5 hazardous attitudes: 1) Anti-authority, 2) Impulsivity, 3) Invulnerability, 4) Macho, 5) Resignation. Each has an antidote statement. CRM training teaches pilots to recognize and counter these attitudes.

humanperf_96.brief: Complacency risk increases with cockpit automation as pilots become over-reliant on systems.
humanperf_96.detailed: Automation complacency: over-trust in automated systems leads to reduced monitoring, slower manual intervention, and skill degradation. Studies show pilots in glass cockpits may take longer to detect failures than those in conventional cockpits.

humanperf_97.brief: The antidote to resignation is: 'I am not helpless. I can make a difference.'
humanperf_97.detailed: Resignation antidote: 'I am not helpless. I can do something about this. I can make a difference.' Recognizing the attitude is the first step. Counter-statement techniques help pilots challenge hazardous thoughts.

humanperf_98.brief: Stress affects all cognitive functions: attention, concentration, responsiveness, and memory.
humanperf_98.detailed: The Yerkes-Dodson Law: performance increases with stress (arousal) up to an optimal level, then decreases. Under high stress: attention narrows (tunnel vision), working memory degrades, risk assessment suffers, reaction time may slow.

humanperf_99.brief: Excessive stress causes cognitive tunneling - reduced ability to process additional information.
humanperf_99.detailed: Cognitive tunneling (attentional narrowing): under high stress, pilots focus on a single task while ignoring other critical information. Example: focusing on an engine failure while ignoring the altitude (contributing to CFIT).

humanperf_100.brief: Fatigue is a major cause of increased errors, tunnel vision, and reduced attention.
humanperf_100.detailed: Fatigue effects: increased reaction time (20-50%), reduced situational awareness, impaired decision making, mood changes (irritability), increased error rate, microsleeps (brief involuntary sleep episodes). Management: proper rest, recognizing personal limits.

met_1.brief: Air is composed of approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and 1% other gases including argon and carbon dioxide. This composition remains constant up to about 100 km.
met_1.detailed: The composition of dry air in the atmosphere is remarkably consistent: nitrogen (N2) ~78.08%, oxygen (O2) ~20.95%, argon (Ar) ~0.93%, and carbon dioxide (CO2) ~0.04%. Water vapour content varies from 0-4% but is not part of dry air. This composition is fundamental to understanding gas laws in meteorology.

met_2.brief: Weather phenomena occur primarily in the troposphere, the lowest layer of the atmosphere extending from the surface to approximately 8-15 km altitude.
met_2.detailed: The troposphere contains about 80% of the atmosphere mass and virtually all its water vapour. Temperature decreases with height at an average lapse rate of 6.5 C/km. All weather phenomena develop within this layer, making it the most relevant layer for aviation meteorology.

met_3.brief: The correct order from the surface upward is: Troposphere, Stratosphere, Mesosphere, Thermosphere (Ionosphere).
met_3.detailed: The atmospheric layers from Earth outward: Troposphere (0-8/15 km) weather zone; Stratosphere (8/15-50 km) ozone layer, stable; Mesosphere (50-85 km) meteors burn up; Thermosphere/Ionosphere (85-600 km) aurora, radio reflection.

met_4.brief: Oxygen makes up approximately 21% of dry air by volume.
met_4.detailed: The percentage of oxygen in the atmosphere is constant at approximately 20.95% (21%) by volume up to about 100 km altitude. It is the partial pressure of oxygen that decreases with altitude, not the percentage.

met_5.brief: ISA lapse rate is ~2°C/1000 ft (0.65°C/100 m).
met_5.detailed: In ISA, temperature decreases at 0.65°C per 100 m (~2°C per 1000 ft) up to the tropopause at 36,000 ft.

met_6.brief: The tropopause is the boundary layer between the troposphere and the stratosphere.
met_6.detailed: The tropopause is a defined boundary where the temperature lapse rate decreases to 2 C/km or less. Its altitude varies: approx 8-10 km at the poles and 15-18 km at the equator.

met_7.brief: Meteorological aviation services in Europe use degrees Celsius (C) for temperature reporting.
met_7.detailed: In European aviation meteorology, temperatures are reported in degrees Celsius as standardized by ICAO and WMO. International aviation uses Celsius.

met_8.brief: An inversion layer is an atmospheric layer where temperature increases with height, opposite to the normal decrease.
met_8.detailed: Normally temperature decreases with altitude. An inversion occurs when temperature increases with height, creating a stable layer that suppresses vertical air movement. Inversions can be caused by radiation cooling, subsidence, or frontal activity.

met_9.brief: Latent heat transfer during phase changes of water is crucial for horizontal and vertical heat transport in the atmosphere.
met_9.detailed: When water evaporates, it absorbs heat (latent heat of vaporization ~2500 J/g). This heat is released when water vapour condenses into clouds, driving weather systems.

met_10.brief: The mean temperature lapse rate in the troposphere according to ISA is 0.65 C per 100 m.
met_10.detailed: The ISA standard lapse rate is 0.65 C/100 m (6.5 C/km) or approx 2 C/1000 ft. The dry adiabatic lapse rate is higher at 1 C/100 m.

met_11.brief: The Foehn wind requires stable conditions to develop, with air flowing over a mountain barrier.
met_11.detailed: Foehn conditions develop when stable air is forced to rise over a mountain barrier. Initial ascent causes cooling and precipitation on the windward side, descending air on the leeward side warms adiabatically, creating warm dry winds.

met_12.brief: A high environmental lapse rate indicates an unstable air mass, as it promotes vertical motion.
met_12.detailed: Stability is determined by comparing the environmental lapse rate (ELR) to the adiabatic lapse rates. When the ELR is greater than 1 C/100m, rising air parcels remain warmer than their environment and continue rising.

met_13.brief: A steady or increasing temperature with height indicates a stable air mass that resists vertical movement.
met_13.detailed: A stable air mass has a low ELR (temperature decreases slowly or increases inversion). This suppresses vertical motion. Signs: stratiform clouds, poor visibility, smooth flying conditions.

met_14.brief: A subsidence inversion at ~5000 ft is caused by widespread descending air within a high-pressure area.
met_14.detailed: In high-pressure systems, air descends slowly (subsidence). As it descends, it warms adiabatically, creating a layer of warm air at about 1000-2000 m above the surface with cooler air below.

met_15.brief: A ground inversion (radiation inversion) is caused by cooling of the ground surface during clear nights.
met_15.detailed: On clear nights with light winds, the Earth surface radiates heat rapidly, cooling the air immediately above it. This creates a shallow layer where temperature increases with height.

met_16.brief: At FL180, ISA standard pressure is approximately 500 hPa, half of the sea-level pressure.
met_16.detailed: Pressure decreases exponentially with altitude. At FL180/18,000 ft the pressure is approximately 500 hPa. At FL350 pressure is approx 250 hPa.

met_17.brief: QNH is used to set the altimeter to indicate altitude above mean sea level (MSL).
met_17.detailed: QNH is the barometric pressure adjusted to MSL using ISA conditions. Setting QNH on the altimeter makes it read the airfield elevation when on the ground.

met_18.brief: Isobars are lines of equal QFF (atmospheric pressure reduced to MSL using actual temperature conditions).
met_18.detailed: On surface weather charts, isobars connect points of equal QFF. They are typically drawn at 5 hPa intervals. Closely spaced isobars indicate strong winds.

met_19.brief: When flying from low to high pressure without adjusting the altimeter, the true altitude becomes higher than indicated.
met_19.detailed: The altimeter assumes standard pressure. When flying into higher pressure, the aircraft is actually higher for a given altimeter reading (safe condition). The opposite is true when flying into low pressure.

met_20.brief: QFF is the pressure measured at a ground station and reduced to MSL using actual atmospheric conditions.
met_20.detailed: QFF uses actual temperature profile (real atmosphere) while QNH uses ISA conditions. QFF is used for meteorological analysis, QNH for aviation altimeter settings.

met_21.brief: Air density decreases when temperature increases and/or pressure decreases through the gas law.
met_21.detailed: According to the ideal gas law (PV=nRT), density = P/(RxT). Density decreases when temperature increases or pressure decreases, degrading aircraft performance.

met_22.brief: Increasing humidity decreases air density because water vapour molecules (M=18) are lighter than oxygen (M=32) and nitrogen (M=28) molecules.
met_22.detailed: Moist air is less dense than dry air at the same temperature and pressure. This is why humid air degrades aircraft performance: lower density means less lift and longer takeoff distances.

met_23.brief: Standard pressure at MSL in ISA conditions is 1013.25 hPa.
met_23.detailed: ISA defines standard sea-level pressure as 1013.25 hPa, equivalent to 29.92 inches of mercury or 760 mmHg.

met_24.brief: The ICAO Standard Atmosphere allows conversion from pressure values to altimeter readings by providing a standardized pressure-altitude relationship.
met_24.detailed: The ISA provides a standardized model of pressure, temperature, and density variation with altitude, enabling consistent altimeter calibration and aircraft performance calculations.

met_25.brief: ISA assumes 0% relative humidity completely dry air.
met_25.detailed: The International Standard Atmosphere defines dry air with 0% relative humidity, avoiding the complexity of variable water vapour content.

met_26.brief: A barometric altimeter indicates height above a selected reference pressure level, adjustable via the subscale setting.
met_26.detailed: The altimeter is a barometer calibrated in feet or meters. By adjusting the subscale, the pilot selects the reference pressure: QNH (MSL), QFE (airfield), or standard 1013.25 hPa (flight levels).

met_27.brief: Elevation is the vertical distance of a point on the Earth surface measured from mean sea level (MSL).
met_27.detailed: Elevation is a fixed property of terrain height above MSL. It differs from altitude (height above MSL) and height (vertical distance above a specific reference).

met_28.brief: Altitude is defined as height above mean sea level (MSL).
met_28.detailed: Altitude specifically refers to vertical distance above MSL. Height refers to distance above ground level. Flight Level refers to pressure altitude at standard setting.

met_29.brief: The transition altitude is the altitude below which the pilot sets QNH, and above which standard pressure 1013.25 hPa is used.
met_29.detailed: Transition altitude varies by country (typically 3000-5000 ft in Europe). Above it, Flight Levels based on standard 1013.25 hPa ensure consistent vertical separation.

met_30.brief: The altimeter can be checked on the ground by setting QNH and comparing the indication with the known airfield elevation.
met_30.detailed: Before takeoff, set the current QNH. The altimeter should read the published airfield elevation (within +/-75 ft). Setting QFE should read zero at the airfield reference point.

met_31.brief: With QFE set, the altimeter indicates height above the pressure level at airfield elevation (approx zero on the ground).
met_31.detailed: QFE is the barometric pressure at the airfield reference point. On the runway it reads near zero. For en-route flights, QNH is more commonly used.

met_32.brief: Adjusting the pressure subscale sets the entire altimeter system to the selected pressure reference value.
met_32.detailed: The altimeter subscale adjusts the internal reference pressure. Moving the setting changes the displayed altitude for the same ambient static pressure.

met_33.brief: With standard 1013.25 hPa setting, the altimeter displays pressure altitude above the 1013.25 hPa pressure level.
met_33.detailed: Pressure altitude is used for flight levels (FL) and aircraft performance calculations. It differs from true altitude when non-standard pressure or temperature exists.

met_34.brief: Wind speed and direction on surface charts are shown by arrows with barbs: each full barb = 10 kt, half barb = 5 kt, pennant = 50 kt.
met_34.detailed: Wind direction is shown by the arrow shaft pointing into the station circle (direction wind is coming FROM). Wind speed is indicated by barbs on the arrow.

met_35.brief: Wind is caused by the pressure gradient force: air moves from high to low pressure areas, deflected by Coriolis.
met_35.detailed: The primary force driving wind is the horizontal pressure gradient force. Coriolis deflects moving air to the right in NH. Friction near the surface slows wind and causes it to cross isobars at an angle.

met_36.brief: Above the friction layer (approx 2000-3000 ft AGL), wind flows parallel to isobars (geostrophic wind).
met_36.detailed: In the free atmosphere, the pressure gradient force balances the Coriolis force, resulting in geostrophic wind that flows parallel to straight isobars.

met_37.brief: Wind forms due to pressure gradients created by differential heating of the Earth surface by the sun.
met_37.detailed: Uneven solar heating creates temperature differences, leading to pressure differences, which create pressure gradient forces. The global circulation distributes heat from equator to poles.

met_38.brief: Mountainous areas with vegetation cover create the greatest friction, reducing wind speed the most.
met_38.detailed: Surface friction depends on roughness: mountains with forests = highest friction, flat land = medium, oceans = least. The friction angle is largest over rough terrain (~30 degrees) and smallest over water (~10 degrees).

met_39.brief: The frictional effect of the Earth surface on wind extends to approximately 3000 ft AGL over land.
met_39.detailed: The planetary boundary layer extends to about 2000-3000 ft (600-1000 m) over land. Within this layer, wind speed decreases toward the surface.

met_40.brief: Convergence is the movement of air flowing together horizontally.
met_40.detailed: Convergence causes mass accumulation, forcing air to rise (upward vertical motion), leading to cloud formation and precipitation. Divergence causes descending air and clearing skies.

met_41.brief: Convergence at ground level forces air to rise, producing ascending air and cloud formation.
met_41.detailed: When air converges (flows together) near the surface, it accumulates. Since the ground blocks downward movement, the air must ascend. This ascending air cools adiabatically, potentially reaching the condensation level to form clouds. Convergence is a key mechanism in low-pressure systems. Divergence has the opposite effect: descending air and clearing skies.

met_42.brief: Convergence close to the ground always results in upward airflow because the air has no other escape path.
met_42.detailed: Near the surface, air cannot go downward (blocked by ground). When convergence forces air to pile up, it must ascend. This upward motion is essential for cloud formation.

met_43.brief: Central Europe is mainly influenced by polar cold air from the north and subtropical warm air from the south.
met_43.detailed: Central Europe lies in the mid-latitudes where polar and subtropical air masses meet along the polar front, creating the frontal weather patterns characteristic of the region.

met_44.brief: General circulation refers to the large-scale vertical airflow systems that transport heat from equator to poles.
met_44.detailed: The general circulation consists of three cells in each hemisphere: Hadley (0-30 degrees), Ferrel (30-60 degrees), and Polar (60-90 degrees), distributing heat energy.

met_45.brief: Winds blowing uphill during the day due to solar heating of mountain slopes are called anabatic winds.
met_45.detailed: During daytime, mountain slopes heat up faster than surrounding air. The warmed air rises along the slope, creating an up-valley/anabatic wind.

met_46.brief: Air descending behind a mountain range is defined as katabatic wind (downslope wind).
met_46.detailed: Katabatic winds are gravity-driven flows of dense air moving downslope. These can be very strong and turbulent, posing hazards to aviation.

met_47.brief: The Mistral is a wind phenomenon arising mainly due to orography (mountain-induced).
met_47.detailed: The Mistral is a strong cold northerly wind flowing down the Rhone Valley in France into the Mediterranean, caused by channeling of cold air through the valley.

met_48.brief: The Bora is a cold katabatic wind that occurs at the Adriatic Sea.
met_48.detailed: The Bora is a strong cold gusty wind from the Dinaric Alps down to the Adriatic coast, occurring when cold continental air spills over the mountains.

met_49.brief: Mountain-valley circulation is caused by diurnal temperature variation from solar radiation.
met_49.detailed: During the day, valley air warms and rises creating anabatic wind. At night, cool air drains down the slopes (katabatic). This daily cycle is driven by solar heating.

met_50.brief: The Foehn wind develops when stable air crosses a mountain barrier.
met_50.detailed: Moist air rises on the windward side, cools at the saturated adiabatic rate, precipitates. Descending on the lee side, it warms at the dry adiabatic rate, creating warm, dry winds.

met_51.brief: A rotor is a roll-shaped cloud on the leeside of a mountain in strong wind, indicating severe turbulence.
met_51.detailed: Rotors are part of mountain wave systems. Beneath wave crests, closed circulations (rotors) form, marked by roll clouds containing severe turbulence.

met_52.brief: Light turbulence is always expected below cumulus clouds due to thermal convection.
met_52.detailed: Cumulus clouds form at the top of rising thermals. Below and within these clouds, the rising air creates turbulence. Even small fair-weather cumulus produce some light turbulence.

met_53.brief: Water exists in the atmosphere in all three states: liquid (rain), solid (ice, snow), and gaseous (water vapour).
met_53.detailed: Water is unique in existing as solid, liquid, and gas within normal atmospheric temperature and pressure ranges. Understanding phase changes is fundamental to meteorology.

met_54.brief: Water vapour is the component of the atmosphere responsible for weather phenomena.
met_54.detailed: Water vapour makes up only 0-4% of the atmosphere but is responsible for essentially all weather: clouds, precipitation, fog, and storms.

met_55.brief: Water occurs in the atmosphere in gaseous (vapour), liquid (droplets), and solid (ice crystals) phases.
met_55.detailed: Water freely changes phase within the Earth temperature/pressure range, allowing the hydrological cycle to operate.

met_56.brief: As temperature decreases, the dew point remains constant but relative humidity increases because the air capacity for moisture decreases.
met_56.detailed: Dew point is the temperature at which air becomes saturated. It doesnt change when temperature changes. Relative humidity increases when temperature decreases because cooler air can hold less water vapour.

met_57.brief: When temperature increases, the spread (temperature minus dew point) increases and relative humidity decreases.
met_57.detailed: As temperature rises at constant moisture content, the air capacity to hold water vapour increases, so the actual moisture represents a lower percentage of capacity (lower RH).

met_58.brief: Decreasing temperature results in decreasing spread and increasing relative humidity.
met_58.detailed: When temperature falls toward the dew point, the spread decreases. Cooler air holds less moisture, so the same amount represents a higher percentage of capacity.

met_59.brief: During fog, temperature equals the dew point, relative humidity is close to 100%, and the spread is zero.
met_59.detailed: Fog forms when air is cooled to its dew point, reaching saturation. At this point: temperature = dew point, spread = 0, RH approx 100%.

met_60.brief: Relative humidity = (actual water content / maximum possible water content) x 100% = (4.6/9.2) x 100% = 50%.
