met_60.detailed: Relative humidity measures how close the air is to saturation. With 4.6 g/m3 actual content and 9.2 g/m3 capacity, RH = 50%.

met_61.brief: A smaller spread brings air closer to saturation, which may cause fog or mist, reducing visibility.
met_61.detailed: When the spread is small, the air is nearly saturated. Saturated air can produce fog, mist, or low clouds, all reducing visibility.

met_62.brief: Latent heat is released into the upper troposphere during condensation (cloud formation).
met_62.detailed: When water vapour condenses into cloud droplets, it releases latent heat (~600 cal/g) absorbed during evaporation, warming the surrounding air and driving further upward motion.

met_63.brief: Evaporation is the phase transition from liquid to gaseous state (water to water vapour).
met_63.detailed: Evaporation requires energy (latent heat of vaporization). It is the primary way moisture enters the atmosphere from oceans, lakes, and wet surfaces.

met_64.brief: Sublimation is the direct transition from solid (ice/snow) to gas (water vapour) without passing through liquid.
met_64.detailed: Sublimation occurs when ice or snow evaporates directly into water vapour, common on cold clear dry days when snow disappears without melting.

met_65.brief: The saturated adiabatic lapse rate is lower than the dry adiabatic lapse rate because condensation releases latent heat, partially offsetting cooling.
met_65.detailed: SALR is approx 0.6 C/100m, less than DALR of 1 C/100m. Condensation releases latent heat, warming the air parcel and reducing the cooling rate.

met_66.brief: The dry adiabatic lapse rate is approximately 1.0 C per 100 m (10 C per km).
met_66.detailed: The DALR is the rate at which an unsaturated air parcel cools when rising without heat exchange with its environment. At 1.0 C/100m, determined by g/cp.

met_67.brief: Conditional instability produces towering cumulus clouds, isolated showers of rain or thunderstorms.
met_67.detailed: Conditional instability occurs when the ELR lies between the DALR and SALR. An unsaturated parcel is stable, but a saturated parcel becomes unstable.

met_68.brief: An adiabatic process involves changes in volume and temperature during vertical movement with no heat exchange with the environment.
met_68.detailed: Adiabatic (from Greek "adiabatos" meaning impassable) describes a process with zero heat transfer. In the atmosphere, when air rises, it expands and cools due to decreasing pressure. When it descends, it compresses and warms. No heat is exchanged with the surrounding environment - all temperature change is from pressure-volume work. Dry adiabatic lapse rate = 1 C/100m.

met_69.brief: The saturated adiabatic process occurs when saturated air ascends and cools by less than 1 C/100m due to latent heat release from condensation.
met_69.detailed: As saturated air rises and cools, water vapour condenses releasing latent heat, partially offsetting the cooling. The exact rate depends on temperature and pressure.

met_70.brief: Clouds are basically distinguished into two types: cumulus (heap/vertical) and stratiform (layered).
met_70.detailed: Cloud classification: cumulus (heap clouds, vertical development), stratus (layer clouds, flat), cirrus (high, wispy), and nimbus (rain-bearing).

met_71.brief: Clouds in high layers use the prefix 'cirro-', indicating ice-crystal composition above 20,000 ft.
met_71.detailed: High-level clouds (above 20,000 ft / FL 200 in temperate regions) are prefixed with 'cirro-' or 'cirrus'. They are composed of ice crystals due to the low temperatures at those altitudes. Examples include cirrus (Ci), cirrocumulus (Cc), and cirrostratus (Cs). Middle-level clouds use 'alto-' (altocumulus, altostratus) and low-level clouds have no special prefix (stratus, cumulus, stratocumulus).

met_72.brief: Clouds are categorised by height into low clouds (0-6500 ft), medium clouds (6500-20000 ft), high clouds (above 20000 ft), and clouds with large vertical extension.
met_72.detailed: ICAO cloud classification divides clouds into four families by height: low clouds (surface to 6500 ft AGL – stratus, stratocumulus, cumulus), medium clouds (6500 to 20000 ft AGL – altocumulus, altostratus), high clouds (above 20000 ft AGL – cirrus, cirrocumulus, cirrostratus), and clouds with large vertical extension (nimbostratus, cumulonimbus) that can span multiple levels.

met_73.brief: Clouds are categorised by their elemental composition as water clouds, ice clouds, or mixed-content clouds.
met_73.detailed: Cloud composition depends on temperature. Water clouds consist entirely of liquid water droplets. Ice clouds are composed of ice crystals (typically at temperatures below -40°C). Mixed-content clouds contain both supercooled water droplets and ice crystals, which is particularly important for aircraft icing risk – the most severe icing occurs in mixed-phase clouds between 0°C and -20°C.

met_74.brief: Nimbostratus (Ns) and cumulonimbus (Cb) have large vertical extents, spanning from low to high levels.
met_74.detailed: Nimbostratus is a thick, dark grey cloud layer with continuous rain or snow, extending through low and middle levels. Cumulonimbus is the towering thunderstorm cloud that can extend from near the surface to above the tropopause, reaching 30,000-60,000 ft. Both are classified as clouds with large vertical development.

met_75.brief: Stratus clouds most commonly develop from the gradual lifting of a large, stable air mass, forming a uniform grey layer.
met_75.detailed: Stratus clouds form when a relatively stable air mass is lifted gradually over a broad area, or when moist air cools to its dew point through advection over a colder surface. Unlike cumulus (convective), stratus is stratiform – horizontally extensive with little vertical development. It often produces drizzle or light precipitation and can reduce visibility significantly.

met_76.brief: An inversion layer acts as a lid, limiting vertical development of cumulus clouds and flattening their tops.
met_76.detailed: Cumulus clouds grow as thermals rise through an unstable layer. When the rising air encounters an inversion (a layer where temperature increases with height), the thermal cannot penetrate the stable layer, so the cloud top spreads horizontally, forming a flat top. The height of the inversion directly determines the maximum cloud top height.

met_77.brief: A rising cloud base followed by a ceiling rise indicates the cumulus top is being capped by an inversion or isotherm layer.
met_77.detailed: Morning cumulus forms as the sun heats the ground. As the day warms, the lifting condensation level (LCL) rises, so the cloud base lifts. If an inversion or isothermal layer exists aloft, it blocks further vertical development, so the ceiling (height of the cloud base above ground) also rises.

met_78.brief: Low stratus ('high fog') forms under a winter high-pressure system when an inversion traps moisture near the ground.
met_78.detailed: In winter, high-pressure systems produce subsidence inversions. Moisture near the surface (from earlier precipitation or high humidity) is trapped beneath the inversion, forming extensive low stratus or 'high fog'. Unlike radiation fog, high fog already has a cloud base (the inversion itself) which may lift or burn off as the day warms.

met_79.brief: Fog formation is indicated by a low temperature-dewpoint spread (spread) and falling temperature.
met_79.detailed: Fog forms when the air temperature falls to the dew point (spread approaches zero). A small spread (1-2°C) indicates near-saturation. Further cooling (e.g., from night-time radiation, cold advection, or evaporation) will result in saturation and fog once the spread reaches zero and condensation begins.

met_80.brief: The main fog types are radiation fog, advection fog, and mixing fog (also steam fog and upslope fog).
met_80.detailed: Radiation fog forms on clear, calm nights when the ground cools by radiation, cooling the air above to the dew point. Advection fog forms when warm, moist air moves (advects) over a colder surface. Mixing fog occurs when two unsaturated air masses mix to produce saturation. Other types include steam fog (cold air over warm water), upslope fog (air cooling as it rises up terrain), and frontal fog.

met_81.brief: Overcast cloud cover prevents radiation fog by trapping outgoing longwave radiation and insulating the ground.
met_81.detailed: Radiation fog requires clear skies at night so the ground can cool efficiently by emitting infrared radiation. Cloud cover acts as a blanket, reflecting longwave radiation back to the surface, keeping the ground warmer. Without ground cooling, the air above does not cool to saturation, so radiation fog cannot form.

met_82.brief: Radiation fog is the most common fog type over Central Europe, especially in autumn and winter.
met_82.detailed: Central Europe experiences frequent clear, calm nights in autumn and winter, ideal for radiation fog. Valleys and low-lying areas are particularly susceptible as cold air drains downhill, collecting in hollows. Radiation fog typically forms after midnight and may persist until mid-morning or longer in winter.

met_83.brief: Radiation fog dissipates with wind increase (turbulent mixing) and temperature increase (warming above dew point).
met_83.detailed: As the sun rises, surface heating evaporates fog droplets and raises the temperature above the dew point. Wind of 5-15 kt mixes the fog layer with drier air above, thinning or lifting the fog into low stratus. Too much wind (above 15 kt) prevents fog formation entirely; too little (calm) allows dense fog to persist.

met_84.brief: Advection fog forms when warm, moist air moves horizontally over a colder surface, cooling to saturation.
met_84.detailed: Advection fog is common when warm, humid maritime air moves over a colder land mass or cold sea current. Unlike radiation fog, it can form in windy conditions (up to 20-25 kt) and at any time of day. It can persist for days and cover large areas (hundreds of km). Classic examples: sea fog off Newfoundland, or warm air moving over snow-covered ground.

met_85.brief: Steam fog (evaporation fog) develops when very cold air moves over a warm, moist surface, causing evaporation and immediate re-condensation.
met_85.detailed: Steam fog, also called sea smoke or evaporation fog, occurs when cold air (well below freezing) passes over warmer water (5-10°C or more). The water evaporates into the cold air, quickly saturates it, and immediately re-condenses as fog. The fog rises in wispy columns resembling steam.

met_86.brief: Mixing fog does not depend on ground temperature; it forms when two unsaturated air masses of different temperatures mix.
met_86.detailed: Mixing fog occurs when two nearly saturated air masses at different temperatures mix, and the mixture becomes supersaturated. For example, when warm, moist air mixes with cold air, the resulting mixture may exceed 100% relative humidity. This type can form at any height and is not reliant on ground cooling.

met_87.brief: Orographic (hill) fog forms when warm, moist air is forced to rise over elevated terrain, cooling adiabatically to saturation.
met_87.detailed: Orographic fog is a type of upslope fog. As moist air is forced upward by hills or mountains, it expands and cools adiabatically. When it cools to the dew point, condensation occurs, enveloping the higher terrain in fog. The windward side of hills is most affected.

met_88.brief: Precipitation formation in clouds requires freezing temperatures (below 0°C) and moderate to strong updrafts to sustain droplet growth.
met_88.detailed: In warm clouds, precipitation forms by collision-coalescence. In cold clouds (below 0°C), the Bergeron-Findeisen process dominates: ice crystals grow at the expense of supercooled water droplets. For significant precipitation, strong updrafts are needed to keep growing droplets/crystals aloft until they are large enough to fall as rain, snow, or hail.

met_89.brief: Strong updrafts are required to keep precipitation particles suspended long enough to grow to medium or large sizes.
met_89.detailed: Precipitation particles grow by collecting smaller droplets as they fall. Updrafts within a cloud support the growing particles, allowing multiple cycles through the cloud (especially important for hail formation). Without strong updrafts, particles fall out too quickly to reach significant size.

met_90.brief: Hail and sleet require precipitation particles to repeatedly cross the freezing level through multiple updrafts and downdrafts.
met_90.detailed: For solid precipitation like hail to form, supercooled water droplets must freeze onto an ice nucleus and grow by accretion. Strong updrafts carry the particle upward through supercooled water regions; when it becomes too heavy, it falls, then may be caught in another updraft. Each cycle adds another layer of ice, producing layered hailstones.

met_91.brief: Flying through cumulonimbus (Cb) clouds risks heavy rain, hail, severe turbulence, heavy icing, and lightning.
met_91.detailed: Cumulonimbus clouds contain violent updrafts and downdrafts, supercooled water droplets (causing severe icing), large hailstones, heavy rain, and lightning. The turbulence within a Cb can exceed the structural limits of an aircraft. EASA rules require aircraft to avoid Cb by at least 5 NM.

met_92.brief: Stratiform clouds (St) produce low precipitation, calm air, and light turbulence – steady conditions.
met_92.detailed: Stratiform clouds are horizontally extensive with weak vertical motions. They produce steady, light precipitation (drizzle or light rain) rather than showery precipitation. Turbulence is generally light or nil. Icing risk exists in freezing conditions but is less severe than in Cb.

met_93.brief: Flying beneath a Cb cloud still exposes the aircraft to sudden heavy rain, hail, turbulence, and lightning strikes.
met_93.detailed: Even when flying below the cloud base of a cumulonimbus, the aircraft is at risk from precipitation falling out of the cloud (heavy rain and hail), low-level turbulence and gust fronts, and lightning discharges that can extend from the cloud. VFR flight should maintain at least 5 NM clearance.

met_94.brief: Continental polar (cP) air is cold, dry air originating over northern Russia/Siberia, bringing cold winter weather to Central Europe.
met_94.detailed: Continental polar air forms over the cold land masses of Russia/Scandinavia. It is cold and dry. When it moves into Central Europe in winter, it brings clear skies, very cold temperatures, and good visibility. In summer it produces cool, stable conditions.

met_95.brief: Unstable air masses show cumulus clouds, strong vertical development, showers, and large water droplets.
met_95.detailed: An unstable air mass has a steep lapse rate (environmental lapse rate > dry adiabatic), allowing thermals to rise freely. This produces cumulus clouds with vertical development, showery precipitation, good visibility between showers, and characteristic 'cauliflower' cloud tops.

met_96.brief: Air mass character is determined by its region of origin and the path it has taken (track) to reach the area.
met_96.detailed: The source region gives the air mass its initial temperature and humidity (e.g., polar vs tropical, continental vs maritime). As the air mass moves, it is modified by the underlying surface: a continental air mass crossing a sea becomes more moist; a polar air mass moving southwards warms from below, becoming unstable.

met_97.brief: 'Maritime climate' means the climate is influenced by Atlantic-maritime air masses, bringing mild, moist, changeable weather.
met_97.detailed: The maritime climate of Western Europe is dominated by air masses from the Atlantic Ocean, particularly the polar maritime (Pm) and tropical maritime (Tm) air masses. Maritime air is moist, with small diurnal and seasonal temperature variations, and brings frequent frontal systems.

met_98.brief: A continental air mass (dry) can be modified by moving over widespread humid areas, gaining moisture and becoming less stable.
met_98.detailed: As a continental air mass moves over a sea or large lake, it absorbs moisture from evaporation. The lower layers become more humid and warmer (if the water is warmer than the air), increasing instability. This may trigger cumulus formation and showers.

met_99.brief: Air mass properties are given by its region of origin (source region) and its track (path) during movement.
met_99.detailed: The source region defines the initial temperature and humidity (e.g., continental = dry, maritime = moist, polar = cold, tropical = warm). The track determines modification: a polar air mass tracking over warm ocean becomes unstable and moist; over cold land, it remains stable.

met_100.brief: Advection is the horizontal movement of air, which can take place at any height in the atmosphere.
met_100.detailed: Advection refers to horizontal transport of air properties (temperature, moisture). Unlike convection (vertical motion), advection moves air laterally and can occur at all levels. Warm advection (warm air moving in) and cold advection (cold air moving in) are key processes in weather forecasting.

met_101.brief: Transformation (modification) of an air mass refers to the changes in its properties as it moves away from its source region.
met_101.detailed: As an air mass travels, it is modified by the underlying surface through heating, cooling, moistening, or drying. For example, cP air moving over the North Sea becomes cP(m) as it picks up moisture. The rate of transformation depends on the temperature difference between air and surface.

met_102.brief: A front is the boundary between two different air masses, associated with distinct weather phenomena.
met_102.detailed: A front is the transition zone between two air masses of different temperature, humidity, and density. Fronts are named by the advancing air mass: warm front (warm air advancing), cold front (cold air advancing), stationary front (neither advancing), or occluded front (cold front overtakes warm front).

met_103.brief: A cold front forms when advancing cold air undercuts and lifts the warmer air ahead of it.
met_103.detailed: In a cold front, the cold air is denser and moves faster than the warm air. It pushes under the warm air, forcing it to rise rapidly. This causes adiabatic cooling, cloud formation (often cumulonimbus), and heavy showers or thunderstorms. After the front passes, wind veers and pressure rises.

met_104.brief: A gradual increase in cirrus clouds (Ci) often indicates the approach of a warm front.
met_104.detailed: In a warm front, warm air overrides the colder air ahead. The first sign is high cirrus clouds, which gradually thicken to cirrostratus, then altostratus, and finally nimbostratus with steady precipitation. The sequence can take 12-24 hours. Cirrus may appear 500-1000 km ahead.

met_105.brief: Altostratus (As) and cirrostratus (Cs) clouds typically appear 400-800 km ahead of an approaching warm front.
met_105.detailed: The typical cloud sequence for an approaching warm front is: cirrus (Ci) → cirrostratus (Cs) → altostratus (As) → nimbostratus (Ns). The As and Cs bands are the middle stage, arriving several hundred km ahead of the surface front. As the front nears, the cloud base lowers.

met_106.brief: VFR flight through a warm front is hazardous due to low ceiling, poor visibility, and steady rain.
met_106.detailed: Warm fronts produce extensive stratiform clouds (nimbostratus), steady rain, and very low ceilings. Visibility is reduced by rain and fog. The large area of cloud and precipitation (often 200-400 km wide) makes it difficult to find VFR gaps.

met_107.brief: Near a cold front, VFR pilots encounter moderate visibility, heavy showers, thunderstorms, and gusty winds.
met_107.detailed: Cold front weather is more violent but narrower than warm-front weather. Heavy showers, thunderstorms, and hail are common. Visibility can be poor in heavy rain but clears rapidly behind the front. The main hazards are reduced visibility, strong gusty winds, wind shear, and turbulence.

met_108.brief: Cumulonimbus (Cb) is the typical cold-front cloud in summer, producing heavy showers and thunderstorms.
met_108.detailed: In summer, the strong temperature contrast across a cold front causes vigorous uplift, forming cumulonimbus clouds along the frontal line. These can develop into a squall line. Cb clouds produce the most severe weather: large hail, dangerous turbulence, and lightning.

met_109.brief: During cold front passage, wind direction veers (clockwise in NH) from SW to NW and wind speed increases.
met_109.detailed: Before a cold front, the wind is typically from the south or southwest (in the warm sector). As the front passes, the wind veers sharply to the northwest (clockwise in NH), and speed increases due to the stronger pressure gradient behind the front.

met_110.brief: A cold front is associated with a sharp wind shift (veering) and narrow band of heavy weather.
met_110.detailed: The passage of a cold front brings abrupt changes: temperature drop, pressure rise, wind veer and increase, and a band of heavy showers or thunderstorms. The width of the frontal zone is typically 50-100 km, much narrower than a warm front.

met_111.brief: In the warm sector of a depression during summer, expect medium-to-high cloud fields with little precipitation and moderate visibility.
met_111.detailed: The warm sector lies between the warm front and cold front of a mid-latitude depression. Air here is typically mild and moist (tropical maritime). Clouds are often altocumulus or stratocumulus with little or no precipitation. Visibility may be reduced by haze.

met_112.brief: Behind a cold front, gusty winds, scattered cumulus, and occasional showers are typical.
met_112.detailed: After the cold front passes, the air mass is cold and unstable. Cold air over a warmer surface causes convection, producing scattered cumulus (Cu) and cumulonimbus (Cb) with showers. The winds remain gusty. Visibility is good except in showers.

met_113.brief: An occlusion line forms when a cold front overtakes a warm front, lifting the warm air completely off the ground.
met_113.detailed: In a mature depression, the cold front moves faster than the warm front and eventually catches up. The warm air is lifted aloft, and the two cold air masses merge at the surface. The occlusion line is where the lifting occurs, often with extensive stratus and steady precipitation.

met_114.brief: A cold-front occlusion occurs when the air behind the occlusion is colder than the air ahead.
met_114.detailed: In a cold occlusion, the advancing air is colder than the air ahead of the warm front. The colder air undercuts both the warm air and the cooler air ahead. The weather typically includes a thick band of stratus and steady rain.

met_115.brief: A stationary front occurs when cold polar and warm subtropical air masses meet but neither advances.
met_115.detailed: A stationary front marks a boundary where the wind on both sides is parallel to the front, with no net movement. The weather can persist for days, with extensive cloud and precipitation. Stationary fronts can become wave disturbances and develop into active depressions.

met_116.brief: Frontal low-pressure areas in the northern hemisphere move along the warm sector isobars, typically from SW to NE.
met_116.detailed: Mid-latitude depressions (frontal lows) are steered by the upper-level winds, typically along the direction of the warm sector isobars. In Europe, they move from the Atlantic toward the east or northeast, bringing the sequence of warm front, warm sector, and cold front.

met_117.brief: During polar front low passage in Central Europe, wind backs during warm front passage and veers during cold front passage.
met_117.detailed: As a frontal low approaches, the wind backs (turns counterclockwise) during warm front passage. As the cold front passes, the wind veers (turns clockwise). This backing-then-veering pattern is characteristic of a depression passing to the north of the observer.

met_118.brief: High-pressure areas are predominantly found at around 30° N/S, where descending air from the Hadley circulation creates divergence.
met_118.detailed: At approximately 30° latitude both north and south, the Hadley circulation produces descending air, creating subtropical high-pressure belts (e.g., Azores High, Bermuda High). These semi-permanent highs are responsible for stable, dry weather.

met_119.brief: In summer, high-pressure areas typically produce scattered cumulus and altocumulus clouds.
met_119.detailed: Summer highs bring subsidence inversions that cap convection, limiting cumulus to shallow fair-weather Cu and Ac. There is little or no precipitation, light winds, and good visibility.

met_120.brief: A ridge of high pressure is an elongated area of high pressure extending between two low-pressure areas.
met_120.detailed: A ridge is an extension of a high-pressure area, shown on weather charts as isobars bulging outward from the high. Weather in a ridge is generally fair, with light winds and stable conditions.

met_121.brief: Winter high-pressure areas bring fog, high fog (low stratus), and occasional light precipitation.
met_121.detailed: In winter, high pressure often brings clear skies at night, leading to strong radiational cooling and radiation fog. If the fog deepens, it becomes low stratus ('high fog'). Persistent fog can severely impact aviation with low ceilings and poor visibility.

met_122.brief: Cold air inflow in high tropospheric layers (upper trough) creates instability, resulting in showers and thunderstorms.
met_122.detailed: When cold air aloft moves into a region, the environmental lapse rate steepens, increasing instability. This can trigger convection even without a frontal boundary, producing showers and thunderstorms.

met_123.brief: An upper-level trough is an area of cold air aloft where pressure levels are lower than surrounding areas.
met_123.detailed: In an upper trough, the height of pressure surfaces (e.g., 500 hPa) is lower, indicating colder, denser air. Upper troughs are associated with instability, cloud formation, and potential thunderstorm development.

met_124.brief: The polar front separates subtropical (warm) air from polar (cold) air, the main frontal boundary across Central Europe.
met_124.detailed: The polar front is the semi-permanent boundary between polar easterlies and mid-latitude westerlies. It is the primary zone of cyclogenesis in the northern hemisphere, where wave disturbances develop into the frontal depressions that bring precipitation to Central Europe.

met_125.brief: Climate is defined as the average weather cycle over a period of at least 30 years (WMO standard).
met_125.detailed: The WMO defines climate as the statistical description of weather (mean and variability) over at least 30 years. This distinguishes climate from weather (day-to-day conditions). Climate normals are used as reference baselines.

met_126.brief: A 'westerly' situation brings changeable weather with passing frontal lines, typical of mid-latitude maritime climates.
met_126.detailed: In a westerly weather pattern, the prevailing wind is from the west, bringing a succession of frontal systems from the Atlantic. This results in changeable weather with alternating rain and clearer conditions.

met_127.brief: Summer high pressure brings calm weather, cloud dissipation, and few high cumulus clouds.
met_127.detailed: With a summer high, subsidence inhibits convection, causing clouds to dissipate. There may be some fair-weather cumulus in the afternoon but generally skies are clear or with thin high cloud.

met_128.brief: In areas with no prevailing pressure gradient (col or flat pressure), winds are variable and local wind systems develop.
met_128.detailed: When isobars are widely spaced, the pressure gradient is weak and synoptic winds are light. Local effects dominate: sea breezes along coasts, anabatic winds during the day, katabatic winds at night.

met_129.brief: A small horizontal pressure gradient causes light winds (a light breeze).
met_129.detailed: Wind speed is proportional to the pressure gradient force (the rate of change of pressure over distance). When isobars are far apart, the gradient is small, resulting in light winds. A strong gradient produces strong winds.

met_130.brief: On the windward side of a mountain range during Foehn, expect layered clouds, mountains obscured, poor visibility, and rain.
met_130.detailed: Foehn conditions occur when moist air is forced to rise over a mountain barrier. On the windward side, the air cools adiabatically, condenses into layered clouds, and produces moderate to heavy precipitation. Mountains are often obscured, and visibility is poor.

met_131.brief: The Bora is a cold, katabatic wind blowing from the northeast into the Adriatic Sea along the Croatian coast.
met_131.detailed: The Bora is a cold, gusty, downslope wind (katabatic) that flows from the Dinaric Alps onto the Adriatic coast. It forms when cold continental air spills over the mountains. It can exceed 100 kt and is dangerous for aviation, producing severe turbulence and wind shear.

met_132.brief: Moist air forced up a mountain range causes cloud and precipitation on the windward side with Foehn clearance and good visibility on the leeward side.
met_132.detailed: When strong moist airflow hits a mountain range perpendicularly, it is forced to rise, causing clouds and precipitation on the windward side. The air then descends on the lee side, warming adiabatically (Foehn effect), creating clouds down the valleys on the lee side as well.

met_133.brief: Ice accretion is most favourable at temperatures between 0°C and -12°C in the presence of supercooled water droplets.
met_133.detailed: Aircraft icing occurs when supercooled water droplets (liquid water below 0°C) strike the aircraft surface and freeze. The temperature range 0°C to -12°C is the most critical because supercooled droplets are most abundant. Below -20°C, most water has already frozen into ice crystals.

met_134.brief: Temperatures between 0°C and -12°C are the most dangerous for aircraft icing.
met_134.detailed: The highest concentration of supercooled liquid water exists between 0°C and -12°C. In this range, droplets remain liquid despite below-freezing temperatures. When they strike an airframe, they freeze instantly. This is the classic 'icing range' in aviation weather training.

met_135.brief: The main factors for aircraft icing are air temperature, humidity (moisture content), and droplet size.
met_135.detailed: Temperature determines whether water is supercooled. Humidity provides the water available for freezing. Droplet size affects the type of ice: small droplets produce rime ice; large droplets produce clear ice.

met_136.brief: Rime ice forms from very small supercooled water droplets freezing instantly on leading edges, creating opaque deposits.
met_136.detailed: Rime ice forms when small supercooled droplets (< 20 microns) freeze immediately on impact, trapping air between frozen droplets. It appears white, opaque, and rough. It accumulates on leading edges. While it disturbs airflow (increasing drag), it is easier to remove than clear ice.

met_137.brief: The primary types of icing are rime ice, clear ice (glaze), and hoarfrost.
met_137.detailed: Rime ice forms from small supercooled droplets. Clear ice (glaze) forms from larger supercooled droplets that spread before freezing. Hoarfrost is not in-flight ice but results from sublimation on cold surfaces on the ground; it must be removed before takeoff.

met_138.brief: Clear ice develops when large supercooled droplets spread across the aircraft surface before freezing.
met_138.detailed: Clear ice forms when large supercooled droplets (above 30-40 microns) hit the aircraft and spread before freezing, creating a smooth, transparent sheet. Clear ice is denser, harder to remove, and aerodynamically more dangerous than rime ice.

met_139.brief: Rime ice adds weight and disrupts aerodynamic shape, increasing drag and reducing lift.
met_139.detailed: Rime ice accumulates on leading edges. Its rough texture disturbs smooth laminar airflow over the wing, causing early boundary-layer separation. This results in a significant loss of lift and increase in drag, raising stall speed.

met_140.brief: Yes, snow accumulation on wings severely deteriorates aerodynamic characteristics, making take-off unsafe.
met_140.detailed: Even a thin layer of snow or frost on the wing disrupts the smooth airflow required for lift generation. It increases surface roughness (drag), reduces the stall margin, and adds weight. EASA regulations require a clean aircraft before take-off.

met_141.brief: Vertical wind shear is a change in wind speed/direction over a small vertical distance.
met_141.detailed: Wind shear can be vertical (change with height) or horizontal (change with distance). Vertical wind shear is particularly hazardous during take-off and landing because the aircraft experiences sudden changes in headwind/tailwind, affecting indicated airspeed and lift.

met_142.brief: Severe wind shear may occur during final approach after a heavy shower has passed within the last 30 minutes.
met_142.detailed: After a heavy shower or thunderstorm passes, the cold downdraft air spreads out horizontally, creating a gust front. This can produce severe low-level wind shear for up to 30-60 minutes after the storm has passed.

met_143.brief: Thunderstorms produce hazardous gusts and turbulence from strong updrafts, downdrafts, and outflow winds.
met_143.detailed: The primary hazards of thunderstorms are: severe turbulence (updrafts/downdrafts up to 3000 ft/min), gust fronts (outflow winds), hail, lightning, heavy rain, and icing.

met_144.brief: Thunderstorm formation requires warm, humid air and a conditionally unstable lapse rate.
met_144.detailed: For thunderstorms: (1) moist air near the surface, (2) an unstable lapse rate, and (3) a triggering mechanism (heating, frontal uplift, or orographic lifting). Conditional instability allows air parcels to become buoyant once they saturate.

met_145.brief: Mandatory conditions for thunderstorm formation: conditionally unstable atmosphere, high temperature, and high humidity.
met_145.detailed: High temperature and humidity provide the energy source (latent heat release). Conditional instability means the air is stable for unsaturated parcels but unstable once saturated. These conditions, together with a lifting mechanism, produce cumulonimbus clouds.

met_146.brief: Frontal thunderstorms develop at any time of day along a frontal boundary, especially along cold fronts.
met_146.detailed: Unlike air-mass thunderstorms (which peak in afternoon heat), frontal thunderstorms can occur at any hour because the lifting mechanism is the frontal surface, not solar heating.

met_147.brief: The expected vertical speed in a cumulonimbus downdraft is about 10-15 m/s (2000-3000 ft/min).
met_147.detailed: Cumulonimbus downdrafts are caused by precipitation drag and negative buoyancy from evaporative cooling. Downdraft speeds of 10-15 m/s (2000-3000 ft/min) are common and can force an aircraft into the ground even with full power.

met_148.brief: Strong updrafts and downdrafts appear during the mature stage of a thunderstorm cell.
met_148.detailed: A thunderstorm cell has three stages: cumulus (developing), mature (updraft and downdraft coexist, heavy rain and lightning), and dissipating (downdraft dominates). The mature stage is the most hazardous for aviation.

met_149.brief: A typical thunderstorm cell lasts about 15-30 minutes.
met_149.detailed: Individual thunderstorm cells are short-lived: the cumulus stage ~15 min, mature stage 15-30 min, and dissipating stage ~30 min. However, multicell clusters can last for hours.

met_150.brief: In the dissipating stage, rain continues but lightning ceases as downdrafts dominate.
met_150.detailed: During dissipation, the downdraft cuts off the inflow of warm, moist air. The updraft weakens. Precipitation continues as light-to-moderate rain, but electrical activity ceases.

met_151.brief: A lightning strike can damage the aircraft's electrical system and navigation equipment.
met_151.detailed: When an aircraft is struck by lightning, the current flows through the conductive skin (Faraday cage) and exits via static wicks. However, sensitive electronics may be damaged. P-static can cause instrument errors, radio failure, and structural damage in severe cases.

met_152.brief: Heavy downdrafts and wind shear are expected near the rainfall areas of heavy showers or thunderstorms.
met_152.detailed: The downdraft is strongest where precipitation loading is greatest. As it approaches the ground, it spreads out horizontally, creating the gust front with strong wind shear. These hazards are most dangerous within 5 NM of the storm.

met_153.brief: The cold air downdraft from a mature thunderstorm spreads out upon reaching the ground, creating a 'gust front'.
met_153.detailed: The gust front is the boundary between the cold thunderstorm outflow and surrounding warm air. It behaves like a mini cold front with sharp wind shift, increased wind speed, and often a roll cloud. It can extend 15-30 km ahead of the storm.

met_154.brief: The minimum safe distance for circumnavigating a thunderstorm is 5 NM (9 km).
met_154.detailed: ICAO and EASA recommend avoiding thunderstorms by at least 5 NM (some say 10 NM for severe storms). Hail can be thrown up to 5 NM from the cloud edge. Severe turbulence can extend beyond the visible cloud.

met_155.brief: When taking off in a ground inversion, expect a sudden decrease in speed and climb performance.
met_155.detailed: The aircraft takes off in cold, dense air (good performance). As it climbs through the inversion into warmer, less dense air, performance drops suddenly. The rate of climb and airspeed decrease sharply.

met_156.brief: When passing a mountain range, frontal weather weakens on the lee side and strengthens on the windward (luv) side.
met_156.detailed: Mountains act as a barrier to fronts. On the windward side, forced uplift enhances clouds and precipitation. On the lee side, descending air (Foehn effect) weakens frontal activity.

met_157.brief: Lenticular (lens-shaped) clouds form on the lee side of a mountain range, above the ridge, in standing waves.
met_157.detailed: Lenticularis are lens-shaped clouds that form in the crests of mountain waves (lee waves). They indicate strong winds aloft, turbulence (rotor), and mountain wave activity.

met_158.brief: A 'roll cloud' at the leading edge of a gust front or in mountain lee waves contains heavy turbulence.
met_158.detailed: Roll clouds are horizontal tube-shaped clouds associated with gust fronts or mountain wave rotors. They indicate severe turbulence due to strong wind shear. In mountain waves, the rotor can produce violent, dangerous turbulence.

met_159.brief: Mist is defined as reduced visibility between 1 km and 8 km with relative humidity of at least 80%.
met_159.detailed: Mist (BR in METAR) is a suspension of water droplets reducing visibility to between 1000 m and 5000 m, with RH ≥ 80%. Fog (FG) is when visibility falls below 1000 m.

met_160.brief: Haze development is favoured by stable atmospheric layering with a strong inversion.
met_160.detailed: Haze (HZ) consists of dry particles (dust, smoke, pollutants) suspended in the air. A stable layer with a strong inversion prevents vertical mixing, so particles accumulate near the surface.

met_161.brief: A surface weather chart shows actual air pressure reduced to MSL, with pressure centres, fronts, and isobars.
met_161.detailed: The surface chart is the most common meteorological chart. It presents isobars (lines of equal pressure at MSL), pressure centres (H/L), and weather fronts.

met_162.brief: A transmissometer measures runway visual range (RVR) by measuring light extinction over a known baseline.
met_162.detailed: RVR is the distance a pilot can see down the runway from the cockpit. Transmissometers measure visibility along the runway using a light source and detector.

met_163.brief: Satellite images provide an overview of cloud cover, front lines, and weather systems.
met_163.detailed: Meteorological satellites provide visible and infrared imagery. Visible shows cloud cover; infrared shows cloud top temperatures/heights. They help pilots identify fronts, thunderstorms, and fog.

met_164.brief: Weather radar images help determine if a thunderstorm can be circumnavigated.
met_164.detailed: Weather radar detects precipitation by reflectivity. Images show location, intensity, and movement of precipitation areas including thunderstorms and squall lines.

met_165.brief: From the flight deck, pilots can determine horizontal visibility, vertical visibility, and slant visibility.
met_165.detailed: Horizontal visibility is lateral distance visible. Vertical visibility is the height visible upward. Slant visibility is visibility along the approach path, which can differ from horizontal due to fog layers.

met_166.brief: Radar echoes of precipitation are NOT found on Low-Level Significant Weather Charts (LLSWC).
met_166.detailed: LLSWC forecast significant weather below FL 240, including thunderstorms, turbulence, icing, and clouds. They do not show radar echoes (real-time precipitation radar is a different product).

met_167.brief: 'FRQ TS' on a LLSWC means frequent, clearly separated thunderstorms.
met_167.detailed: FRQ TS indicates frequent, separated thunderstorms covering > 50% of the area. Other abbreviations: OCNL TS (occasional), SQL TS (squall line), EMBD TS (embedded in cloud layers).

met_168.brief: Low-Level Significant Weather Charts are updated every 6 hours.
met_168.detailed: LLSWCs are issued four times daily (00, 06, 12, 18 UTC) with validity covering 6-24 hours. They are a key pre-flight planning tool.

met_169.brief: LLSWC shows cloud coverage in eighths (oktas), ceiling height, and cloud tops.
met_169.detailed: Cloud information includes total cloud cover in oktas, cloud base (ceiling) in hundreds of feet, and cloud tops. SCAT, BKN, or OVC describe coverage.

met_170.brief: A surface weather chart displays measured pressure distribution at MSL and corresponding frontal systems.
met_170.detailed: The surface analysis chart presents observed pressure (QFF) using isobars, with analysed fronts and pressure centres. It is the primary chart for understanding current synoptic weather.

met_171.brief: A high pressure gradient is recognised by closely spaced isobars, indicating strong winds.
met_171.detailed: Isobars connect points of equal pressure. Close spacing means a large pressure change over a short distance, producing a strong pressure gradient force and strong winds.

met_172.brief: In METAR, '+RA' designates heavy rain (RA = rain, '+' = heavy intensity).
met_172.detailed: METAR abbreviations: RA = rain, DZ = drizzle, SN = snow. '+' = heavy, '-' = light. '+RA' means heavy rain.

met_173.brief: When haze (HZ) is reported in METAR, the visibility is between 1000 m and 5000 m.
met_173.detailed: Haze (HZ) is reported when visibility is 1000-5000 m due to suspended dry particles. Below 1000 m, it is reported as fog (FG).

met_174.brief: In GAFOR, 'M' means ground visibility < 3 km (≥ 1.5 km) and/or ceiling < 1000 ft (≥ 500 ft).
met_174.detailed: GAFOR uses letters A-to-M for VFR weather severity. 'M' is the worst: visibility < 3 km and/or ceiling < 1000 ft. 'A' is the best.

met_175.brief: With cloud base 2000 ft and visibility 20 km, the GAFOR code is DELTA (D).
met_175.detailed: GAFOR codes: A (vis ≥ 8 km, ceiling ≥ 1000 ft), B (≥ 5 km, ≥ 1000 ft), C (≥ 5 km, ≥ 500 ft), D (≥ 3 km, ≥ 500 ft).

met_176.brief: The TREND message of a METAR covers a 2-hour forecast period.
met_176.detailed: TREND is a short-term forecast appended to METAR, valid for 2 hours. It describes expected changes: BECMG, TEMPO, or NOSIG.

met_177.brief: 'NOSIG' means no significant change is expected in the 2-hour TREND period.
met_177.detailed: NOSIG (No Significant Change) is used when conditions are expected to remain within the current METAR criteria. If no TREND is given, NOSIG is implied.

met_178.brief: 'BECMG' in a TAF indicates a transition to another weather state.
met_178.detailed: BECMG (becoming) indicates a gradual change to described conditions. It includes a time period (e.g., BECMG 1012 means change between 10 and 12 UTC).

met_179.brief: BECMG 1214 means the change is expected between 12 UTC and 14 UTC.
met_179.detailed: The new weather state after BECMG is expected to be fully established by the end of the period (14 UTC). The old conditions gradually give way.

met_180.brief: FM1220 means a new weather situation starting from 1220 UTC.
met_180.detailed: FM (from) in a TAF indicates an abrupt change at the specified time. Conditions after FM replace previous conditions immediately.

met_181.brief: Cloud bases in a METAR are indicated in feet above reference height (airfield elevation).
met_181.detailed: Cloud heights in METAR are given in feet above aerodrome level. 'BKN030' means a broken layer at 3000 ft AAL.

met_182.brief: The METAR reports temperature 15 °C, dew point 12 °C, and QNH 1015 hPa.
met_182.detailed: METAR LEPA ... 15/12 means temperature 15 °C and dew point 12 °C. SCT005 = 3-4/8 at 500 ft, BKN010 = 5-7/8 at 1000 ft, RA = rain, QNH 1015 hPa.

met_183.detailed: METAR cloud coverage: FEW = 1-2 oktas, SCT = 3-4, BKN = 5-7, OVC = 8. BKN and OVC are ceilings.

met_184.brief: AIRMETs are issued when significant weather phenomena like severe icing or turbulence occur.
met_184.detailed: AIRMETs are in-flight advisories for light aircraft for less severe conditions than SIGMETs: moderate icing, moderate turbulence, reduced visibility.

met_185.brief: A GAMET is issued for 3 hours, 8 times a day.
met_185.detailed: GAMET is a low-level area forecast for VFR flights, issued 8 times daily (every 3 hours). It covers an FIR for flights below FL 100.

met_186.brief: ATIS provides weather and operational information about the destination aerodrome during flight.
met_186.detailed: ATIS broadcasts: active runways, wind, visibility, clouds, temperature, QNH, QFE. Updated every 30 minutes.

met_187.brief: Flights in the traffic circuit do NOT require a weather briefing before departure.
met_187.detailed: For local flights remaining in the circuit, a formal briefing is not needed as the pilot can observe conditions directly.

met_188.brief: SIGMET should be checked before each flight for information about en-route hazards.
met_188.detailed: SIGMET warns of severe icing, severe turbulence, thunderstorms, volcanic ash, and radioactive clouds. Issued for each FIR/UIR.

met_189.brief: SIGMET warnings are issued for FIRs/UIRs.
met_189.detailed: SIGMETs cover the airspace of an FIR or UIR, issued by the meteorological watch office. Valid for up to 4-6 hours.

met_190.brief: SIGMET includes warnings about thunderstorms at squall lines (SQL TS).
met_190.detailed: SQL TS indicates a line of thunderstorms with continuous heavy precipitation and strong gusts. SIGMET also covers TS (isolated, frequent, or embedded).

comm_1.brief: HX means 'no specific opening hours' – the station has no published operating schedule.
comm_1.detailed: HX is a standard service abbreviation in aeronautical information publications (AIPs). It indicates the station operates without fixed hours, available on request or by arrangement. Other service abbreviations: H24 (24-hour service), HJ (daytime only), HN (night only), HO (by arrangement).

comm_2.brief: Blind transmissions are used when a pilot cannot establish two-way communication but needs to transmit important information.
comm_2.detailed: Blind transmissions begin with 'Blind' followed by the message. The pilot transmits position, altitude, and intentions but does not expect acknowledgement. This procedure is specified in SERA.

comm_3.brief: 'ABM' is the standard abbreviation for 'abeam' – a position laterally adjacent to a specific point.
comm_3.detailed: ABM = abeam, a position where the aircraft's beam is directly in line with a navigation point. Other position abbreviations: CL (centre line), DCT (direct), O/H (overhead).

comm_4.brief: FIS stands for Flight Information Service – providing information useful for safe and efficient flight.
comm_4.detailed: FIS includes weather (SIGMET, AIRMET), traffic information, navigation assistance, and operational information. It does not provide separation service (that is ATC).

comm_5.brief: FIR stands for Flight Information Region – designated airspace within which FIS and alerting service are provided.
comm_5.detailed: Each FIR is defined by ICAO regional agreements. FIR boundaries often follow national borders. Upper FIRs (UIRs) apply above a certain altitude.

comm_6.detailed: H24 indicates a station operates 24 hours. Other abbreviations: HJ (day only), HN (night only), HO (by arrangement), HX (no specific hours).

comm_7.brief: QFE is the barometric pressure at the aerodrome; setting QFE makes the altimeter read zero on the runway.
comm_7.detailed: QFE is pressure adjusted to aerodrome elevation. When set, the altimeter indicates height above the aerodrome. Used for circuit flying and landing at some airports.

comm_8.brief: With QNH set, the altimeter displays altitude above mean sea level (MSL).
comm_8.detailed: QNH is pressure reduced to MSL using standard atmosphere. With QNH set, the altimeter reads elevation above MSL. Standard setting for VFR flights below transition altitude.

comm_9.brief: With QFE set, the altimeter displays height above the reference airfield pressure level.
comm_9.detailed: QFE shows height above the aerodrome. At the runway threshold, the altimeter reads approximately 0 ft. Not all airports provide QFE.

comm_10.brief: QUJ is the Q-code for true bearing to the station (from aircraft to station).
comm_10.detailed: Q-codes are standardised three-letter codes. QUJ = true bearing to station. QTE = true bearing from station. QDM = magnetic heading to station (zero wind). QDR = magnetic bearing from station.

comm_11.brief: QTE is the Q-code for true bearing from the station (from station to aircraft).
comm_11.detailed: QTE is used in VHF direction finding (VDF). The ground station measures the bearing and returns QTE. The pilot can plot QTE on a chart for a position line.

comm_12.brief: QUJ is used for the true bearing to the station.
comm_12.detailed: QUJ is the reciprocal of QTE. If QTE = 090°, then QUJ = QTE + 180° = 270°.

comm_13.brief: Message priority: Distress > Urgency > Direction finding > Flight safety > Flight regularity.
comm_13.detailed: ICAO message priority order: 1) Distress MAYDAY, 2) Urgency PAN-PAN, 3) Direction finding, 4) Flight safety, 5) Flight regularity.

comm_14.brief: A flight safety message is used for air traffic control.
comm_14.detailed: Flight safety messages include ATC instructions, position reports, clearances. They have priority over flight regularity and other messages (SERA).

comm_15.brief: Distress messages concern aircraft, watercraft, or other vehicle/person in grave and imminent danger.
comm_15.detailed: MAYDAY (repeated three times) indicates grave and imminent danger requiring immediate assistance. Highest priority in radiotelephony.

comm_16.brief: Request QDM (magnetic heading to station) is classified as a flight safety message.
comm_16.detailed: QDM requests are flight safety messages because they provide essential navigational assistance. Flight safety is second only to distress and urgency.

comm_17.brief: The call sign HB-YKM is transmitted as 'Hotel Bravo Yankee Kilo Mike'.
comm_17.detailed: ICAO phonetic alphabet: A=Alpha, B=Bravo, C=Charlie, D=Delta, E=Echo, F=Foxtrot, G=Golf, H=Hotel, I=India, J=Juliett, K=Kilo, L=Lima, M=Mike, N=November, O=Oscar, P=Papa, Q=Quebec, R=Romeo, S=Sierra, T=Tango, U=Uniform, V=Victor, W=Whiskey, X=X-ray, Y=Yankee, Z=Zulu.

comm_18.brief: Altitude 4500 ft is transmitted as 'four thousand five hundred feet'.
comm_18.detailed: Standard RT: altitudes spoken as 'two thousand', 'four thousand five hundred'. 'Feet' after the number. Flight levels: 'flight level three five zero'. Headings: digits individually.

comm_19.brief: Directional information '12 o'clock' is transmitted as 'Twelve o'clock'.
comm_19.detailed: Clock code indicates direction relative to the aircraft's nose: 12 o'clock = ahead, 3 = right, 6 = behind. Spoken as words, not digits.

comm_20.brief: After a transmission with no answer, wait 10 seconds before re-transmitting.
comm_20.detailed: Standard RT: wait 10 seconds (VHF) before repeating a call. For HF, the wait is longer due to propagation delays.

comm_21.brief: 'Roger' means 'I have received all of your last transmission' (not compliance).
comm_21.detailed: 'Roger' confirms receipt only. 'Wilco' (Will Comply) means understood and will be complied with. 'Roger' comes from Morse code 'R' for 'Received'.

comm_22.brief: 'Correction' indicates an error in the last transmission, followed by the correct version.
comm_22.detailed: When a mistake is made, say 'Correction' (not abbreviated), pause briefly, then repeat the corrected part.

comm_23.brief: 'How do you read?' checks the readability (signal quality) of a transmission.
comm_23.detailed: Readability scale 1-5: 1 = unreadable, 2 = readable now and then, 3 = with difficulty, 4 = readable, 5 = perfectly readable. Response: 'Readability 5'.

comm_24.brief: 'Request' is used when a pilot wants to fly through controlled airspace.
comm_24.detailed: 'Request' precedes a specific request: 'Request join controlled airspace'. Standard procedure for transiting controlled airspace.

comm_25.brief: 'Request take-off' is the phrase when a pilot is ready for departure.
comm_25.detailed: The correct phraseology is 'Request take-off'. Not 'Ready for departure' or 'Ready for take-off'. Defined in ICAO Doc 9432 and SERA.

comm_26.brief: The call sign of aerodrome control (tower) is 'Tower'.
comm_26.detailed: Standard call signs: Tower (aerodrome control), Approach/Radar (approach), Ground (ground control), Information (FIS), Control (area control). Preceded by facility name.

comm_27.brief: The call sign of Flight Information Service is 'Information'.
comm_27.detailed: FIS uses 'Information' (e.g., 'Zürich Information'). FIS provides weather, traffic, and navigation information without issuing control instructions.

comm_28.brief: The pilot may abbreviate the call sign only after the ground station has used the abbreviated form.
comm_28.detailed: To reduce congestion, call signs may be abbreviated once the ground station initiates it. Some call signs cannot be abbreviated.

comm_29.brief: Leaving a control frequency (except at final parking) must be reported.
comm_29.detailed: Report when changing frequency or leaving controlled airspace. Exception: reaching the final parking position.

comm_30.brief: The correct acknowledgement is 'Call tower on 121.275' (restating the instruction).
comm_30.detailed: Readback is mandatory for frequency changes, runway info, altitude, headings, and clearances. Frequencies spoken as individual digits.

comm_31.brief: Readability 1 means the transmission is unreadable.
comm_31.detailed: ICAO scale: 1 = Unreadable, 2 = Readable now and then, 3 = With difficulty, 4 = Good, 5 = Perfect.

comm_32.brief: Readability 2 means the transmission is readable now and then.
comm_32.detailed: Signal is weak or affected by interference. Message understood only in parts. Blind transmission procedures may be required if conditions do not improve.

comm_33.brief: A test transmission should last a maximum of 10 seconds.
comm_33.detailed: Standard: '(Unit) this is (call sign), radio check'. Response includes readability level. Limited to 10 seconds to avoid frequency congestion.

comm_34.brief: Wind information does NOT require readback.
comm_34.detailed: Items requiring mandatory readback: runway, altitude, heading, speed, frequency, transition level, and conditional clearances. Wind and weather do not.

comm_35.brief: Readback includes callsign and all assigned parameters (altitude, heading, runway, clearance).
comm_35.detailed: Mandatory readback confirms each critical element. Prevents hearback/readback errors.

comm_36.brief: 'Wilco' acknowledges 'Next report PAH', confirming understanding and compliance.
comm_36.detailed: 'Wilco' (Will Comply) confirms both receipt and action. 'Roger' is receipt only.

comm_37.brief: 'Roger' acknowledges entering airspace Delta (confirms receipt of information).
comm_37.detailed: When informed of entering airspace (advisory), 'Roger' is appropriate. 'Wilco' implies an instruction.

comm_38.brief: 'SCT' means scattered clouds covering 3 to 4 oktas.
comm_38.detailed: METAR cloud coverage: FEW = 1-2, SCT = 3-4, BKN = 5-7, OVC = 8. SCT is not a ceiling.

comm_39.brief: For visibility ≥ 10 km, the standard ICAO term is 'Good'.
comm_39.detailed: ICAO visibility terms: <1 km Poor, 1-4 km Moderate, 5-9 km Good, ≥10 km Good (or state actual value). 'Very good' is not standard.

comm_40.brief: Visibility ≥ 5 km is reported in kilometers; <5 km in meters.
comm_40.detailed: ICAO convention: Visibility < 5 km in meters (e.g. '4000 m'), ≥5 km in kilometers (e.g. '10 km').

comm_41.brief: VOLMET broadcasts meteorological information (weather reports and forecasts) for airports.
comm_41.detailed: VOLMET (vol + météo) is a continuous broadcast of METAR, TAF, and trends for major airports.

comm_42.brief: An ATIS is valid for 30 minutes.
comm_42.detailed: ATIS is updated every 30 minutes or when significant changes occur. Each ATIS is identified by a phonetic letter (Alpha, Bravo, etc.).

comm_43.brief: Transponder code 7600 indicates radio communication failure.
comm_43.detailed: Standard codes: 7500 = hijack, 7600 = radio failure, 7700 = emergency. On radio failure, set 7600 and follow SERA procedures.

comm_44.brief: A blind transmission begins with 'Transmitting blind'.
comm_44.detailed: When unable to receive but able to transmit, the standard ICAO phrase is 'Transmitting blind' followed by the message.

comm_45.brief: Blind transmissions should be made on the current frequency.
comm_45.detailed: First attempt on the current frequency. If unsuccessful, continue on that same frequency or 121.500 MHz.

comm_46.brief: During radio failure in Class D airspace, leave using a standard routing.
comm_46.detailed: Radio failure procedures: continue in VMC, land at nearest suitable aerodrome, squawk 7600, watch for light signals, leave via standard routing.

comm_47.brief: Distress messages concern safety of aircraft, watercraft, or person in immediate danger.
comm_47.detailed: Preceded by MAYDAY (x3). Message includes: station called, aircraft ID, nature of distress, intention, position, altitude.

comm_48.brief: The correct frequency for initial distress is the current frequency.
comm_48.detailed: Use the frequency currently in use with ATC. If no contact, use 121.500 MHz (VHF emergency).

comm_49.brief: 'Pan Pan' is repeated three times before an urgency message.
comm_49.detailed: PAN PAN indicates a serious situation requiring priority but no immediate danger. Different from MAYDAY (grave and imminent danger).

comm_50.brief: Urgency messages concern safety of aircraft/vehicle/person but not requiring immediate assistance.
comm_50.detailed: Urgency (PAN PAN) = situation concerning safety, no immediate danger (e.g., medical, partial engine failure). Priority over all except distress.

comm_51.brief: 118.75 MHz is a VHF frequency designated for voice communication.
comm_51.detailed: Aviation VHF band: 118.000-136.975 MHz. Uses: 118-121.4 = ATC, 121.5 = emergency, 122.2-123.6 = FIS, 128.8-132 = ATIS, 132-136.975 = airline ops.

comm_52.brief: The band 118.000-136.975 MHz is called VHF (Very High Frequency).
comm_52.detailed: VHF (30-300 MHz) provides line-of-sight propagation. Aviation voice is 118-137 MHz. HF (2-30 MHz) for long range.

comm_53.brief: Altitude affects VHF reception because VHF waves travel as quasi-optical (line-of-sight) waves.
comm_53.detailed: Higher altitude increases distance to radio horizon. Range ≈ 1.23 × √(height in ft) NM. At 1000 ft: ~39 NM; at 10,000 ft: ~123 NM.

pof_1.brief: Static pressure of gases acts equally in all directions (Pascal's principle).
pof_1.detailed: In a fluid at rest, pressure acts with equal magnitude in all directions. For an aerofoil in flight, static pressure is measured perpendicular to the airflow. Total pressure (pitot) = static + dynamic.

pof_2.brief: Bernoulli's equation: total pressure = dynamic pressure + static pressure.
pof_2.detailed: For inviscid, incompressible flow, the sum of static and dynamic pressure (½ρV²) is constant along a streamline. As air speeds up over the curved upper wing surface, static pressure decreases, generating lift.

pof_3.brief: Total pressure remains constant when air flows through a pipe with changing cross-sections (ideal flow).
pof_3.detailed: Bernoulli's principle: as the pipe narrows, velocity increases (continuity: A₁V₁ = A₂V₂), so dynamic pressure increases and static decreases. Total pressure is conserved. Used in carburettor venturi.

pof_4.brief: Any body in an airflow always produces drag but not necessarily lift.
pof_4.detailed: Drag is produced by any body moving through a fluid. Lift requires specific shape (aerofoil) and angle of attack to create a pressure differential.

pof_5.brief: Angle of attack is the angle between the chord line and the relative airflow.
pof_5.detailed: The chord line runs from leading edge to trailing edge. Relative airflow is the vector sum of aircraft velocity and wind. AoA is distinct from pitch angle and is critical for lift.

pof_6.brief: The point where all aerodynamic forces act is the centre of pressure (CP).
pof_6.detailed: The CP is on the chord line where the resultant force acts. It moves with AoA changes. For a symmetrical profile, the CP stays fixed.

pof_7.brief: Aerodynamic force is the vector sum of lift and drag.
pof_7.detailed: Total aerodynamic force R = √(L² + D²). Lift is perpendicular to relative airflow; drag is parallel.

pof_8.brief: Profile depth (chord) is the distance between leading edge and trailing edge.
pof_8.detailed: The chord is the fundamental aerofoil dimension. Mean chord is used for tapered wings. Aspect ratio = span² / area = span / mean chord.

pof_9.brief: A symmetrical profile has identical upper and lower surface curvatures, with mean camber line equal to chord line.
pof_9.detailed: At zero AoA, a symmetrical profile produces zero lift. Used for tail surfaces and aerobatic aircraft.

pof_10.brief: Aspect ratio is the ratio of wing span to mean chord (AR = b²/S).
pof_10.detailed: High AR (gliders) has low induced drag. Low AR (fighters) has higher induced drag but better manoeuvrability.

pof_11.brief: A rectangular wing has the highest induced drag due to inefficient lift distribution.
pof_11.detailed: Rectangular wings have constant chord, causing strong tip vortices and highest induced drag. Elliptical wings have the lowest induced drag.

pof_12.brief: When the incidence angle is smaller at the tip than the root, this is geometric twist (washout).
pof_12.detailed: Washout causes the root to stall before the tip, preserving aileron effectiveness at high AoA.

pof_13.brief: Vortex development starts when lift is generated during take-off rotation.
pof_13.detailed: Wingtip vortices form as soon as the wing produces lift. The pressure difference causes air to flow around wingtips, creating trailing vortices.

pof_14.brief: The transition point is where airflow changes from laminar to turbulent.
pof_14.detailed: Laminar flow has low skin friction. At the transition point, the boundary layer becomes turbulent (higher friction but more resistant to separation). It moves forward with increasing AoA.

pof_15.brief: At the stagnation point, streamlines divide above and below the profile.
pof_15.detailed: The stagnation point is where airflow velocity is zero and static pressure is maximum. Flow splits into upper (faster, lower pressure) and lower paths.

pof_16.brief: Low pressure above and higher pressure below the profile creates the net upward force (lift).
pof_16.detailed: Bernoulli: curved upper surface accelerates airflow, reducing pressure. Flatter lower surface has higher pressure. The pressure difference produces lift.

pof_17.brief: On a positively cambered profile, the CP moves toward the trailing edge as AoA decreases.
pof_17.detailed: At high AoA, CP is forward. As AoA decreases, CP moves aft. This affects pitching moment and must be balanced by the tailplane.

pof_18.brief: A symmetrical profile has a fixed centre of pressure regardless of AoA.
pof_18.detailed: The CP of a symmetrical profile remains at about 25% chord. This makes it predictable for tail surfaces.

pof_19.brief: Excessive AoA causes loss of lift and airflow separation (stall).
pof_19.detailed: At the critical AoA (15-18°), the boundary layer separates from the upper surface, causing sudden lift loss and drag increase. Critical AoA is independent of airspeed.

pof_20.brief: As AoA decreases, the centre of pressure moves aft.
pof_20.detailed: A lower AoA shifts the stagnation point upward, shifting the resultant force toward the trailing edge.

pof_21.brief: Lift is directly changed in flight by changing the angle of attack.
pof_21.detailed: The pilot controls lift via elevator (pitch). Increasing AoA increases lift (up to stall). Other methods: changing airspeed, deploying flaps, or altitude changes.

pof_22.brief: Aerodynamic washout ensures the wing root stalls before the tip, retaining aileron effectiveness.
pof_22.detailed: Washout reduces tip incidence. At high AoA, the root stalls first while tips still produce lift, keeping ailerons effective during stall approach.

pof_23.brief: Separation begins at the trailing edge and moves forward as AoA increases.
pof_23.detailed: Adverse pressure gradient on the upper surface causes separation starting at the trailing edge. At critical AoA, separation reaches the leading edge and the wing stalls.

pof_24.brief: A too-large AoA results in a loss of lift (stall) at any airspeed.
pof_24.detailed: Every aerofoil has a critical AoA. Exceeding it causes boundary layer separation and stall, even at high speed (e.g., steep turn or pull-up).

pof_25.brief: Lift and drag decrease proportionally with decreasing air density.
pof_25.detailed: L = ½ρV²SCL, D = ½ρV²SCD. Both are proportional to density (ρ). At altitude, TAS must increase to maintain the same lift at constant IAS.

pof_26.brief: Lift depends on CL, V², ρ, and S: L = ½ρV² × S × CL.
pof_26.detailed: The lift equation is fundamental: lift increases with airspeed squared, density, wing area, and lift coefficient (which increases with AoA up to the stall).

pof_27.brief: The drag coefficient cannot be lower than a non-negative minimum value.
pof_27.detailed: Total CD = CD0 + CDi. There is always some skin friction and pressure drag, so CD has a positive minimum.

pof_28.brief: A thicker aerofoil generates more drag AND more lift at the same speed.
pof_28.detailed: Thicker profiles create more lift (higher maximum Cl) but also more form drag due to greater frontal area and flow separation.

pof_29.detailed: D = ½ρV²SCD. Doubling speed (100 to 200 kt) gives four times the drag.

pof_30.brief: Pressure compensation between upper and lower surfaces occurs at the wing tips.
pof_30.detailed: High-pressure air beneath the wing escapes around the tip to the low-pressure area above, creating wingtip vortices. This is the source of induced drag.

pof_31.brief: A small aspect ratio produces large induced drag due to strong tip vortices.
pof_31.detailed: Induced drag CDi ∝ CL²/(π×AR×e). Low AR wings have higher induced drag. Gliders have high AR for efficiency.

pof_32.brief: Induced drag is generated at the trailing edge as a result of wingtip vortices.
pof_32.detailed: Tip vortices tilt the local lift vector backward, creating induced drag. Highest at low speeds (high CL).

pof_33.brief: Interference drag is generated at the wing root (and other junctions).
pof_33.detailed: Interference drag occurs where two surfaces meet. The interaction of boundary layers creates additional drag. Fairings are used to reduce it.

pof_34.brief: Pressure drag, interference drag, and friction drag are all forms of parasite drag.
pof_34.detailed: Parasite drag = form drag + skin friction + interference drag. It is non-lift-related and increases with V².

pof_35.brief: As airspeed decreases during cruise, induced drag increases (higher CL needed).
pof_35.detailed: At slower speeds, higher CL is needed to maintain lift = weight. Higher CL means higher induced drag (CDi ∝ CL²).

pof_36.brief: As airspeed increases, induced drag decreases and parasite drag increases.
pof_36.detailed: Low speed: high induced drag, low parasite drag. High speed: low induced drag, high parasite drag. Total drag has a minimum at best glide speed.

pof_37.brief: A streamlined body has the smallest drag for its cross-sectional area.
pof_37.detailed: Streamlining reduces form drag by keeping airflow attached, minimising the wake. Teardrop shape = low drag.

pof_38.brief: When approaching a stall, lift decreases and drag increases significantly.
pof_38.detailed: At the critical AoA, airflow separates from the upper surface. Lift drops sharply and drag increases dramatically due to the separated flow wake.

pof_39.brief: When approaching a stall, lift decreases and drag increases significantly.
pof_39.detailed: At the critical AoA, airflow separates from the upper surface. Lift drops sharply and drag increases dramatically due to the separated flow wake.

pof_40.brief: The critical angle of attack is independent of weight.
pof_40.detailed: Critical AoA depends only on the aerofoil shape, not weight, speed, or altitude. Heavier aircraft stall at a higher IAS because more lift is needed, but the AoA at stall is the same.

pof_41.brief: A strong decrease in lift occurs suddenly when nearing the stall speed.
pof_41.detailed: As the aircraft slows, required AoA increases. When AoA exceeds the critical value, the wing stalls: lift decreases sharply and drag increases.

pof_42.brief: The stall warning activates just before reaching VS (stall speed).
pof_42.detailed: VS is the stalling speed in a specified configuration. The stall warning (horn/light) activates 5-10% above actual stall speed.

pof_43.brief: Higher wing load increases the minimum flight speed (stall speed).
pof_43.detailed: VS = √(2W/(ρSCLmax)). Higher weight means higher stall speed.

pof_44.brief: Wing twist (washout) causes the inner wing to stall first, maintaining aileron effectiveness.
pof_44.detailed: Washout decreases incidence toward the wingtip. The root stalls first while the tip (with ailerons) continues producing lift. This also reduces induced drag.

pof_45.brief: Stall warning is activated by a change of the stagnation point on the wing's leading edge.
pof_45.detailed: As AoA increases, the stagnation point moves downward and aft on the lower surface, triggering the stall warning device.

pof_46.brief: During spin recovery, keep ailerons neutral, apply opposite rudder, then forward elevator.
pof_46.detailed: Standard PARE recovery: Power idle, Ailerons neutral, Rudder opposite, Elevator forward. Ailerons neutral is critical because applying aileron worsens the spin.

pof_47.brief: Setting flaps to a lower position increases both lift and drag.
pof_47.detailed: Flaps increase camber (and sometimes area), increasing CLmax and lowering stall speed. Drag increases, which steepens the approach path in landing configuration.

pof_48.brief: Increasing aerofoil camber provides a lift-increasing effect.
pof_48.detailed: Flaps increase camber, raising CL for the same AoA. Other lift-increasing methods: increasing wing area, using slats/slots, boundary-layer control.

pof_49.brief: Flaps should not be retracted suddenly near the ground due to sudden lift loss.
pof_49.detailed: Retracting flaps reduces camber, decreasing lift and stall margin. Near the ground at low speed, this could cause the aircraft to sink into the ground.

pof_50.brief: Take-off with flaps in take-off position shortens the take-off run.
pof_50.detailed: Take-off flaps (10-15°) increase CL, lowering lift-off speed. However, increased drag reduces climb gradient.

pof_51.brief: Extending landing flaps increases lift by enlarging profile camber.
pof_51.detailed: Landing flaps (30-40°) significantly increase CLmax (50-80%), lowering approach speed. Increased drag steepens the approach path.

pof_52.brief: Flaps in landing position decrease minimum speed and steepen the glide path.
pof_52.detailed: Lower stall speed allows lower approach speed. Higher drag means steeper descent without gaining speed.

pof_53.brief: Extending flaps increases the wing's CLmax and shifts the CL-α curve upward.
pof_53.detailed: Flaps increase CLmax through increased camber, area, and/or slot effect.

pof_54.brief: Maximum lift and minimum speed are achieved with full flaps extended.
pof_54.detailed: Full flaps give maximum CLmax = lowest stall speed (VSO). The bottom of the white arc on the ASI.

pof_55.brief: Slats and flaps are secondary flight controls used to increase lift at low speeds.
pof_55.detailed: Slats increase critical AoA. Flaps increase camber and drag. Both are used during take-off, approach, and landing.

pof_56.brief: The tailplane ensures longitudinal stability around the lateral axis.
pof_56.detailed: The tailplane produces a downward (negative lift) force counteracting the nose-down pitching moment from the wing, creating stable balance.

pof_57.brief: Longitudinal stability requires the CG forward of the centre of pressure.
pof_57.detailed: CG ahead of the neutral point = stability. If the nose rises, the CP moves forward, creating a nose-down moment restored by the tailplane.

pof_58.brief: An aircraft is stable in pitch if the CG is forward of the neutral point.
pof_58.detailed: Neutral point (NP) is the CG position for neutral stability. CG forward of NP = positive stability. The static margin (NP-CG) determines stability strength.

pof_59.brief: Longitudinal stability is provided by the tailplane acting behind the CG.
pof_59.detailed: The tailplane provides restoring leverage. If the nose pitches up, tailplane down-force increases, pushing the tail down and nose back down.

pof_60.brief: Dihedral (upward wing angle) provides lateral stability.
pof_60.detailed: When a wing drops, the lower wing gets increased AoA and lift, creating a restoring roll moment. Anhedral reduces lateral stability.

pof_61.brief: The elevator controls pitch around the lateral axis.
pof_61.detailed: Pulling back raises the elevator, increasing tail-down force and raising the nose. Effectiveness depends on airspeed.

pof_62.brief: The rudder controls yaw around the vertical axis and coordinates turns.
pof_62.detailed: Right rudder yaws right. Rudder coordinates turns (prevents slip/skid) and counteracts adverse yaw.

pof_63.brief: In a coordinated left turn, left aileron up, right aileron down, with left rudder.
pof_63.detailed: Ailerons roll the aircraft. Adverse yaw requires coordinating rudder input to keep the ball centred.

pof_64.brief: During right turn entry, the nose tends to yaw left due to adverse yaw.
pof_64.detailed: The down-going left aileron creates more drag on the left wing, yawing left. Pilot compensates with right rudder.

pof_65.brief: Angle of incidence is the fixed mounting angle of the wing to the fuselage.
pof_65.detailed: Angle of incidence is a geometric property, not to be confused with angle of attack (which varies in flight).

pof_66.brief: An aft CG reduces longitudinal stability but improves manoeuvrability.
pof_66.detailed: Aft CG reduces the tailplane's restoring moment. The aircraft becomes less stable with lighter elevator forces. The stall margin is also reduced.

pof_67.brief: The CG is the point where the entire weight acts; it must remain within certified limits.
pof_67.detailed: CG limits are in the flight manual. Forward of limit: elevator may not raise nose. Aft of limit: aircraft becomes unstable.

pof_68.brief: MTOM can be limited by either structural limitations or performance limitations.
pof_68.detailed: Structural MTOM is the certificated maximum. Performance-limited MTOM may be lower (runway length, density altitude, climb gradient). The lower of the two applies.

pof_69.brief: VA is the speed at which full control deflection will not exceed the aircraft's load factor limits.
pof_69.detailed: Below VA, the wing stalls before exceeding limit load factor (+3.8g/-1.52g for normal category). Above VA, abrupt inputs could overstress the airframe. VA decreases with weight.

pof_70.brief: The maximum crosswind in the flight manual is a demonstrated value, not a structural limit.
pof_70.detailed: The demonstrated crosswind is the maximum tested during certification. Exceeding it increases the risk of losing directional control.

pof_71.brief: The static vent is located in undisturbed air to measure ambient static pressure.
pof_71.detailed: The static port is on the fuselage side, away from propeller slipstream and wing pressure fields.

pof_72.brief: A blocked static vent causes altimeter, VSI, and ASI to give incorrect readings.
pof_72.detailed: If the static port is blocked: altimeter freezes, VSI shows zero, ASI reads inaccurately. Emergency static source should be selected.

pof_73.brief: The VSI measures the rate of change of static pressure to determine climb/descent rate.
pof_73.detailed: The VSI compares current static pressure (trapped in a calibrated leak) with instantaneous static pressure.

pof_74.brief: The ASI compares pitot (total) pressure with static pressure; the difference is dynamic pressure.
pof_74.detailed: The ASI diaphragm receives pitot pressure, the case receives static. The difference (dynamic pressure, ½ρV²) drives the needle.

pof_75.brief: If both pitot and static are blocked by ice, the ASI acts as an altimeter.
pof_75.detailed: With both blocked, trapped pressure is constant. As the aircraft climbs, the pressure difference decreases, showing decreasing airspeed. Pitot heat is essential.

pof_76.brief: The barometric altimeter uses static pressure relationships from the standard atmosphere.
pof_76.detailed: An evacuated aneroid capsule expands/contracts with static pressure. Calibrated to ISA: 1013.25 hPa at MSL, decreasing with height.

pof_77.brief: QFE setting makes the altimeter read zero on the runway.
pof_77.detailed: QFE is the pressure at the aerodrome. The altimeter shows height above that aerodrome.

pof_78.brief: Tailwind increases the distance to climb to reach a given height.
pof_78.detailed: Tailwind increases ground speed. With the same climb rate, the aircraft travels further horizontally while climbing.

pof_79.brief: Rate of climb decreases when ambient temperature increases.
pof_79.detailed: Higher temperature reduces air density, reducing engine power, propeller efficiency, and lift.

pof_80.brief: An absolute altimeter (radio altimeter) measures actual height above terrain using radio waves.
pof_80.detailed: Radio altimeters measure true height above ground using reflected signal time delay. Used for approaches (DH) and terrain warning.

pof_81.brief: The elevator is the primary pitch control; the trim tab is a secondary control.
pof_81.detailed: Primary controls (elevator, aileron, rudder) directly control attitude. Trim tabs relieve control forces by deflecting to aerodynamically centre the main surface.
