pof_82.brief: Trim works by deflecting a tab on the trailing edge of the control surface.
pof_82.detailed: The tab deflects opposite to the desired surface movement. Airflow hitting the tab creates a force that moves the main surface to neutral.

pof_83.brief: Trim tabs balance the aircraft so no constant control force is needed.
pof_83.detailed: Trim sets the elevator neutral for current speed and CG. Proper trimming reduces pilot fatigue.

pof_84.brief: The turn coordinator uses a gyroscope to indicate roll rate and yaw rate.
pof_84.detailed: The turn coordinator senses both roll and yaw. The slip indicator ball shows coordination (centred = coordinated).

pof_85.brief: The artificial horizon uses a gyroscope to provide an artificial reference to the natural horizon.
pof_85.detailed: The attitude indicator displays pitch and bank relative to the earth's horizon using a vertical gyro.

pof_86.brief: A gyroscope's rigidity in space provides a stable reference regardless of aircraft motion.
pof_86.detailed: Gyroscopic inertia keeps the spin axis fixed. The attitude indicator uses this to maintain a stable artificial horizon.

pof_87.brief: Wing loading is the weight of the aircraft divided by the wing area (W/S).
pof_87.detailed: Higher wing loading = higher stall speed, longer take-off/landing, better gust response. Lower wing loading = better manoeuvrability and shorter field performance.

pof_88.brief: The maximum permissible speed (VNE) must never be exceeded.
pof_88.detailed: VNE (Never Exceed) is marked as a red line on the ASI. Exceeding VNE risks flutter, structural failure, or control surface damage.

pof_89.brief: Manoeuvring speed (VA) is the maximum speed for full, abrupt control deflections.
pof_89.detailed: At or below VA, the aircraft stalls before exceeding limit load factor. Above VA, full deflection could generate loads exceeding structural limits.

pof_90.brief: An upward gust increases load factor by abruptly increasing AoA and lift.
pof_90.detailed: An upward gust changes relative airflow direction, increasing AoA and lift. This additional lift increases the 'g' force on the aircraft.

pof_91.brief: A downward gust reduces effective AoA, momentarily decreasing lift and load factor.
pof_91.detailed: A downward gust changes relative airflow, reducing effective AoA. This decreases lift momentarily, causing a negative load factor change.

pof_92.brief: A constant-speed propeller varies blade pitch to maintain a set RPM.
pof_92.detailed: The constant-speed unit (governor) uses oil pressure to change blade pitch. When power (MAP) increases, the governor increases pitch to maintain RPM.

pof_93.brief: Propeller blade twist ensures a nearly constant effective AoA along the blade.
pof_93.detailed: The tip travels faster than the root, so it needs a lower geometric angle to maintain a constant effective AoA. This ensures uniform thrust.

pof_94.brief: After engine failure, the windmilling propeller generates drag rather than thrust.
pof_94.detailed: A windmilling propeller creates significant drag. Feathering (on constant-speed props) stops windmilling and dramatically reduces drag.

pof_95.brief: During descent at idle, moving the propeller lever back increases pitch and sink rate.
pof_95.detailed: Coarse pitch increases blade angle, presenting a larger face to the airflow, increasing drag and sink rate for a steeper descent.

pof_96.brief: In a left spin with a clockwise engine, adding power enforces the spin.
pof_96.detailed: A clockwise engine produces left-turning tendency from torque and P-factor. In a left spin, these compound the spin direction. Recovery requires power idle.

pof_97.brief: Wing load is mass per wing surface area (kg/m²).
pof_97.detailed: Wing loading = mass / wing area. It determines stall speed, turn radius, and field performance.

pof_98.brief: After increasing AoA at best gliding speed, lift and drag initially increase.
pof_98.detailed: Increasing AoA increases CL and CD simultaneously. Initially both lift and drag rise together.

pof_99.brief: In a turn, the horizontal component of lift provides centripetal force.
pof_99.detailed: In a coordinated turn, lift is increased and its horizontal component acts as centripetal force toward the turn center. Total lift supports both weight and the centrifugal component.

pof_100.brief: The spin tendency is greater with an aft centre of gravity position.
pof_100.detailed: An aft CG reduces stability and makes the aircraft more prone to entering and staying in a spin. Forward CG improves spin recovery characteristics.

ops_1.brief: Flight time is the period from first movement for takeoff to final rest.
ops_1.detailed: Under EASA Part-FCL, flight time is the total time from the moment an aircraft first moves for the purpose of taking off until it finally comes to rest at the end of the flight. Block time (engine start to shutdown) is different.

ops_2.brief: For scheduled overwater flights where land cannot be reached, life jackets or lifeboats must be available for all passengers.
ops_2.detailed: EASA regulations (Part-NCO and Part-CAT) require life jackets or life rafts for all occupants when flying beyond gliding distance from land. The specific distance depends on the aircraft type and the availability of ditching equipment.

ops_3.brief: In a spin, the aircraft is stalled and autorotating; recovery requires opposite rudder. In a spiral dive, the aircraft is not stalled and speed increases rapidly.
ops_3.detailed: A spin involves an asymmetric stall with autorotation. Recovery: power idle, ailerons neutral, opposite rudder, forward elevator. A spiral dive is a steep turning descent without stall; recovery involves reducing power and levelling the wings.

ops_4.brief: When about to stall, reduce pull on the elevator (lower the nose) and increase power.
ops_4.detailed: Stall recovery: reduce angle of attack by lowering the nose (forward elevator), apply full power, and level the wings. This breaks the stall and regains flying speed.

ops_5.brief: Apply carburettor heat when the temperature indicator moves near the yellow range to prevent carburettor icing.
ops_5.detailed: Carburettor icing occurs when moisture in the air freezes in the venturi due to evaporative cooling. The yellow range on the carburettor temperature gauge indicates potential icing conditions. Applying carb heat reduces the temperature drop and prevents ice formation.

ops_6.brief: Carburettor icing is the most common type of icing for VFR flights.
ops_6.detailed: Carburettor icing can occur even on warm days (up to 20°C) when humidity is high, because the evaporative cooling in the venturi can drop temperatures below freezing. It is a greater risk than airframe icing for most VFR flights in light aircraft.

ops_7.brief: During refuelling: ignition and magnetos OFF, attach ground cable (earthing).
ops_7.detailed: Refuelling safety: the ground cable prevents static discharge sparks. Ignition/magnetos off prevents accidental engine start. No smoking, no open flames. Fuel type and quantity must be checked.

ops_9.brief: A rough-running engine after descending from 8000 ft may be caused by not enriching the mixture during descent.
ops_9.detailed: At altitude, the mixture must be leaned. During descent, the air becomes denser, so the mixture becomes leaner. If not enriched, the engine may run rough or lose power due to an excessively lean mixture.

ops_10.brief: Bird strikes are most common in spring and autumn during migration seasons.
ops_10.detailed: Bird migration peaks in spring (March-May) and autumn (August-October). Birds are also more active near airports in spring/summer breeding seasons. The risk is highest at low altitudes during take-off and landing.

ops_11.brief: A blocked static pressure system can cause a malfunction of the altitude indicator.
ops_11.detailed: The altimeter relies on static pressure. A blocked static port causes the altimeter to freeze at the last reading. The VSI also fails (shows zero). The ASI gives incorrect readings.

ops_12.brief: When inadvertently entering an icing area, leave the area as soon as possible.
ops_12.detailed: The primary action in icing conditions is to exit the area by changing altitude or course. Activate de-icing equipment (pitot heat, propeller anti-ice) and avoid using flaps which increase the icing surface.

ops_13.brief: Wing area icing results in a higher stall speed.
ops_13.detailed: Ice on the wing disrupts the smooth airflow, reducing CLmax. With reduced CLmax, the stall speed increases (VS = √(2W/(ρSCLmax))). Higher approach speeds are required.

ops_14.brief: If the electrical flap motor fails, first check the flaps' circuit breaker.
ops_14.detailed: If a circuit breaker has tripped, resetting it may restore flap operation. If not, the emergency flap extension system (if available) or manual extension should be used per the flight manual.

ops_15.brief: All snow and ice must be removed before take-off to ensure an undisrupted, smooth airflow over the wings.
ops_15.detailed: Even a thin layer of frost or snow disrupts the smooth airflow required for lift. It increases drag, reduces lift, adds weight, and raises stall speed. A 'clean aircraft' is mandatory per regulations.

ops_16.brief: Sudden downdrafts are the greatest danger to an aircraft during a thunderstorm.
ops_16.detailed: Thunderstorm downdrafts can exceed 3000 ft/min and force an aircraft into the ground even with full power. Avoiding thunderstorms by at least 5 NM is the best strategy.

ops_17.brief: Wrinkles in fuselage skin may indicate previous structural damage or overstress.
ops_17.detailed: Wrinkles in the skin indicate that the structure has been loaded beyond its yield point. This may have occurred during a heavy landing, turbulence, or ground handling incident. The aircraft must be inspected by a qualified engineer.

ops_18.brief: Haze can lead to spatial disorientation, especially when flying over water.
ops_18.detailed: Haze reduces contrast and eliminates the visible horizon. Over water, the lack of ground features makes it difficult to judge attitude and altitude, which can lead to disorientation and loss of control.

ops_19.brief: If the rudder is stuck in neutral, manoeuvre with elevator and aileron, using small bank angles.
ops_19.detailed: Without rudder, turns must be coordinated using aileron and elevator only. Use shallow bank angles to avoid adverse yaw. Land at the nearest suitable airfield.

ops_20.brief: To minimise noise, fly a high approach with minimum power, late descent and late configuration along established routes.
ops_20.detailed: Noise abatement procedures: use the lowest practical power setting, keep the aircraft high until necessary to descend, reduce power early, and avoid low-level manoeuvring over built-up areas.

ops_21.brief: Turns at low altitude above villages should be avoided in horizontal flight for noise abatement.
ops_21.detailed: Level turns at low altitude project engine noise over a wider area. Noise-sensitive areas should be overflown at the highest possible altitude, avoiding turns at low level.

ops_22.brief: Piston engines are susceptible to carburettor fire, which can occur during starting or hot-soak conditions.
ops_22.detailed: A carburettor fire happens when the fuel-air mixture ignites in the induction system rather than the cylinders. It is most likely during engine start (backfire) or after shutdown (hot-soak with residual fuel).

ops_23.brief: Pumping the throttle in cold weather may flood the engine and cause carburettor icing.
ops_23.detailed: Repeated throttle pumping injects excess fuel, flooding the cylinders. The evaporative cooling from excess fuel can also cause carburettor icing. The correct cold-start procedure is in the flight manual.

ops_24.brief: Carbon monoxide (CO) is the most dangerous gas during an engine fire.
ops_24.detailed: CO is odourless, colourless, and highly toxic. It binds to haemoglobin more readily than oxygen, causing hypoxia and incapacitation. CO can enter the cabin through a leaking exhaust or heater system.

ops_25.brief: Engine fire when fire extinguisher is used from outside: engine fuel shut-off valve closed, engine cutoff, master switch off.
ops_25.detailed: The emergency procedure for an engine fire on the ground: close the fuel shut-off valve, cut off the engine (mixture idle cut-off, ignition off), turn the master switch off, and evacuate. An external fire extinguisher may be used.

ops_26.brief: Halon fire extinguisher: disarm safety, hold upright, aim at base of fire from 1-1.5 m, use side-to-side motion.
ops_26.detailed: The correct P-A-S-S technique: Pull the pin, Aim at the base of the fire, Squeeze the handle, Sweep side to side. Halon is effective for class B (fuel) and C (electrical) fires but is being phased out.

ops_27.brief: Water is the least suitable extinguishing agent for aircraft fires due to electrical shock risk and fuel spreading.
ops_27.detailed: Water conducts electricity (risk of shock from electrical systems) and can spread fuel fires. CO₂, dry powder, or Halon are preferred for aircraft fires.

ops_28.brief: In case of an electrical cable fire during flight, turn off the master switch first.
ops_28.detailed: Cutting electrical power removes the source of ignition. After turning off the master switch, the pilot should proceed according to the flight manual and consider landing at the nearest airport.

ops_29.brief: For a burning electrical wire: master switch off, proceed according to the flight manual.
ops_29.detailed: After isolating the electrical system, the fire should subside due to lack of power. The pilot should then plan for a precautionary landing as soon as practical.

ops_30.brief: If smoke emerges from behind the panel and an engine fire is suspected, turn off the master switch.
ops_30.detailed: Smoke in the cockpit is a serious emergency. Turning off the master switch isolates the electrical system. If the fire persists (engine fire), proceed with engine fire procedures.

ops_31.brief: Wind shear is a vertical or horizontal change of wind speed and wind direction over a short distance.
ops_31.detailed: Wind shear is hazardous because it causes sudden changes in headwind/tailwind component, affecting indicated airspeed and lift. It is commonly associated with fronts, thunderstorms, inversions, and mountain waves.

ops_32.brief: After take-off into decreasing headwind (wind shear), the aircraft flies below the estimated climb path.
ops_32.detailed: A decreasing headwind reduces indicated airspeed and lift. The aircraft sinks below the intended flight path. Recovery requires immediate power application and lowering the nose to maintain airspeed.

ops_33.brief: An increase in headwind of 20 kt in a microburst could be followed by a downdraft and tailwind of up to 40 kt.
ops_33.detailed: Microbursts produce a strong downdraft that spreads out horizontally on reaching the ground. An aircraft flying through experiences: increasing headwind (lift), then downdraft, then increasing tailwind (lift loss). The total wind change can be double the initial headwind gain.

ops_34.brief: Wind shear can be expected during an inversion, where wind speed and direction change rapidly across the inversion layer.
ops_34.detailed: Inversions create a stable layer with a large temperature gradient. The wind above the inversion can be much stronger and from a different direction than below. This creates significant wind shear when climbing or descending through the inversion.

ops_35.brief: During approach with decreasing headwind (windshear), the path becomes lower and TAS decreases.
ops_35.detailed: A decreasing headwind reduces the lift, causing the aircraft to descend below the glide path. True airspeed also decreases initially due to the reduced headwind component.

ops_36.brief: Gusts are the most hazardous weather phenomenon during approach and landing near frontal thunderstorms.
ops_36.detailed: Thunderstorm gusts can exceed 50 kt, causing sudden changes in airspeed and lift. Wind direction changes can exceed 90°. The gust front can arrive well before the rain.

ops_37.brief: Wind shear is expected during climb through an inversion layer.
ops_37.detailed: Climbing through an inversion exposes the aircraft to sudden changes in wind speed and direction. This can result in a significant performance loss as the aircraft transitions between air masses.

ops_38.brief: Avoid wind shear by not taking off or landing during the passage of heavy showers.
ops_38.detailed: The best avoidance strategy for wind shear is to delay take-off or landing until thunderstorm activity has passed. Wait at least 30 minutes after a heavy shower passes the airfield.

ops_39.brief: A much stronger than expected airspeed rise after lift-off may be followed by a decreased climb rate and airspeed.
ops_39.detailed: This pattern indicates entering a gust front or wind shear. The initial headwind gain increases airspeed, but the aircraft then encounters a downdraft and/or tailwind, causing reduced climb performance.

ops_40.brief: The greatest danger in mountainous terrain is downdrafts exceeding climb capability.
ops_40.detailed: Strong downdrafts on the lee side of ridges may exceed the aircraft's climb performance, leading to terrain impact. This is the primary hazard of mountain flying.

ops_41.brief: When crossing a mountain pass at the end of a narrow valley, reach the required altitude shortly before the pass.
ops_41.detailed: Crossing passes requires reaching a safe altitude before the pass to avoid terrain. The required crossing altitude should be achieved before entering the pass, not after, due to rising terrain and potential downdrafts.

ops_42.brief: Wake turbulence develops as the aircraft lifts off (rotation).
ops_42.detailed: Wake turbulence (wingtip vortices) starts when the wing generates lift. During take-off, the vortices begin at rotation and are strongest when the aircraft is heavy, slow, and clean.

ops_43.brief: Wake turbulence develops after rotation during departure.
ops_43.detailed: As the nose rotates and the wing generates lift at low speed, the high angle of attack produces strong wingtip vortices. These trail behind and descend below the flight path.

ops_44.brief: Wake turbulence intensity depends on the weight of the aeroplane.
ops_44.detailed: Heavier aircraft produce stronger wingtip vortices. The vortex strength is proportional to the weight and inversely proportional to the speed and span. Heavy, slow aircraft (landing or departing) produce the strongest wake.

ops_45.brief: Wake turbulence is particularly strong at a high aeroplane weight.
ops_45.detailed: Wake turbulence is most severe when the generating aircraft is heavy, slow, and in a clean configuration. This is why heavy airliners produce dangerous wake vortices for light aircraft.

ops_46.brief: To avoid wake turbulence when landing behind a larger aircraft, make a shallow approach and land beyond the heavy aircraft's touchdown point.
ops_46.detailed: Wingtip vortices sink and move laterally. Landing beyond the preceding aircraft's touchdown point keeps the light aircraft above the wake. A shallow approach also maintains a higher altitude for longer.

ops_47.brief: Wake turbulence is expected below and behind the generating aircraft's flight path.
ops_47.detailed: Wingtip vortices descend at about 500-800 ft/min and move laterally with the crosswind. The strongest wake is behind and slightly below the generating aircraft.

ops_48.brief: The minimum separation behind a larger wake turbulence category aircraft is 2 minutes.
ops_48.detailed: ICAO wake turbulence categories: Heavy (H) > 136,000 kg, Medium (M) 7,000-136,000 kg, Light (L) < 7,000 kg. The required separation for a Light behind a Medium or Heavy is 2 minutes.

ops_49.brief: A harvested field is the most suitable terrain for a forced landing.
ops_49.detailed: Harvested fields provide a relatively smooth, firm surface with fewer obstacles. Crops have been removed, reducing the risk of the aircraft nosing over. The field is typically flat and open.

ops_50.brief: A large, even field in the direction of the wind, without obstacles, is most adequate for a precautionary landing.
ops_50.detailed: The ideal off-field landing site is: (1) into wind to reduce ground speed, (2) long and flat, (3) firm and dry, (4) free of obstacles (fences, power lines, trees), (5) accessible for rescue.

ops_51.brief: During an emergency landing on water, expect a severe impact with a strong nose-over tendency.
ops_51.detailed: Ditching: the aircraft should be landed at the lowest possible speed, parallel to the swell direction (along the waves). Impact can be violent, and the aircraft may flip over. Life vests should be donned before impact but inflated after leaving the aircraft.

ops_52.brief: The correct approach to an unprepared field involves a terrain investigation to determine approach points and landing direction.
ops_52.detailed: Overfly the field at a safe altitude to assess the surface, length, obstacles, and wind direction. Plan the approach path carefully, and if any doubts remain, select an alternative field.

ops_53.brief: A harvested cornfield is suitable for an off-field landing.
ops_53.detailed: Harvested fields offer a firm surface without crops that could cause the aircraft to nose over. Avoid fields with standing crops, livestock, power lines, or fences.

ops_54.brief: A meadow without livestock is most suitable for an off-field landing.
ops_54.detailed: A mown meadow provides a good surface without standing crops. Livestock should be avoided for safety reasons (risk to animals and pilot).

ops_55.brief: When weather drops below VMC minimums, maintain visual ground contact and land at the nearest suitable airfield.
ops_55.detailed: VFR pilots encountering deteriorating weather should maintain ground contact, turn back if possible, or land at the nearest airfield. Climbing through cloud requires an instrument rating.

ops_56.brief: If unable to reach the destination before nightfall, land at the nearest airfield during daylight.
ops_56.detailed: Night VFR may not be permitted depending on the pilot's ratings. If the pilot is not night-rated, the safest action is to land before sunset at the nearest suitable airfield.

ops_57.brief: For extended overwater flights, carry life vests or a life raft for all occupants.
ops_57.detailed: Regulations require life jackets or rafts for all occupants when flying beyond gliding distance from land. The equipment must be readily accessible and occupants must be briefed on its use.

ops_58.brief: Overheated brakes can cause tyres to burst in the radial direction or along the tread.
ops_58.detailed: Brake heat can ignite tyre rubber or cause the tyre to burst from internal pressure build-up. The burst is often radial (sidewall) or along the tread. Park with the brakes cool and approach hot brakes from front or back (not the side) if inspection is needed.

ops_59.brief: Approach hot brakes and wheels from the front or back side – the sides of the tyre are the most likely burst direction.
ops_59.detailed: Tyres burst radially (sidewall). Approaching from the front or back minimises the risk of injury. Use gloves, stay clear of the tyre sidewall, and wait for brakes to cool.

ops_60.brief: After a forced landing in uneven terrain, check the aircraft for possible damage before leaving it.
ops_60.detailed: Inspect the aircraft for structural damage, fuel leaks, and electrical hazards. If the ELT has not activated, activate it manually. Stay with the aircraft unless it is unsafe.

ops_61.brief: An Emergency Locator Transmitter (ELT) automatically transmits in case of an accident to help determine the location.
ops_61.detailed: ELTs operate on 121.500 MHz and/or 406 MHz (Cospas-Sarsat). They activate automatically on impact and transmit a distress signal to aid search and rescue. Portable ELTs can be activated manually.

ops_62.brief: In a ditching, life vests should be inflated after disembarking the aircraft.
ops_62.detailed: If inflated inside the aircraft, the vest could make it difficult to exit through a narrow opening or trap the wearer in a submerged cabin. Don the vest before impact but inflate it only after exit.

ops_63.brief: Wet grass increases both take-off distance and landing distance.
ops_63.detailed: Wet grass reduces tyre friction (increased rolling resistance for take-off, reduced braking for landing). It also increases drag on the aircraft during the ground roll.

ops_64.brief: A runway is considered contaminated when at least 25% of the surface is covered with ice or snow.
ops_64.detailed: Contaminated runway definition per ICAO: more than 25% of the runway surface area is covered by standing water, slush, snow, or ice. Performance calculations must account for runway contamination.

ops_65.brief: If tyres are getting deeply stuck in wet, softened ground, do not take off because rolling resistance is too high.
ops_65.detailed: Soft ground increases rolling resistance, preventing the aircraft from reaching take-off speed. Attempting take-off could cause damage or a rejected take-off into obstacles.

ops_66.brief: For landing on an icy paved runway: directional control with rudder, elevator fully up, minimum braking.
ops_66.detailed: On ice, directional control is maintained with the rudder. The elevator should be held fully back to maximise weight on the tail wheel (nose wheel aircraft: back pressure reduces nose wheel loading). Braking should be minimal to avoid skidding.

ops_67.brief: Wet snow on a runway increases rolling resistance during take-off.
ops_67.detailed: Wet snow creates drag on the tyres and can also create suction, increasing the take-off distance required. If slush is present, there is also a risk of hydroplaning.

ops_68.brief: When hydroplaning is suspected, avoid braking and maintain directional control with rudder.
ops_68.detailed: Hydroplaning occurs when the tyre rides on a film of water, losing contact with the runway. Braking in this condition is ineffective and can cause loss of control. Light braking or aerodynamic braking (elevator up) should be used instead.

ops_69.brief: After a heavy rain shower, the landing aircraft faces a longer braking distance due to aquaplaning.
ops_69.detailed: Aquaplaning (hydroplaning) on a wet runway significantly reduces braking effectiveness. Land at the slowest safe speed, use minimum braking, and expect longer landing distance.

ops_70.brief: If collision with an obstacle is unavoidable during a forced landing, steer the aircraft fuselage away from the obstacle to let the wing absorb the impact.
ops_70.detailed: The wing is designed to absorb impact energy and acts as a crumple zone. Directing the fuselage away from the obstacle allows the wing to strike first, protecting the cockpit occupants.

perf_1.brief: Exceeding the maximum allowed aircraft mass is not permissible and is essentially dangerous.
perf_1.detailed: Operating above the maximum certificated mass reduces structural margins, increases stall speed, lengthens take-off/landing distances, reduces climb performance, and can lead to loss of control.

perf_2.brief: An overweight aircraft risks structural damage and impaired handling.
perf_2.detailed: Overweight operation stresses the airframe beyond design limits, reduces the safety margin for turbulence and manoeuvring, impairs climb and cruise performance, and increases the risk of structural failure.

perf_3.brief: If minimum weight cannot be achieved, additional ballast must be added.
perf_3.detailed: Minimum weight is specified for CG range compliance and structural reasons. Ballast (secured weight) is added in designated locations to bring the aircraft to the minimum weight.

perf_4.brief: The CG must be located between the forward and rear CG limits.
perf_4.detailed: The CG limits are specified in the flight manual. Keeping the CG within limits ensures adequate longitudinal stability and elevator authority for all phases of flight.

perf_5.brief: A rear CG position decreases stability (reduced static margin).
perf_5.detailed: An aft CG reduces the tailplane's restoring moment. The aircraft becomes more manoeuvrable (lighter elevator forces) but less stable. Stall and spin characteristics worsen.

perf_6.brief: The aircraft must be loaded so the CG stays within limits for both stability and controllability.
perf_6.detailed: CG limits ensure both stability (return to original attitude after disturbance) and controllability (sufficient elevator authority for pitch control in all phases).

perf_7.brief: An aft CG beyond the limit makes the aircraft uncontrollable in certain circumstances.
perf_7.detailed: With the CG aft of the limit, the aircraft lacks sufficient longitudinal stability and may be impossible to recover from a stall or spin. The manufacturer's CG limits are mandatory.

perf_8.brief: Basic empty mass includes the aircraft plus standard items (unusable fuel, full oil).
perf_8.detailed: Basic empty mass (BEM) = mass of the aircraft + unusable fuel + full operating fluids (oil) + standard equipment. Useful load = MTOM - BEM.

perf_9.brief: The total weight at any particular time is called gross weight.
perf_9.detailed: Gross weight (all-up weight) = basic empty mass + payload + usable fuel. It varies during flight as fuel is consumed. Must be within MTOM at take-off and MLM at landing.

perf_10.brief: Empty mass includes the mass of all installed instruments.
perf_10.detailed: Empty mass (or basic empty mass) includes the aircraft structure, engine, instruments, avionics, seats, upholstery, and all standard equipment.

perf_11.brief: The density of AVGAS 100LL at 15°C is 0.72 kg/l.
perf_11.detailed: AVGAS 100LL specific gravity = 0.72. 1 litre = 0.72 kg. Conversion: litres × 0.72 = kg.

perf_12.detailed: 1 kg = 2.20462 lb (approx 2.205). Many aircraft use pounds for weight and balance.

perf_13.brief: Unsecured baggage/cargo shift may cause uncontrollable attitudes, structural damage, and injury risk.
perf_13.detailed: Load shift changes the CG position. Rearward shift could make aircraft uncontrollable. Forward shift could make it impossible to flare. All items must be properly secured.

perf_14.brief: Loads must be adequately secured to avoid CG movement in flight.
perf_14.detailed: Even small CG shifts affect handling. Cargo, baggage, and equipment must be tied down.

perf_15.brief: Total weight acts vertically through the centre of gravity.
perf_15.detailed: The CG is the point where the entire weight can be considered to act. It is the balance point.

perf_16.brief: The CG defines the point on the longitudinal axis from which moments are measured.
perf_16.detailed: CG position relative to the wing's centre of pressure determines longitudinal stability.

perf_17.brief: The datum is a reference point on the longitudinal axis from which all arms are measured.
perf_17.detailed: The datum is an arbitrary reference point (often the firewall). Stations measured from it.

perf_18.brief: Moment = mass × arm. Product of a mass and its distance from the datum.
perf_18.detailed: Total moment / total mass = CG location. Moment determines the balance.

perf_19.brief: Balance arm (lever arm) is the distance from the datum to the CG of an item.
perf_19.detailed: The balance arm (or station) is used to compute total moment in weight and balance.

perf_20.brief: Before weighing an aircraft, drain all usable fuel.
perf_20.detailed: Weighing requires an empty aircraft with all usable fuel drained and fluids at specified level.

perf_21.brief: After changing power setting at constant altitude, the elevator trim will not need adjustment.
perf_21.detailed: If properly trimmed for level flight, a power change will change pitch attitude but the trim setting remains correct for that airspeed.

perf_22.brief: After fuel burn, CG moves aft as fuel is consumed from the forward station.
perf_22.detailed: New CG = (total moment after burn) / (total mass after burn). CG movement depends on the station of the fuel tank.

perf_23.brief: After fuel burn, CG shifts forward: (total moment - fuel moment) / (total mass - fuel mass).
perf_23.detailed: Takeoff: 746 kg × 0.371 m = 276.766 kg·m. Fuel: 30.5 L × 0.72 kg/L = 21.96 kg at 0.45 m = 9.882 kg·m. After: mass = 724.04 kg, moment = 266.884 kg·m, CG = 36.9 cm.

perf_24.detailed: Original moment: 151200 lb·in. Added fuel: 310 lb × 90 in = 27900 lb·in. New total: 179100 lb·in.

perf_25.brief: For normal category (CS-23), aeroplane maximum weight is below 5700 kg, no aerobatics/spinning, bank angles limited to 60°.
perf_25.detailed: Normal category: MTOM < 5670 kg. Load factor limits of +3.8g/-1.52g limit bank angle to about 60° in level flight.

perf_26.brief: When climbing at constant speed and power, lift is less than weight.
perf_26.detailed: In a steady climb, the lift vector is slightly less than weight because thrust supports part of the weight.

perf_27.brief: A steep turn at constant altitude and airspeed requires increased power and angle of attack.
perf_27.detailed: In a level turn, load factor increases (n = 1/cos(φ)). More lift needed, so higher AoA and power.

perf_28.brief: Power changes affect pitch because the thrust line is not aligned with the drag line.
perf_28.detailed: The thrust line is typically offset from the CG, creating a pitching moment when power changes.

perf_29.brief: High temperatures reduce air density, lowering density altitude and decreasing performance.
perf_29.detailed: High temperature = low density = higher density altitude = reduced power, longer take-off/landing.

perf_30.brief: Higher flap setting decreases ground roll and lift-off speed but reduces climb gradient.
perf_30.detailed: Take-off flaps increase lift at low speed but increase drag, reducing climb gradient.

perf_31.brief: Headwind reduces take-off distance (more airflow over the wing, higher initial relative wind).
perf_31.detailed: Headwind increases the relative airflow, allowing the aircraft to reach flying speed in a shorter roll.

perf_32.brief: Water on the wing disturbs the airflow, decreasing aerodynamic performance.
perf_32.detailed: Rain or standing water on the wing disrupts the boundary layer, reducing CLmax and increasing drag.

perf_33.brief: Grass increases rolling resistance, increasing both take-off and landing distance.
perf_33.detailed: Grass runways increase rolling resistance compared to paved surfaces. Take-off distance increases and braking effectiveness decreases.

perf_34.brief: A strong headwind shortens both take-off and landing distance.
perf_34.detailed: Headwind reduces ground speed required to fly and the landing roll. Tailwind has the opposite effect.

perf_35.brief: Reduced air density (high density altitude) increases the full-throttle take-off distance.
perf_35.detailed: Low density reduces engine power and propeller efficiency. Higher TAS needed for same IAS.

perf_36.brief: A downsloping runway increases take-off distance required but decreases landing distance.
perf_36.detailed: Downslope helps deceleration (landing) but hinders acceleration to flying speed (take-off).

perf_37.brief: Even light frost on a wing increases weight and drag and significantly reduces lift.
perf_37.detailed: Frost disrupts the smooth airflow, causing early boundary layer separation. Lift reduced by 20-30%.

perf_38.brief: A 15% increase in landing weight increases landing distance by approximately 25%.
perf_38.detailed: Landing distance increases at roughly 1.5-2 times the percentage weight increase.

perf_39.brief: If TAS is significantly less than GS, there is a tailwind.
perf_39.detailed: GS = TAS + tailwind component (or - headwind). GS > TAS = tailwind.

perf_40.brief: Taking off into the wind reduces the take-off distance.
perf_40.detailed: Headwind increases relative airflow, allowing lift-off with shorter ground roll.

perf_41.brief: A 10% increase in take-off mass increases take-off distance to 50 ft by approximately 20%.
perf_41.detailed: Take-off distance increases disproportionately to weight. Heavier = slower acceleration and higher lift-off speed.

perf_42.brief: Approach on a hot summer day: fly with normal IAS (correct margin above stall).
perf_42.detailed: On a hot day, TAS is higher for a given IAS, but stall speed also increases. Normal IAS ensures correct margin.

perf_43.brief: Vx is the speed for best angle of climb (minimum horizontal distance to gain altitude).
perf_43.detailed: Vx is used for obstacle clearance after take-off. It is lower than Vy.

perf_44.brief: Increasing gross weight decreases the rate of climb.
perf_44.detailed: Rate of climb = (excess power) / weight. Heavier = less excess power available.

perf_45.brief: Steady flight is unaccelerated flight where thrust = drag and lift = weight.
perf_45.detailed: In steady flight, the four forces are balanced. Any imbalance results in acceleration.

perf_46.brief: Vy is the speed for best rate of climb (maximum altitude gain per unit time).
perf_46.detailed: Vy gives the fastest climb to altitude. Higher than Vx.

perf_47.brief: Vy (best rate of climb speed) is used to reach a desired altitude in minimum time.
perf_47.detailed: Vy provides the maximum excess power, giving the highest climb rate in ft/min.

perf_48.brief: A wing stalls when the angle of attack is increased too far (beyond the critical AoA).
perf_48.detailed: Stall is purely a function of AoA, not airspeed. Can occur at any speed if critical AoA is exceeded.

perf_49.detailed: Vref (approach speed) = 1.3 × VSO. Provides 30% margin above stall.

perf_50.brief: Increasing approach speed above the POH recommended speed increases landing distance.
perf_50.detailed: Higher approach speed = more kinetic energy to dissipate. Landing distance increases with speed squared.

perf_51.brief: Flaps decrease the stalling speed (lower VSO).
perf_51.detailed: Flaps increase CLmax, which reduces stall speed.

perf_52.brief: The shortest landing distance at 10°C, 3000 ft PA, 9 kt headwind is approximately 370 m.
perf_52.detailed: This value is read from the landing distance chart in the flight manual for the given conditions.

perf_53.brief: Fuel consumption at 6000 ft, standard temp, 60% power is approximately 18.5 l/h.
perf_53.detailed: Cruise performance tables provide fuel consumption for given altitude, power, and mixture.

perf_54.brief: Cruise performance table data refers to the maximum aeroplane mass and correctly leaned mixture.
perf_54.detailed: Actual fuel consumption varies with actual weight and mixture setting.

perf_55.brief: Increasing gross weight decreases the rate of climb.
perf_55.detailed: Higher weight = more lift needed = more drag = reduced excess power for climbing.

perf_56.brief: Carburettor heat reduces engine RPM because warmer air is less dense, reducing oxygen available for combustion.
perf_56.detailed: When carb heat is selected, air passes through a heat exchanger before entering the carburettor. The heated air is less dense (fewer oxygen molecules per volume), which reduces the engine power output. The mixture becomes richer (same fuel flow with less oxygen), further contributing to the RPM drop. This is normal - RPM should recover when carb heat is turned off. Apply carb heat when icing conditions exist (temp 0 to -12 C, visible moisture).

perf_57.brief: Higher ambient temperature decreases both air density and engine power available.
perf_57.detailed: Temperature increase reduces density, reducing engine power and aerodynamic efficiency.

perf_58.brief: Temperature, pressure, density, and humidity affect aircraft performance.
perf_58.detailed: These four variables determine air density, which affects engine power, lift, and drag.

perf_59.brief: Maximum endurance is achieved at lower speed than max range, at the lowest safe altitude.
perf_59.detailed: Maximum endurance = minimum fuel per time = minimum drag speed (Vmd).

perf_60.brief: With a tailwind, optimum TAS for best range is slightly lower than in still air.
perf_60.detailed: Tailwind reduces the fuel-per-distance benefit of higher TAS. The still-air best-range TAS only applies in zero wind conditions.

perf_61.brief: When gliding for max range, heavier aircraft requires higher airspeed and steeper glide path.
perf_61.detailed: Glide range depends on L/D. Heavier = higher TAS for best L/D = steeper path.

perf_62.brief: With L/D 6:1 at 6000 ft, maximum glide distance = 6 NM.

perf_63.brief: Maximum range in a piston aircraft is achieved at just above the minimum drag speed.
perf_63.detailed: Best range speed = speed for max L/D, slightly above Vmd.

perf_64.brief: Maximum Elevation Figure (MEF) = highest elevation + 1000 ft safety margin, rounded up.
perf_64.detailed: MEF on VFR charts = highest point in 30′×30′ area + 1000 ft, rounded to next higher 100 ft.

perf_65.brief: VFR semicircular rules are based on magnetic track.
perf_65.detailed: Magnetic track 000-179° = odd FLs, 180-359° = even FLs. Applies above transition altitude.

perf_66.brief: TC 181°, VAR 3°E: MC = 178° (southerly). Lowest VFR FL = 065.
perf_66.detailed: MC = TC - VAR(E) = 181 - 3 = 178°. Southerly track = odd FLs. FL 065 is the lowest.

perf_68.brief: Climb from 1500 ft at 600 ft/min, GS 85 MPH: distance from aerodrome = 12 NM.
perf_68.detailed: Time to climb = (target altitude - elevation) / ROC. Distance = time × GS.

perf_69.detailed: Convert lb to kg (divide by 2.205), then kg to litres (divide by density 0.72).

perf_72.brief: Total fuel = start-up/taxi/run-up + trip + reserve = 32 Imp gals.
perf_72.detailed: Fuel planning includes start/taxi/run-up, trip, and 30-minute reserve.

perf_73.brief: 'Z' in METAR timestamps denotes Zulu time (UTC).
perf_73.detailed: The 'Z' appended to aviation time stamps indicates Zulu time, synonymous with UTC (Coordinated Universal Time).

perf_74.brief: EOBT in the ATS flight plan is specified in UTC.
perf_74.detailed: All aviation times are in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC).

perf_75.brief: Cross-border flights require a flight plan.
perf_75.detailed: ATS flight plan is typically mandatory for international flights.

perf_76.brief: A flight plan can be filed in-flight at the Flight Information Service (FIS).
perf_76.detailed: In-flight flight plans can be submitted via radio to the FIS unit.

agk_1.brief: An overstressed aircraft must have an appropriate entry made in the aircraft technical log.
agk_1.detailed: When an aircraft has been overstressed (exceeded limit loads), the pilot must record it in the technical log. The aircraft must then be inspected by a qualified engineer before the next flight to ensure no structural damage occurred.

agk_2.brief: Maintenance not concurring with the maintenance schedule invalidates the previous certificate of release to service.
agk_2.detailed: The Certificate of Release to Service (CRS) is only valid when maintenance is performed according to the approved maintenance schedule. Non-compliant maintenance breaks the chain of airworthiness.

agk_3.brief: Max permissible RPM drop during magneto check is per the flight manual.
agk_3.detailed: Limits vary by engine type. Always check the aircraft flight manual. Common limits exist but the correct answer is to consult the manual.

agk_4.brief: Electrical fuel pumps shall be switched on according to the flight manual.
agk_4.detailed: The electric fuel pump is used for take-off, landing, and during critical phases to prevent vapour lock and ensure fuel pressure. The specific operation is defined in the POH/AFM.

agk_5.brief: If the ASI is unserviceable, the aircraft may only be operated when it has been repaired.
agk_5.detailed: For VFR flight, certain instruments may be inoperative per the Master Minimum Equipment List (MMEL). However, the airspeed indicator is a mandatory instrument for all flights.

agk_6.brief: Damage to any supporting parts (primary structure) causes loss of airworthiness.
agk_6.detailed: Damage to primary structural components (spars, longerons, bulkheads, control surface hinges) renders the aircraft unairworthy. The aircraft must not be flown until repaired and certified.

agk_7.brief: The mass and balance report must be certified by any competent person.
agk_7.detailed: The mass and balance report can be completed by the pilot or any person trained in the procedure. The pilot-in-command is ultimately responsible for ensuring the aircraft is within limits.

agk_8.brief: Wing thickness is the distance between the upper and lower side at the thickest part.
agk_8.detailed: The thickness-to-chord ratio (t/c) defines the aerofoil's thickness. A thick aerofoil has higher drag but can achieve higher CLmax. The maximum thickness is typically at 25-30% chord.

agk_9.brief: A tubular steel construction with a non-self-supporting skin is grid construction.
agk_9.detailed: Grid (truss) construction uses welded steel tubes forming the framework. The fabric skin is not structural; it only provides aerodynamic shape. Used in many classic aircraft.

agk_10.brief: A construction of frames and straps with a supporting skin is monocoque or semi-monocoque.
agk_10.detailed: In monocoque construction, the skin carries all structural loads. In semi-monocoque, the skin is reinforced by stringers, frames, and bulkheads. Most modern aircraft use semi-monocoque.

agk_11.brief: The major components of an aircraft's tail (empennage) are the elevator and rudder.
agk_11.detailed: The empennage consists of the horizontal stabiliser (with elevator) for pitch control and the vertical stabiliser (with rudder) for yaw control. Some aircraft also have a trim tab.

agk_12.brief: Sandwich structure consists of two thin layers (skins) and a light core material.
agk_12.detailed: Sandwich construction uses two thin, strong skins bonded to a lightweight core (honeycomb, foam). The core keeps the skins apart, increasing the moment of inertia for high stiffness at low weight.

agk_13.brief: Ribs (or ribs) are the structural elements that give the wing its profile shape.
agk_13.detailed: Ribs are the chord-wise structural members that define the aerofoil shape. They attach to the spars and support the skin. Ribs can be truss-type, stamped sheet metal, or composite.

agk_14.brief: Load factor 'n' describes the relationship between lift and weight (n = L/W).
agk_14.detailed: In level flight, n = 1 (lift = weight). In turns or turbulence, n increases. Limit load factor for normal category is +3.8g / -1.52g.

agk_15.brief: The maximum speed for full rudder deflection is VA (manoeuvring speed).
agk_15.detailed: VA is the speed below which full control deflection will not exceed the limit load factor. Above VA, abrupt rudder input could overstress the fin and rudder.

agk_16.brief: Fuselage components of wooden and metal aircraft are planking, frame, and longitudinal straps (stringers).
agk_16.detailed: The fuselage structure consists of longitudinal members (longerons, stringers), transverse members (frames, formers, bulkheads), and the skin (planking for wood, sheet metal for metal).

agk_17.brief: Carbon fiber has the highest strength-to-weight ratio among the listed materials.
agk_17.detailed: Composite materials, particularly carbon fibre reinforced polymer (CFRP), offer superior strength and stiffness compared to aluminium, wood, or fibreglass.

agk_18.brief: A pre-flight inspection from 15 ft (5 m) allows the best recognition of fuselage deformations.
agk_18.detailed: Viewing the aircraft from a distance helps spot asymmetries, wrinkles, or misalignments that might not be visible close-up. This is part of the walk-around inspection.

agk_19.brief: When expecting severe turbulence in mountainous terrain, reduce airspeed to manoeuvring speed (VA).
agk_19.detailed: VA provides protection against overstress from gusts. At or below VA, the aircraft will stall before exceeding the limit load factor in turbulence.

agk_20.brief: A flight control surface that is aerodynamically balanced has a part of the surface forward of the hinge line.
agk_20.detailed: Aerodynamic balancing reduces the control force needed. The horn balance or inset hinge places some area ahead of the hinge, creating a moment that assists the pilot's input.

agk_21.brief: Synthetic hydraulic oil is used in modern aircraft hydraulic systems.
agk_21.detailed: Synthetic phosphate ester-based hydraulic fluids (e.g., Skydrol) are fire-resistant and compatible with modern seals. Mineral oil is used in some older systems.

agk_22.brief: The brake system is installed only on the main gear (nose wheel typically has no brakes).
agk_22.detailed: Brakes are on the main wheels to provide braking force. Nose wheels usually have no brakes to avoid nose-over tendency when braking.

agk_23.brief: The operational reliability of the brake system should be checked during taxi.
agk_23.detailed: Before take-off, the brakes are tested during taxi by applying them at low speed to ensure they function correctly and do not pull to one side.

agk_24.brief: The rudder control is connected to the nose wheel for steering during ground operations.
agk_24.detailed: Nose wheel steering is linked to the rudder pedals. Deflecting the rudder pedals turns the nose wheel via mechanical linkage, enabling directional control on the ground.

agk_25.brief: Tyre creep is monitored by alignment marks on the tyre wall and wheel flange.
agk_25.detailed: Alignment marks (painted lines across the tyre sidewall and wheel rim) indicate if the tyre has slipped on the wheel rim, which would indicate insufficient inflation pressure or excessive braking forces.

agk_26.brief: An aircraft moves about 3 axes: vertical (yaw), lateral (pitch), and longitudinal (roll).
agk_26.detailed: The three axes intersect at the CG. The longitudinal axis runs nose-to-tail (roll). The lateral axis runs wingtip-to-wingtip (pitch). The vertical axis runs top-to-bottom (yaw).

agk_27.brief: Movement around the longitudinal axis (roll) is primarily initiated by the ailerons.
agk_27.detailed: Ailerons on the trailing edge of each wing move in opposition. The down-going aileron increases lift (rolls up), the up-going aileron decreases lift (rolls down).

agk_28.brief: Flight controls on small single-engine piston aircraft are manually actuated through rods and control cables.
agk_28.detailed: Light aircraft use a direct mechanical control system: push-pull rods or control cables transmit pilot inputs from the cockpit controls to the control surfaces.

agk_29.brief: Control inputs on fixed-wing aircraft below 2000 kg are transmitted via wire ropes or control rods.
agk_29.detailed: Below 2000 kg MTOM, mechanical control systems are standard. Above this weight, hydraulic or electric actuation may be used.

agk_30.brief: The rudder control lock on the control yoke should be set for outside parking.
agk_30.detailed: The control lock prevents wind from moving the control surfaces and causing damage while the aircraft is parked outside. It locks the ailerons and elevator in a neutral position.

agk_31.brief: Primary flight controls control movement about three axes (pitch, roll, yaw).
agk_31.detailed: Primary: elevator (pitch), aileron (roll), rudder (yaw). Secondary controls (trim, flaps, slats) improve handling and reduce control forces.

agk_32.brief: Pulling the control yoke back raises the elevator (tail-down force increases), raising the nose.
agk_32.detailed: Backward yoke movement pulls the elevator upward, increasing downward force on the tail, which rotates the aircraft nose-up around the lateral axis.

agk_33.brief: All primary flight controls: elevator, rudder, and aileron.
agk_33.detailed: These three surfaces control pitch (elevator), yaw (rudder), and roll (aileron) respectively.

agk_34.brief: Secondary flight controls improve performance and relieve pilot of excessive control forces.
agk_34.detailed: Secondary controls include trim tabs, flaps, slats, and spoilers. They assist the primary controls and enhance aircraft performance.

agk_35.brief: Moving the trim wheel forward: the trim tab moves up, and the elevator moves down.
agk_35.detailed: The trim tab deflects opposite to the desired elevator deflection. Moving the trim wheel forward lowers the elevator (nose-down trim), so the tab goes up.

agk_36.brief: Trim tab moves opposite to the desired control surface deflection.
agk_36.detailed: For nose-up trim: tab goes down → airflow pushes elevator up → tail goes down → nose goes up.

agk_37.brief: Trimming nose-up: the trim tab moves down.
agk_37.detailed: In some systems (depending on trim tab design), nose-up trim causes the tab to move down, which deflects the elevator upward.

agk_38.brief: Pitot heat prevents icing of the pitot tube, which would block the pitot-static system.
agk_38.detailed: Pitot heat uses an electrical heating element inside the pitot tube. It should be turned on when flying in visible moisture at temperatures near or below freezing.

agk_39.brief: During refuelling: no open fires, obey smoking ban, and apply ground cable (earthing).
agk_39.detailed: Fuel safety precautions: ground cable prevents static sparks, no smoking, no open flames. Correct fuel grade must be verified before refuelling.

agk_40.brief: Tank ventilation prevents underpressure (vacuum) caused by fuel consumption.
agk_40.detailed: As fuel is consumed, air must enter the tank to replace the volume, preventing a vacuum that could stop the fuel flow. Vent lines are part of the fuel system.

agk_41.brief: Before switching to another fuel tank, the fuel pump should be turned on.
agk_41.detailed: The electric fuel pump ensures uninterrupted fuel flow during tank switching, preventing air from entering the fuel lines.

agk_42.brief: A priming pump delivers fuel directly to the induction manifold or inlet valve port.
agk_42.detailed: The primer injects raw fuel into the intake manifold near the cylinders, providing the rich mixture needed for cold starts. It bypasses the carburettor.

agk_43.brief: The idle cut-off valve stops fuel flow when activated.
agk_43.detailed: Pulling the mixture to idle cut-off shuts the fuel supply, stopping the engine.

agk_44.brief: The mixture control regulates the fuel flow (fuel-to-air ratio).
agk_44.detailed: The mixture control adjusts the fuel flow to maintain the correct fuel-air ratio for the current air density. Lean for altitude, rich for take-off and climb.

agk_45.brief: The best mixture setting is reached by reducing fuel flow with the mixture control.
agk_45.detailed: The pilot leans the mixture by pulling the mixture control, reducing fuel flow until the engine runs smoothly. EGT gauge is used for precise leaning.

agk_46.brief: Fuel inspection (draining) should be conducted at latest during the pre-flight inspection before the first flight.
agk_46.detailed: Fuel drains (sumps) at the tank lowest points check for water or contaminants. A clear fuel sample should be obtained from each sump.

agk_47.brief: The voltmeter indicates the electric potential difference (voltage) in the system.
agk_47.detailed: The voltmeter measures system voltage (typically 12V or 24V). A healthy system shows charging voltage (13.5-14.5V or 27-29V) with the alternator running.

agk_48.brief: The unit for voltage is the Volt (V).
agk_48.detailed: Voltage (potential difference) is measured in volts. Current is measured in amperes (A). Resistance is measured in ohms (Ω).

agk_49.brief: Two 12V 40Ah batteries in series = 40 Ah at 24V.
agk_49.detailed: In series: voltage adds (12+12=24V), capacity (Ah) stays the same (40 Ah). In parallel: voltage same (12V), capacity adds (80 Ah).

agk_50.brief: Switching the battery master switch off in flight does not affect engine operation with magneto ignition.
agk_50.detailed: Magneto ignition is independent of the aircraft's electrical system. Magnetos generate their own electricity, so the engine continues to run. However, electrical instruments and radios will fail.

agk_51.brief: Electrically operated flaps can be deployed when the generator has failed, if the battery is charged.
agk_51.detailed: With generator failure, the battery supplies power. As long as the battery has sufficient charge, electric flaps will operate. However, battery life is limited.

agk_52.brief: Static dischargers (static wicks) discharge static charging (P-static) during flight.
agk_52.detailed: Flight through dust, rain, or ice particles builds static electricity on the airframe. Static wicks at the trailing edges discharge this to reduce radio interference and reduce the risk of lightning attachment.

agk_53.brief: The most likely reason for the starter not turning is that the master switch is not on.
agk_53.detailed: The starter motor draws power from the battery via the master switch. If the master switch is off, the starter circuit is not powered and cannot operate.

agk_54.brief: The Horizontal Situation Indicator (HSI) can be supplied by the onboard power supply.
agk_54.detailed: Gyroscopic instruments may be vacuum-driven or electrically driven. The HSI is typically electrically driven and requires electrical power to operate.

agk_55.brief: Electrically driven flight instruments are marked with 'EL'.
agk_55.detailed: Instruments marked 'EL' are electrically powered. Vacuum-driven instruments are marked 'VAC' or 'V'. This helps pilots identify which instruments will fail with electrical loss.

agk_56.brief: Horizontally opposed (flat) engines are commonly used on small aircraft and motor gliders.
agk_56.detailed: Horizontally opposed engines have cylinders on opposite sides of the crankshaft. They offer a low profile, good cooling, and smooth operation. Common in Lycoming/Continental engines.

agk_57.brief: The crankshaft converts reciprocating (linear) movement into rotary motion.
agk_57.detailed: The pistons move up and down (reciprocating). The connecting rods transfer this to the crankshaft, converting it to rotational motion to drive the propeller.

agk_58.brief: The four-stroke engine is the most common piston engine type for low/medium power.
agk_58.detailed: The four-stroke cycle: intake, compression, power (ignition), and exhaust. Four-stroke engines are reliable, efficient, and widely used in light aircraft.

agk_59.brief: A rough-running engine during magneto check may indicate a defective spark plug.
agk_59.detailed: If the engine runs rough on one magneto but smooth on both, the suspect magneto has a problem (fouled spark plug, broken wire, or magneto timing issue).

agk_60.brief: Compression ratio = Volume at BDC / Volume at TDC.
agk_60.detailed: The compression ratio is the cylinder volume at bottom dead center divided by the volume at top dead center.

agk_61.brief: Light aircraft engines typically use a flat (horizontally opposed) cylinder arrangement.
agk_61.detailed: Horizontally opposed engines (4 or 6 cylinders) offer excellent cooling, low vibration, and a low profile that fits well in aircraft cowlings.

agk_62.brief: Correct four-stroke sequence: Intake, Compression, Ignition (Power), Exhaust.
agk_62.detailed: Intake stroke: piston moves down, intake valve open. Compression: piston up, valves closed. Power: spark ignites mixture, piston forced down. Exhaust: piston up, exhaust valve open.

agk_63.brief: Cylinder fins (cooling fins) dissipate heat from the combustion process to the surrounding air.
agk_63.detailed: Air-cooled engines rely on fins to increase the surface area for heat transfer. The fins are designed to maximise airflow contact for efficient cooling.

agk_64.brief: Condensation water converges at the lowest position in the fuel tank.
agk_64.detailed: Water is heavier than fuel and settles at the lowest point of the tank. The fuel sump drain is located at this lowest point for water removal.

agk_65.brief: The fuel drain procedure should be carried out before each flight.
agk_65.detailed: Before the first flight of the day, drain fuel from each sump until clear fuel flows. Check for water, sediment, or contamination.

agk_66.brief: The highest absorption of humidity in fuel occurs in almost empty tanks.
agk_66.detailed: An empty tank has more air volume, allowing more moisture to condense from the air. Keeping tanks full reduces the air gap and humidity absorption.

agk_67.brief: The octane rating (fuel grade) describes the anti-knock rating of the fuel.
agk_67.detailed: Octane rating measures the fuel's resistance to detonation (knocking). Higher octane fuels can withstand higher compression ratios without pre-ignition.

agk_68.detailed: Avgas colour codes: 80/87 = red, 100/130 = green, 100LL (low lead) = blue, UL91 (unleaded) = purple. Colour helps prevent misfuelling.

agk_69.brief: The carburettor's major task is to produce an ignitable air/fuel mixture.
agk_69.detailed: The carburettor atomises liquid fuel and mixes it with incoming air in the correct ratio (approximately 14.7:1 for stoichiometric, richer for power).

agk_70.brief: A carburettor engine continues running at idle because it has an independent idle run system.
agk_70.detailed: The carburettor has an idle circuit that supplies fuel through a separate jet when the throttle butterfly is closed, allowing the engine to idle.

agk_71.brief: Carburettor icing results in a reduction of engine power.
agk_71.detailed: Ice forms in the venturi, restricting airflow and disturbing the fuel-air mixture. The engine loses power and runs rough. Application of carburettor heat melts the ice.

agk_72.brief: When the carburettor temperature gauge enters the yellow range, apply carburettor heat.
agk_72.detailed: The yellow range on the carburettor temperature gauge indicates potential icing conditions. Applying carb heat raises the carburettor temperature above freezing.

agk_73.brief: Carburettor heating must be switched OFF during take-off, even if icing is expected.
agk_73.detailed: Carb heat reduces engine power (hot air is less dense), which is undesirable for take-off. It should be off for full power, and only used in cruise/descent.

agk_74.brief: Carburettor icing is most likely in high humidity and temperatures between -5°C and +20°C.
agk_74.detailed: The evaporative cooling in the venturi can drop temperatures by 15-20°C, so even warm days (up to 20°C) with high humidity risk carburettor icing.

agk_75.brief: Cooling fins on air-cooled engines provide quick heat transfer to the surrounding airflow by expanding the surface area.
agk_75.detailed: The large surface area of the fins allows efficient heat dissipation from the hot cylinders to the cooling airflow directed by the cowling and baffles.

agk_76.brief: Cylinder head temperature (CHT) indication relates to the critical (hottest) cylinder.
agk_76.detailed: CHT is typically measured on the hottest cylinder (usually the rear cylinder, which has the least cooling airflow). Multiple cylinders may be monitored.

agk_77.brief: Cowlings duct air around cylinders for cooling and reduce drag by streamlining the engine.
agk_77.detailed: Engine cowlings serve two purposes: (1) direct cooling air over the cylinders, (2) reduce aerodynamic drag by providing a smooth outer surface.

agk_78.brief: Deflector plates (baffles) ensure ideal cooling for all cylinders.
agk_78.detailed: Baffles between cylinders force the cooling air to flow past each cylinder, preventing air from bypassing the cylinders and ensuring uniform cooling.

agk_79.brief: Mixing fully synthetic oil with mineral oil should be done according to the flight manual.
agk_79.detailed: Some engines allow mixing, others do not. The engine manufacturer's recommendations (in the flight manual) must be followed.

agk_80.brief: Oil pressure above the green arc after start indicates the oil is still cold (viscous).
agk_80.detailed: Cold oil is thick, creating higher resistance and thus higher indicated pressure. As the oil warms up, viscosity decreases and pressure returns to the green range.

agk_81.brief: During oil filter clogging, a bypass valve opens, allowing circulation to continue (but unfiltered).
agk_81.detailed: The oil filter bypass valve prevents complete oil starvation if the filter clogs. Dirty oil circulates unfiltered but at least lubrication is maintained.

agk_82.brief: When oil temperature reaches the red arc during climb, stop the climb until temperature returns to normal.
agk_82.detailed: High oil temperature indicates inadequate cooling. Level off, increase airspeed (more cooling airflow), and reduce power to allow engine temperatures to stabilise.

agk_83.brief: When the magneto switch is OFF, the primary circuit is closed and grounded (shorted).
agk_83.detailed: The magneto switch shorts the primary winding to ground, preventing the magnetic field from collapsing and inducing a spark. This stops the engine.

agk_84.brief: Piston engines of aircraft have two independent ignition systems (dual magnetos).
agk_84.detailed: Redundancy: each cylinder has two spark plugs, each powered by a separate magneto. If one system fails, the other provides backup for continued operation.

agk_85.brief: If the short circuit cable of the ignition system is broken, the engine continues to run (cannot be shut off with mags).
agk_85.detailed: A broken ground wire means the magneto primary is not grounded when the switch is OFF. The engine cannot be stopped by the ignition switch alone.

agk_86.brief: The magneto check before engine shutdown checks if both magnetos are correctly grounded (off).
agk_86.detailed: The 'mag drop' check ensures the P-leads are properly grounding the magnetos so the engine can be shut down with the key switch.

agk_87.brief: Fuel mixtures with a high amount of fuel (rich mixture) are called 'rich'.
agk_87.detailed: Rich mixtures have excess fuel beyond the stoichiometric ratio. This provides cooling for the cylinders (extra fuel absorbs heat) and prevents detonation.

agk_88.brief: During acceleration at constant power with a fixed-pitch propeller, engine RPM increases.
agk_88.detailed: A fixed-pitch propeller acts like a fixed gear. As airspeed increases, the propeller unloads (less angle of attack on the blades), allowing RPM to increase.

agk_89.brief: Carburettor engine power decreases with altitude because air density decreases.
agk_89.detailed: Less dense air means fewer oxygen molecules per intake stroke, reducing the fuel that can be burned and thus the power output.

agk_90.brief: With increasing altitude, carburettor engine power decreases (same as q89).
agk_90.detailed: Engine power output is proportional to air density. At 10,000 ft, the engine produces approximately 70% of sea-level power.

agk_91.brief: A higher engine power output causes a greater torque load on the crankshaft.
agk_91.detailed: Torque is the rotational force from the engine. Higher power means higher torque load on the crankshaft and propeller, affecting aircraft handling (left-turning tendency).

agk_92.brief: A broken or congested cylinder fin causes overheating of that cylinder.
agk_92.detailed: Cylinder fins provide essential cooling. If a fin is broken or blocked, the cylinder cannot dissipate heat properly, leading to local overheating and potential damage.

agk_93.brief: Engine warm-up is required because maximum power can only be reached at the correct operating temperature.
agk_93.detailed: Cold engines have high oil viscosity and poor fuel vaporisation. Warm-up ensures proper lubrication and even thermal expansion of engine components.

agk_94.brief: Exceeding maximum RPM can damage the engine, with certain parts potentially failing.
agk_94.detailed: Overspeeding can cause valve float, connecting rod failure, and catastrophic engine damage. RPM limits must be respected.

agk_95.brief: Pre-ignition (detonation) is associated with weak mixtures and high cylinder head temperatures.
agk_95.detailed: A lean mixture burns hotter, increasing CHT. This can cause the fuel to ignite prematurely (detonation) before the spark, leading to engine damage.

agk_96.brief: Engine fire in flight: close throttle, switch off ignition, set up for forced landing.
agk_96.detailed: Close throttle, mixture idle cut-off, fuel shut-off, master switch off, ignition off. If fire persists, set up for forced landing following the flight manual.

agk_97.brief: High CHT can be reduced by enriching the mixture (more fuel cools the combustion chamber).
agk_97.detailed: Additional fuel absorbs heat during vaporisation, cooling the combustion process. Enriching the mixture is the primary method to reduce CHT.

agk_98.brief: Full throttle climb is recommended for internal cooling (extra fuel provides cooling effect).
agk_98.detailed: At full throttle, the mixture is richer (more fuel), which provides internal cooling. The extra fuel absorbs heat from the cylinder walls.

agk_99.brief: When CHT approaches the limit, climb at a higher speed or level off until temperature reduces.
agk_99.detailed: Increasing airspeed improves cooling airflow. Levelling off reduces the power demand and allows the engine to cool.

agk_100.brief: Engine RPM should be kept low after start because efficient lubrication is not immediately available.
agk_100.detailed: Cold oil takes time to reach all engine components. Low RPM prevents damage from inadequate lubrication during the warm-up period.

agk_101.brief: The mixture should be leaned at all altitudes with engine power below 75%.
agk_101.detailed: Below 75% power, leaning improves efficiency and prevents spark plug fouling. Above 75% power, a rich mixture is needed for cooling.

agk_102.brief: A mixture that is too lean can cause overheating of pistons, cylinders, and valves.
agk_102.detailed: Lean mixtures burn hotter, raising combustion temperatures. This can overheat cylinder heads, exhaust valves, and pistons, causing pre-ignition or detonation.

agk_103.brief: To minimise noise after take-off, select max pitch (constant-speed propeller) to climb quickly.
agk_103.detailed: A quick climb to altitude minimises noise over populated areas. Coarse pitch reduces RPM and propeller tip speed, reducing noise.

agk_104.brief: To minimise noise on approach: lowest possible power, flaps retracted, gear up as late as practical.
agk_104.detailed: Low power reduces propeller and engine noise. Late gear/flap extension keeps the aircraft streamlined and reduces drag noise.

agk_105.brief: A Bourdon tube is suitable for measuring pressure.
agk_105.detailed: A Bourdon tube is a curved tube that straightens under pressure. It is used in oil pressure gauges and manifold pressure gauges.

agk_106.brief: The oil pressure sensor is located on the outlet side of the oil pressure pump.
agk_106.detailed: Oil pressure is measured after the pump to ensure adequate pressure is being delivered to the engine bearings.

agk_107.brief: A drop in oil pressure with steady oil temperature may indicate a false indication (sensor failure).
agk_107.detailed: Genuine oil pressure drops are usually accompanied by rising temperature (loss of lubrication). If temperature is steady, the sensor may be faulty.

agk_108.brief: When the engine is not running, manifold pressure equals ambient air pressure at the aircraft's location.
agk_108.detailed: The manifold pressure gauge (MP) measures absolute pressure in the intake manifold. With the engine off, it reads the barometric pressure at that altitude.

agk_109.brief: When the engine is not running, the manifold pressure gauge indicates barometric pressure.
agk_109.detailed: With the engine stopped, the intake manifold is open to atmosphere, so the gauge shows ambient barometric pressure.

agk_110.brief: The Exhaust Gas Temperature (EGT) indicator monitors mixture adjustment.
agk_110.detailed: EGT peaks at the stoichiometric mixture. Leaning the mixture raises EGT; enriching lowers it. Pilots use EGT to find the best power or best economy mixture setting.

agk_111.brief: The green arc on the CHT indicator indicates the normal operating temperature range.
agk_111.detailed: The green arc shows the safe operating range. The yellow arc is a caution range, and the red line indicates the maximum permissible temperature.

agk_112.brief: The fuel flow gauge shows the volume (or mass) of fuel used per unit time.
agk_112.detailed: Fuel flow is displayed in litres/hour or kg/hour (or USG/hour). It is used to monitor engine performance and manage fuel planning.

agk_113.brief: The tachometer may be driven by a flexible shaft from the engine.
agk_113.detailed: The tachometer measures crankshaft RPM. Mechanical tachometers use a flexible rotating cable; electronic ones use a sensor and display.

agk_114.brief: Dynamic pressure quadruples when airspeed is doubled (q ∝ V²).
agk_114.detailed: Dynamic pressure = ½ρV². Doubling V means 4× dynamic pressure. This is why the ASI scale is nonlinear.

agk_115.brief: Static pressure is the pressure of undisturbed (ambient) airflow.
agk_115.detailed: Static pressure is the pressure of the air not affected by the aircraft's motion. It decreases with altitude.

agk_116.brief: The airspeed indicator (ASI) is connected to the pitot tube.
agk_116.detailed: The pitot tube measures total pressure (static + dynamic). The ASI uses the difference between pitot and static pressure to indicate airspeed.

agk_117.brief: Dynamic pressure depends on air density and the square of airflow speed.
agk_117.detailed: q = ½ρV². For a given IAS, dynamic pressure is constant, but TAS varies with altitude.

agk_118.brief: The pitot-static system measures total (pitot) and static air pressure.
agk_118.detailed: The pitot tube measures total pressure. Static ports measure ambient static pressure. The difference is used for airspeed indication.

agk_119.brief: The pitot tube senses total air pressure (static + dynamic).
agk_119.detailed: Total pressure = Pstatic + ½ρV². The pitot tube opening faces directly into the airflow.

agk_120.brief: The airspeed indicator (ASI) is connected to the pitot tube.
agk_120.detailed: The ASI is the primary instrument receiving pitot pressure. It compares pitot (total) with static pressure to derive airspeed.

agk_121.brief: When static ports are blocked, the altimeter, VSI, and ASI show incorrect readings.
agk_121.detailed: All three pitot-static instruments rely on static pressure. Blocked static port causes the altimeter to freeze, VSI to read zero, and ASI to read inaccurately.

agk_122.brief: Blocked static ports cause altimeter, VSI, and ASI errors.
agk_122.detailed: Same as q121. The three instruments affected are altimeter, VSI, and ASI.

agk_123.brief: The barometric altimeter is calibrated in accordance with the standard atmosphere (ISA).
agk_123.detailed: The altimeter assumes ISA conditions: 1013.25 hPa at MSL, temperature lapse rate 0.65°C/100m, pressure decreasing at a standard rate.

agk_124.brief: QFE is the barometric pressure at a reference datum, typically runway threshold.
agk_124.detailed: QFE is the actual barometric pressure at aerodrome elevation. When set, the altimeter reads 0 ft on the runway. Used by some aerodromes for traffic pattern work.

agk_125.brief: The altimeter scale should be set before every flight and during the flight as needed.
agk_125.detailed: The altimeter subscale must be set to the local QNH or QFE before flight. During cross-country flights, QNH is updated when crossing into new pressure regions.

agk_126.brief: The altimeter subscale references the reading to a predetermined level (MSL, aerodrome, or 1013.25 hPa).
agk_126.detailed: The subscale allows the pilot to select QNH (altitude MSL), QFE (height above airfield), or standard 1013.25 hPa (flight levels).

agk_127.brief: The altimeter scale must be set before every flight and during cross-country flight.
agk_127.detailed: Pressure changes along a route require QNH updates. The pilot obtains current QNH from ATIS, ATC, or FIS.

agk_128.brief: The barometric altimeter indication is based on the preselected barometric pressure on the scale.
agk_128.detailed: The altimeter compares the selected pressure (set in the subscale window) with the ambient static pressure. A smaller window value = higher indicated altitude.

agk_129.detailed: In Europe, QNH is given in hPa (same as millibars). In the US, it is given in inches of mercury (inHg). 1013.25 hPa = 29.92 inHg.

agk_130.brief: Increasing QNH from 1000 to 1010 hPa causes ~80 m lower altimeter indication.
agk_130.detailed: 1 hPa ≈ 27 ft ≈ 8.2 m. A 10 hPa increase means the altimeter indicates 10 × 8.2 ≈ 80 m less.

agk_131.brief: With QFE set, the altimeter indicates height above the airfield.
agk_131.detailed: QFE is the pressure at the airfield. With this setting, the altimeter reads zero on the runway and shows height above the airfield during flight.

agk_132.brief: A flight level is a pressure altitude (altimeter set to 1013.25 hPa).
agk_132.detailed: Flight levels are altitudes above the transition altitude based on a standard setting of 1013.25 hPa. FL 100 = 10,000 ft pressure altitude.

agk_133.brief: In colder-than-ISA air, the indicated altitude is higher than the true altitude.
agk_133.detailed: Cold air is denser, so the pressure drops more rapidly with height. The altimeter thinks it's higher than it actually is. Cold weather = 'the aircraft is higher than it says'.

agk_134.brief: In ISA temperature conditions, indicated altitude equals true altitude.
agk_134.detailed: The altimeter is calibrated for ISA conditions. When actual temperature matches ISA, there is no temperature error.

agk_135.brief: With QNH set, the altimeter indicates the airfield elevation above MSL.
agk_135.detailed: On the ground with QNH set, the altimeter reads the published field elevation. This confirms the correct QNH setting.

agk_136.brief: The altimeter can be affected by hysteresis error (mechanical lag in the aneroid capsule).
agk_136.detailed: Hysteresis causes the altimeter to 'stick' or lag, especially after large altitude changes. Tapping the instrument may help the reading settle.

agk_137.brief: Altitude measurement is based on the change of static pressure with height.
agk_137.detailed: The altimeter measures the decreasing static pressure as altitude increases, calibrated to the standard atmosphere.

agk_138.brief: A barometric altimeter always shows altitude above a preselected reference level.
agk_138.detailed: The selected reference is set via the subscale window. Different settings give altitude above MSL (QNH), height above airfield (QFE), or pressure altitude (1013.25 hPa).

agk_139.brief: The VSI measures the present static pressure and compares it to the previous static pressure (via a calibrated leak).
agk_139.detailed: The VSI uses a calibrated capillary to create a pressure differential during climbs and descents, which is displayed as rate of change.

agk_140.brief: A VSI measures the difference between instantaneous static pressure and previous (trapped) static pressure.
agk_140.detailed: The VSI contains an instrument case with a calibrated leak. During climb, the case pressure lags behind the capsule pressure, creating a reading.

agk_141.brief: Calibrated airspeed (CAS) = IAS corrected for instrument and position error.
agk_141.detailed: IAS must be corrected for instrument errors (ASI calibration) and position errors (airflow disturbances at the static port) to obtain CAS.

agk_142.detailed: Rule of thumb: for each 1000 ft above sea level, add 2% of CAS to get TAS. At 10,000 ft, TAS = CAS + 20% = CAS × 1.2.

agk_143.brief: IAS = Indicated Air Speed (the raw reading from the airspeed indicator).
agk_143.detailed: IAS directly from the instrument before any corrections.

agk_144.brief: The ASI measures dynamic air pressure (pitot - static) and converts it to speed.
agk_144.detailed: The difference between pitot (total) and static pressure is dynamic pressure (½ρV²), which is displayed as airspeed.
