agk_145.brief: The green band on the ASI represents the normal operating range (Vno).
agk_145.detailed: Green arc: normal operating speed range. Bottom = VS1 (stall speed clean), top = Vno (maximum structural cruising speed).

agk_146.brief: The ASI measures the difference between total pressure and static pressure.
agk_146.detailed: Total pressure - static pressure = dynamic pressure, which is proportional to the square of airspeed.

agk_147.brief: The white arc on the ASI is the speed range for extended flaps.
agk_147.detailed: White arc: lower limit = VSO (stall speed landing config), upper limit = VFE (maximum flaps extended speed).

agk_148.brief: The yellow arc on the ASI indicates the caution range (avoid in turbulence).
agk_148.detailed: Yellow arc: speeds between Vno and VNE. Fly in this range only in smooth air, not in turbulence.

agk_149.brief: The red line on the ASI indicates the maximum (never-exceed) speed (VNE).
agk_149.detailed: VNE must never be exceeded. Exceeding VNE risks flutter, structural damage, or failure.

agk_150.brief: Equal magnetic poles repel each other.
agk_150.detailed: Like poles repel, opposite poles attract. The magnetic compass needle aligns with the earth's magnetic field.

agk_151.brief: Inclination (magnetic dip) is the angle between the earth's magnetic field lines and the horizontal plane.
agk_151.detailed: At the magnetic poles, inclination is 90° (vertical). At the magnetic equator, inclination is 0° (horizontal).

agk_152.brief: The earth's magnetic field is referenced to the magnetic north pole.
agk_152.detailed: Magnetic north is the direction a compass needle points. It is different from true north (geographic pole). The difference is called variation.

agk_153.brief: A magnetic compass is subject to variation, deviation, turning errors, and acceleration errors.
agk_153.detailed: Variation: difference between true north and magnetic north. Deviation: compass error caused by aircraft magnetic fields. Turning/acceleration: dynamic errors.

agk_154.brief: The fluid in a compass damps compass movements and achieves a smooth indication.
agk_154.detailed: The compass is filled with a viscous fluid (kerosene or alcohol) to dampen oscillations and reduce friction, providing a stable reading.

agk_155.brief: In the northern hemisphere, accelerating on a heading of 090° causes the compass to indicate a greater heading (over-read).
agk_155.detailed: Acceleration error (ANDS rule): Accelerate North, Decelerate South. On E/W headings, acceleration briefly shows a turn to the north (greater heading on 090°).

agk_156.brief: On heading 270° with acceleration, the compass indicates approximately 300° (shows a turn to north).
agk_156.detailed: Acceleration error: on west heading, acceleration makes the compass briefly indicate a more northerly heading (in this case, 300° instead of 270°).

agk_157.brief: Turn and bank indicator and artificial horizon are gyroscopic instruments.
agk_157.detailed: Gyroscopic instruments rely on a spinning gyro for their operation. The artificial horizon uses rigidity in space. The turn indicator uses precession.

agk_158.brief: The heading indicator should be re-aligned with the magnetic compass when the wings are level in straight-and-level flight.
agk_158.detailed: The heading indicator (DG) precesses over time. It should be reset to the compass reading only when the aircraft is in straight, level, unaccelerated flight to avoid compass errors.

agk_159.brief: The apparent drift of a gyro equals 15°/h × sin(latitude).
agk_159.detailed: Apparent drift is caused by the earth's rotation. It varies with latitude: zero at the equator, maximum (15°/h) at the poles.

agk_160.brief: Directional gyro apparent drift is caused by the earth's rotation about its axis.
agk_160.detailed: The earth rotates 15° per hour. The gyro maintains its orientation in space, so the earth's rotation creates an apparent precession in the DG.

agk_161.brief: The bank angle of a 2-minute (standard rate) turn depends on TAS.
agk_161.detailed: For a standard rate turn (3°/s), bank angle = TAS/10 + 7 (approximately). Higher TAS requires more bank angle.

agk_162.brief: A rate-of-turn indicator (turn coordinator) shows movement around the vertical axis (yaw).
agk_162.detailed: The turn coordinator displays the aircraft's rotation rate about the vertical axis, i.e., how fast the heading is changing.

agk_163.brief: A turn and bank coordinator shows the rate of turn and coordination (slip or skid).
agk_163.detailed: The turn coordinator shows the roll and yaw rate (turn needle) and coordination (inclinometer ball). Ball centred = coordinated turn.

agk_164.brief: The turn and bank indicator shows the rate and direction of turn around the vertical axis.
agk_164.detailed: The needle indicates the rate of turn (standard rate = 3°/s). The ball indicates whether the turn is coordinated.

agk_165.brief: A complete 360° turn at 3°/s (standard rate) takes 2 minutes.
agk_165.detailed: Standard rate turn = 3° per second = 360° / 3 = 120 seconds = 2 minutes.

agk_166.brief: The slip indicator shows the apparent vertical (direction of resultant force).
agk_166.detailed: The inclinometer (ball) moves towards the direction of the slip/skid. In a slip, the ball is on the low side; in a skid, it's on the high side.

agk_167.brief: The artificial horizon (attitude indicator) is a gyroscopic instrument.
agk_167.detailed: It uses a gyroscope spinning in the vertical axis to maintain a stable artificial horizon reference regardless of aircraft attitude.

agk_168.brief: The directional gyro (heading indicator) has its axis of rotation vertical to the earth's surface.
agk_168.detailed: The heading indicator gyro spins in the horizontal plane (vertical spin axis), maintaining its orientation in azimuth.

agk_169.brief: The artificial horizon is half-gimballed, movable around all three axes, and maintains its position in space.
agk_169.detailed: The gyro in the attitude indicator is mounted with freedom in roll and pitch but limited in yaw (half-gimballed). It erects to vertical when powered.

agk_170.brief: Gyros suffer from gimbal errors, which occur when the aircraft's attitude exceeds the gyro's gimbal limits.
agk_170.detailed: Gimbal errors occur when the aircraft pitches or banks beyond the gyro's range. The gyro may tumble or give false indications.

agk_171.brief: The standard directional gyro is generally reliable for bank and pitch angles less than 60°.
agk_171.detailed: Beyond 60° of bank or pitch, the DG may experience gimbal lock or precession errors, requiring re-alignment.

agk_172.brief: Precession error can occur with a directional gyro (caused by friction or earth rotation).
agk_172.detailed: Real (mechanical) precession is caused by friction and bearing wear. Apparent precession is caused by the earth's rotation.

agk_173.brief: Red light indicates 'immediate corrective action is required'.
agk_173.detailed: Warning systems use red for warnings (immediate action), amber/yellow for cautions (prompt action), and green for normal indications.

agk_174.brief: ADI stands for Attitude Director Indicator.
agk_174.detailed: The ADI is a modern version of the artificial horizon that includes flight director commands for pitch and roll guidance.

agk_175.brief: The HSI combines the directional gyro and VHF navigation receiver (VOR/ILS) information.
agk_175.detailed: The Horizontal Situation Indicator integrates heading (from the DG) with navigation information (VOR radial, ILS localiser) on a single display.

agk_176.brief: The PFD may include attitude, heading, radial, track, approach course, and flight director.
agk_176.detailed: The Primary Flight Display integrates all primary flight instruments: attitude, airspeed, altitude, vertical speed, heading, and navigation guidance.

agk_177.brief: The ND may include navigational information, heading, track, bearings, wind, and position.
agk_177.detailed: The Navigation Display (ND) shows the aircraft's position relative to navigation aids, waypoints, weather, traffic, and terrain.

agk_178.brief: Carbon monoxide from a leaking exhaust/heat exchanger cannot be detected because it is odourless and colourless.
agk_178.detailed: CO is odourless, colourless, and tasteless. It causes headaches, drowsiness, and unconsciousness. A CO detector in the cabin is essential for heater-equipped aircraft.

nav_1.brief: The Earth orbits the sun on an elliptical path, rotating from west to east on its tilted axis.
nav_1.detailed: The Earth's axis is tilted 23.5° from the perpendicular to the orbital plane (ecliptic). This tilt causes seasons. The Earth rotates west to east at 15°/hour.

nav_2.brief: The distance between Earth and the Sun is approximately 150,000,000 km (1 AU).
nav_2.detailed: One Astronomical Unit (AU) = average Earth-Sun distance = 149.6 million km. This distance varies slightly due to Earth's elliptical orbit.

nav_3.brief: The polar axis is at ~66.5° to the ecliptic plane (23.5° from perpendicular).
nav_3.detailed: Earth's axis is tilted 23.5° from the perpendicular to the orbital plane. Angle between axis and ecliptic: 90° - 23.5° = 66.5°.

nav_4.brief: Seasons are caused by the inclination of the Earth's polar axis to the plane of the ecliptic.
nav_4.detailed: As Earth orbits, the axial tilt causes different hemispheres to receive more direct sunlight at different times of year, creating summer and winter.

nav_5.brief: The rotational axis crosses Earth at the geographic North Pole and South Pole.
nav_5.detailed: The axis passes through the true geographic poles, which are different from the magnetic poles. It emerges at 90°N and 90°S.

nav_6.brief: The polar axis passes through the geographic poles and is perpendicular to the plane of the equator.
nav_6.detailed: The Earth's polar (rotation) axis passes through the geographic North and South Poles and is perpendicular to the equatorial plane. The magnetic poles are offset from the geographic poles.

nav_7.brief: The Earth's shape is best described for navigation as an ellipsoid (oblate spheroid).
nav_7.detailed: The Earth is not a perfect sphere; it is flattened at the poles and bulging at the equator. The ellipsoid model (e.g., WGS84) is used for accurate navigation.

nav_8.brief: A rhumb line (loxodrome) cuts each meridian at the same angle – a constant true course line.
nav_8.detailed: A rhumb line is a path of constant bearing. On a Mercator chart, it appears as a straight line, but it is longer than the great circle route.

nav_9.brief: A small circle does not have the Earth's centre as its centre.
nav_9.detailed: Small circles are any circle on Earth's surface that does not split the Earth into two equal hemispheres. Parallels of latitude (except the equator) are small circles.

nav_10.brief: The shortest distance between two points on Earth is a great circle arc.
nav_10.detailed: A great circle is the intersection of the Earth's surface with a plane passing through the Earth's centre. The equator and all meridians are great circles.

nav_11.brief: The equator is a parallel of latitude (0°).
nav_11.detailed: Parallels of latitude run east-west. The equator is the longest parallel (0°) and is a great circle. All other parallels are small circles.

nav_12.brief: The polar circles (Arctic and Antarctic) are at 66.5° N/S (23.5° from the poles).
nav_12.detailed: The Arctic Circle = 66.5°N. The Antarctic Circle = 66.5°S. These mark the boundary of the polar regions where the midnight sun occurs.

nav_13.brief: The polar circle divides the polar climate zone from the temperate climate zone.
nav_13.detailed: Above the Arctic/Antarctic Circle, the climate is polar (cold year-round). Below them lies the temperate zone. The tropics of Cancer/Capricorn separate temperate from tropical.

nav_14.brief: One degree of latitude = 60 NM (great circle distance).
nav_14.detailed: 1° of latitude = 60 nautical miles. 1' of latitude = 1 NM. This is a constant because meridians are great circles.

nav_15.brief: At the equator, 1° of longitude = 60 NM (111 km).
nav_15.detailed: At the equator only, 1° of longitude = 1° of latitude = 60 NM. Away from the equator, longitude distance decreases by cos(latitude).

nav_16.brief: Two points on the equator 1° apart in longitude are 60 NM apart.
nav_16.detailed: On the equator, 1° of longitude = 60 NM = 111 km.

nav_17.brief: The rhumb line distance between two points on the same parallel (not equator) is less than the great circle distance.
nav_17.detailed: On a parallel of latitude, the rhumb line (constant track) is the parallel itself. The great circle route would be slightly shorter.

nav_18.brief: On 60°N, 1° of longitude = 60 × cos(60°) = 30 NM. 40°W to 000° = 40° = 1200 NM.

nav_19.detailed: Earth rotates 15°/hour. Time = 20°/15° per hour = 1.333 h = 1 h 20 min.

nav_21.detailed: Central European Summer Time = UTC + 2. 16:00 - 2:00 = 14:00 UTC.

nav_22.brief: UTC is the obligatory time reference used in aviation worldwide.
nav_22.detailed: All aviation operations use UTC (Coordinated Universal Time, formerly GMT). Flight plans, weather reports, ATC clearances, and logs use UTC.

nav_23.brief: Crossing the 180° meridian (dateline) from east to west increases the date by one day.
nav_23.detailed: The International Date Line is roughly at 180°. Moving westward across it: +1 day. Moving eastward: -1 day.

nav_24.brief: Sunrise is defined as when the upper edge of the sun's disk first becomes visible above the horizon.
nav_24.detailed: Sunrise is when the upper limb (edge) of the sun appears. Sunset is when the upper limb disappears. These times are published in flight planning documentation.

nav_26.brief: MC = TC + VAR (east west: east = minus, west = plus). MC = TC ± VAR.
nav_26.detailed: MC = TC + VAR east, MC = TC - VAR west. More precisely: MC = TC + VAR (with east positive, west negative).

nav_27.brief: MH = CH + DEV (with east positive, west negative).
nav_27.detailed: Compass heading (CH) corrected for deviation (DEV) gives magnetic heading (MH). DEV east: MH = CH + DEV. DEV west: MH = CH - DEV.

nav_28.detailed: North = 000, East = 090, South = 180, West = 270. SSE: halfway between S (180) and SE (135) = 157.5°.

nav_29.brief: The angle between true course and true heading is the wind correction angle (WCA).
nav_29.detailed: WCA (or drift angle) = TH - TC. Positive WCA = drift to the right (wind from left). Negative WCA = drift to the left (wind from right).

nav_30.brief: Magnetic course (MC) is the angle between magnetic north and the desired track.
nav_30.detailed: MC = TC ± VAR. It is the course direction measured from magnetic north, which is what the pilot would fly in zero wind.

nav_31.brief: True course (TC) is the direction from one point to another measured from true north.
nav_31.detailed: TC is the planned track direction over the earth's surface, measured clockwise from true north (geographic north pole).

nav_32.brief: MC = MH - WCA (magnetic course = magnetic heading minus wind correction angle).
nav_32.detailed: MH = MC + WCA, so MC = MH - WCA. If WCA is positive (drift right), MC < MH.

nav_33.brief: Inclination (magnetic dip) is lowest (0°) at the magnetic equator.
nav_33.detailed: Magnetic dip (inclination) varies from 0° at the magnetic equator to 90° at the magnetic poles.

nav_34.brief: The angle between compass north and magnetic north is called deviation.
nav_34.detailed: Deviation is caused by the aircraft's magnetic fields (metal, electrical equipment). It varies with heading.

nav_35.brief: Compass north (CN) is the direction indicated by the magnetic compass on board.
nav_35.detailed: Compass north differs from magnetic north by deviation. The compass reading is the direction to compass north.

nav_36.brief: Deviation (DEV) is influenced by the aircraft's heading.
nav_36.detailed: As the aircraft turns, the magnetic fields from onboard equipment create different deviations relative to the Earth's field. A compass correction card shows remaining deviation.

nav_37.brief: Official distance units in aeronautical navigation: nautical miles (NM) and kilometres (km).
nav_37.detailed: NM is the primary unit for air navigation (1 NM = 1.852 km). Statute miles (SM) and kilometres are also used in some contexts.

nav_39.brief: The magnetic north pole is located in the Arctic region of Canada.
nav_39.detailed: As of 2024, magnetic north is near 86°N 160°W, moving towards Siberia at approximately 40 km/year.

nav_40.brief: Variation (VAR) depends on the location (varies with position on Earth).
nav_40.detailed: Variation is the angular difference between true north and magnetic north at a given location. It changes slowly over time (secular variation).

nav_41.brief: Deviation depends on the aircraft's magnetic field (heading-dependent).
nav_41.detailed: Deviation is caused by magnetic materials and electrical currents within the aircraft. It must be checked and recorded on a compass correction card.

nav_42.brief: Mercator chart: conformal, convergency 0°, rhumb lines appear as straight lines.
nav_42.detailed: Mercator is a cylindrical projection. It is conformal (angles preserved). Rhumb lines are straight, useful for plotting constant heading routes.

nav_43.brief: On a conformal chart, the angle between longitudes and latitudes is always 90°.
nav_43.detailed: Conformality means angular relationships are preserved. On all conformal projections, meridians and parallels intersect at right angles.

nav_44.brief: Lambert conformal chart: conformal and nearly true to scale.
nav_44.detailed: The Lambert conformal conic projection is the standard for aeronautical charts (ICAO 1:500,000). It is conformal with minimal scale distortion.

nav_45.brief: Pilots use true bearings (QTE) to determine the aircraft's position.
nav_45.detailed: QTE is the true bearing from a station to the aircraft. Plotting two or more QTEs on a chart provides a position fix.

nav_46.detailed: Scale = distance on chart / actual distance. 220 NM = 407.44 km = 40,744,000 cm. 40.744 / 40,744,000 = 1:1,000,000.

nav_47.detailed: MC = TC + VAR west (or - VAR east). 245 + 7 = 252°.

nav_48.detailed: Rule of thumb: TAS = IAS + 2% × (altitude/1000). 150 + 16% = 174 kt.

nav_49.brief: GS = distance / time × 60. 50 NM / 42 min × 60 = 71.4 kt.

nav_51.brief: GS = TAS - headwind = 180 - 25 = 155 kt. Distance = 155 × 2.42 h = 375 NM.

nav_53.brief: CAS 155 kt, FL 80, OAT -15°C. TAS ≈ 168 kt.
nav_53.detailed: Using flight computer (CRP-5): altitude 8000 ft, temp -15°C, CAS 155 gives TAS ~168 kt.

nav_54.brief: Pressure altitude 7000 ft, OAT +21°C, QNH altitude 6500 ft => true altitude = 6500 ft.
nav_54.detailed: True altitude is read when QNH is set. The question provides the QNH altitude directly.

nav_55.detailed: Using wind triangle: TH 250 + wind 010/30 with GS 120 gives TC 263°.

nav_56.detailed: WCA = -5° (wind from right). TH = TC + WCA = 255 - 5 = 250°.

nav_57.detailed: Using wind triangle: TAS 180 with wind 350/30 gives GS ~172 kt.

nav_58.detailed: Wind is calculated from the wind triangle: difference between TAS vector (TH 150, 150 kt) and GS vector (TC 140, 120 kt).

nav_59.detailed: Wind from 150/12 on TC 120 at TAS 120 gives a drift of ~3° to the left.

nav_60.brief: 5 min ahead of schedule with expected GS 120 kt indicates a tailwind of about 25 kt.
nav_60.detailed: 5 min early on a 120 kt schedule means actual GS = 120 × (T/(T-5)) = 144 kt. Tailwind ≈ 24 kt.

nav_61.brief: Deviation of 7 NM right after 55 NM: track error = 7/55 × 60 = 7.6°. Correction to intercept: 8° left.
nav_61.detailed: Using the 1:60 rule: TE = (off-track × 60) / distance gone = (7 × 60) / 55 = 7.6°. To rejoin course: correction = TE + TE × (distance gone / distance remaining). Approx 8° left.

nav_62.brief: 4.5 NM north after 45 NM on heading 090: track error = (4.5/45) × 60 = 6° right.
nav_62.detailed: 1:60 rule: TE = (cross-track / distance) × 60 = (4.5/45) × 60 = 6°. The aircraft drifted right, so correction is 6° to the left.

nav_63.brief: The 1:60 rule states that 1 NM lateral offset at 1° drift after 60 NM.
nav_63.detailed: The 1:60 rule is an approximation: 1° drift causes 1 NM offset over 60 NM distance. It is used for quick track error calculations in flight.

nav_64.brief: Electromagnetic waves propagate at approximately 300,000 km/s (speed of light).
nav_64.detailed: The speed of electromagnetic waves (including radio) = 299,792 km/s ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

nav_65.brief: Types of modulation: amplitude modulation (AM), frequency modulation (FM), phase modulation (PM).
nav_65.detailed: AM varies the amplitude of the carrier wave. FM varies the frequency. PM varies the phase. Aviation voice uses AM (VHF). VOR uses FM on sub-carrier.

nav_66.brief: VHF radio waves (e.g., VOR) travel as quasi-optical waves (line-of-sight).
nav_66.detailed: VHF (30-300 MHz) propagates by direct (line-of-sight) transmission. Range is limited by the radio horizon, affected by transmitter power and receiver altitude.

nav_67.brief: A VHF direction finder (VDF) can determine magnetic bearings from the station to the aircraft.
nav_67.detailed: VDF stations measure the direction of the aircraft's VHF signal. The bearing can be provided as QDM (magnetic heading to station) or QDR (magnetic bearing from station).

nav_68.brief: QDM 138, VAR 10°E: QUJ = QDM + 180 + VAR = 138 + 180 + 10 = 328°? Or QUJ = true bearing to station.
nav_68.detailed: QDM is magnetic heading to station. QUJ is true bearing to station. QUJ = QDM + VAR(E) (or - VAR(W)) but VAR is applied in the correct sense.

nav_69.brief: The earth rotates around its axis from west to east.
nav_69.detailed: Earth's rotation is west-to-east (counter-clockwise when viewed from above the North Pole). This causes the apparent movement of the sun from east to west.

nav_70.brief: The imaginary axis of the Earth passes through the geographic North and South Poles.
nav_70.detailed: The axis of rotation connects the true geographic poles.

nav_71.brief: QDR means magnetic bearing from the station to the aircraft.
nav_71.detailed: QDR is the reciprocal of QDM. If QDM = 045, QDR = 225. QDR is the bearing the station measures to the aircraft.

nav_72.brief: QDM 035 from VDF: aircraft is northeast of the station.
nav_72.detailed: QDM is magnetic heading to the station. QDM 035 means the aircraft is 035 magnetic from the station, which is northeast.

nav_73.brief: The VDF range depends on the aircraft's altitude (higher = greater range).
nav_73.detailed: VDF uses VHF frequencies, which are line-of-sight. Higher altitude extends the radio horizon and increases VDF range.

nav_74.brief: VDF accuracy can be affected by the coastline effect (refraction of radio waves at land/sea boundaries).
nav_74.detailed: Coastal refraction (shoreline effect) bends radio waves when they cross the coastline at an angle, introducing bearing errors in VDF.

nav_75.brief: An Automatic Direction Finder (ADF) is needed on board to receive signals from a Non-Directional Beacon (NDB).
nav_75.detailed: The NDB transmits on LF/MF (200-1750 kHz). The ADF receiver uses a loop antenna to determine the bearing to the NDB.

nav_76.brief: Heading 095 with RBI 350 indicates crosswind increased. Decrease MH.
nav_76.detailed: RBI 350 means the station is 10° to the left (350 = -10 from 360). The aircraft is drifting right, so heading must be decreased (turn left).

nav_77.brief: Locator beacons have a lower range than NDBs (typically < 50 NM vs 100+ NM).
nav_77.detailed: Locator beacons are low-power NDBs used for approach and holding. They have limited range compared to en-route NDBs.

nav_78.brief: Shoreline (coastal) effect is greatest at an acute angle to the coast, below 6000 ft.
nav_78.detailed: Coastal refraction is most pronounced when the aircraft approaches the coast at a shallow angle and at low altitude.

nav_79.brief: Fading (signal strength variation) occurs mainly during the night.
nav_79.detailed: At night, sky wave propagation from distant stations can interfere with ground wave signals, causing fading. This is known as the 'night effect'.

nav_80.brief: The progress of an electromagnetic wave is described by its phase angle.
nav_80.detailed: Phase describes the position of a wave relative to a reference point. It is measured in degrees (0-360°).

nav_81.brief: A VOR radial corresponds to the QDR (magnetic bearing from the VOR station).
nav_81.detailed: A VOR radial is the magnetic bearing from the VOR station to the aircraft. The radial name = magnetic direction from the VOR. QDR is the same.

nav_82.brief: Full CDI deflection means the aircraft is at least 10° from the selected course.
nav_82.detailed: The Course Deviation Indicator (CDI) shows full deflection at 10° off course (or about 2½ dots per degree). At full deflection, the aircraft is more than 10° from the selected radial.

nav_83.brief: DME (Distance Measuring Equipment) operates in the UHF frequency band.
nav_83.detailed: DME uses UHF (960-1215 MHz). It transmits paired pulses and measures the time delay of the reply to determine distance.

nav_84.brief: DME determines distance based on time measurement (pulse timing).
nav_84.detailed: The aircraft interrogates with a pulse pair. The ground transponder replies after a fixed 50 µs delay. The DME calculates distance = (time - 50 µs) × speed of light / 2.

nav_85.brief: The DME reading is a slant range distance (not horizontal distance).
nav_85.detailed: DME measures the line-of-sight (slant) distance to the station. At high altitude close to the station, the slant range error is significant.

nav_86.brief: The maximum number of aircraft obtaining DME distance simultaneously is approximately 100.
nav_86.detailed: DME systems can handle about 100 aircraft interrogations simultaneously using staggered pulse spacing and automatic gain control.

nav_87.brief: DME distance error increases when approaching the DME station (slant range error).
nav_87.detailed: At high altitude near the station, the slant range is much greater than the horizontal distance. As the aircraft passes the station, the DME shows decreasing distance to directly overhead, then increasing.

nav_88.brief: Ground radar (primary radar) provides instantaneous distance and direction (bearing) of targets.
nav_88.detailed: Primary radar transmits radio pulses and measures the echo return. It gives range and azimuth of all reflecting objects. It does not provide altitude or identification.

nav_89.brief: The on-board equipment of SSR (Secondary Surveillance Radar) is called a transponder.
nav_89.detailed: The transponder receives SSR interrogations and replies with a coded response containing the squawk code and (in Mode C/S) altitude.

nav_90.brief: Primary radar uses reflected signals; secondary radar signals are answered (replied to) by the transponder.
nav_90.detailed: Primary radar: transmits a pulse, receives echo from target. Secondary radar (SSR): transmits interrogation, the aircraft transponder replies with encoded data.

nav_91.brief: The transponder code for emergency is 7700.
nav_91.detailed: Standard codes: 7500 = hijack, 7600 = radio failure, 7700 = emergency.

nav_92.brief: Mode C of the transponder transmits pressure altitude.
nav_92.detailed: Mode C reports the aircraft's pressure altitude (1013.25 hPa reference) encoded in Gillham code. ATC can correlate this with the primary return.

nav_93.brief: NAVSTAR/GPS requires 24 active satellites for the space segment.
nav_93.detailed: The GPS constellation has 24 operational satellites (plus spares) in 6 orbital planes at 20,200 km altitude. They provide global coverage.

nav_94.brief: The Arctic and Antarctic circles are 23.5° from the poles (66.5° N/S).

nav_95.brief: Any meridian intersects the equator at an angle of 90°.
nav_95.detailed: Meridians are great circles running north-south. The equator is perpendicular (90°) to all meridians.

nav_96.brief: A small circle does not have its centre in the centre of the Earth.
nav_96.detailed: Only great circles have the Earth's centre as centre. All other circles are small circles.

nav_97.brief: A difference of 10' of latitude = 10 NM.

nav_98.brief: At the equator, 1° of longitude = 60 NM. 010°W to 011°W = 1° = 60 NM.

nav_100.brief: UTC is the time to be used in aviation (formerly GMT).
nav_100.detailed: Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) is the standard time reference for all aviation.

nav_101.brief: Converting from TC to MC: variation is added if east, subtracted if west.
nav_101.detailed: MC = TC + VAR east (or - VAR west). 'East is least' (subtract), 'west is best' (add).

nav_102.brief: Aviation navigation uses NM for distances, ft/min for vertical speed.
nav_102.detailed: Distance: nautical miles (NM). Short distances: m or km. Vertical speed: ft/min or m/s.

nav_103.brief: The vertical deflection of the compass needle (inclination) is largest at the magnetic poles.
nav_103.detailed: At the magnetic poles, the Earth's field is vertical, so dip = 90°. At the magnetic equator, dip = 0°.

nav_104.brief: Magnetic inclination (dip) is 0° at the magnetic equator.
nav_104.detailed: At the magnetic equator, the magnetic field lines are horizontal (parallel to the Earth's surface).

nav_105.brief: When turning onto a southerly heading (NH), the compass under-reads, so stop the turn before the desired heading.
nav_105.detailed: Compass turning errors: on southerly headings, the compass leads (shows a greater turn than actual). Stop the turn before the desired heading is reached.

nav_106.brief: Magnetic variation ranges from 0° to 180° E/W.
nav_106.detailed: Variation is the angular difference between true and magnetic north. It can be up to 180° near the magnetic poles.

nav_107.brief: Lines of constant magnetic variation are called isogonic lines.
nav_107.detailed: Isogonic lines connect points of equal magnetic variation. The agonic line (zero variation) connects points where true north = magnetic north.

nav_108.brief: The directional gyro (DG) should be adjusted after take-off, using the magnetic compass.
nav_108.detailed: The DG should be set in straight-and-level flight after take-off. It is aligned with the magnetic compass and then corrected for precession during flight.

nav_109.brief: On west courses, accelerating descent causes the compass indication to become smaller (decrease).
nav_109.detailed: On west headings, acceleration makes the compass read as if turning north (lower indication). Deceleration gives the opposite effect.

nav_110.brief: Acceleration error occurs on east and west courses (the ANDS rule).
nav_110.detailed: ANDS: Accelerate North, Decelerate South. The error is maximum on E/W headings and zero on N/S headings.

nav_111.brief: Magnetic compass deviation is caused by electrical devices, metal parts (especially iron), and the ignition system.
nav_111.detailed: Any ferrous metal or electrical current in the aircraft creates magnetic fields that deflect the compass needle from magnetic north.

nav_112.brief: A chart projection with straight parallel latitude and longitude lines is a cylindrical projection.
nav_112.detailed: Cylindrical projections (like Mercator) have straight, parallel lines of latitude and longitude intersecting at right angles.

nav_113.brief: HJ means sunrise to sunset (daytime hours only).
nav_113.detailed: Service abbreviation: HJ = from sunrise to sunset (daytime operation). Derived from French 'heures du jour'.

nav_114.brief: A magnetic compass shows the direction relative to compass north.
nav_114.detailed: Compass north is the direction the compass needle points, which differs from magnetic north by deviation.

nav_115.brief: QDM means the magnetic heading to the station (with zero wind).
nav_115.detailed: QDM is the bearing you would steer (magnetic) to fly directly to the station assuming zero wind. It is also called the 'homing' bearing.

nav_116.brief: Horizontal speed in navigation uses kt (knots) or km/h.
nav_116.detailed: Knots (NM/h) is the primary unit. km/h is also used.

nav_119.brief: At the standard parallels of a Lambert conformal chart, the projection is equidistant and true to scale.
nav_119.detailed: The Lambert projection has two standard parallels where the scale is exact. Between them, scale is slightly too small; outside, slightly too large.

nav_120.brief: The ICAO 1:500,000 chart is a conformal conic projection with two standard parallels.
nav_120.detailed: This is the standard VFR chart. It uses the Lambert conformal conic projection with two standard parallels for minimal distortion.

nav_121.brief: A chart is conformal when an angle depicted on the chart equals the angle on Earth's surface.
nav_121.detailed: Conformality preserves angles locally. On a conformal chart, a bearing line drawn on the chart represents the correct angle on the Earth.

nav_122.brief: Aeronautical charts must be up-to-date, useful, and clear.
nav_122.detailed: Charts must be current (check the revision date), legible, and provide the information needed for the flight. Outdated charts can lead to navigation errors.

nav_123.brief: QTE (true bearing from station) can be used to identify the present position.
nav_123.detailed: By plotting QTE from a known station, the pilot can establish a position line. Two or more QTEs provide a fix.

nav_124.brief: The highest spot elevation or highest obstacle on aeronautical charts is marked by a point with the elevation in ft.
nav_124.detailed: Obstacle heights and spot elevations are shown on charts to help pilots determine safe altitudes.

nav_125.brief: Isogonic lines on the ICAO 1:500,000 chart are shown as black, dashed lines.
nav_125.detailed: Isogonic lines show the magnetic variation. They are dashed lines labelled with the variation value in degrees east or west.

nav_127.brief: TH 270, WCA -10: return course TH = 100° (opposite + reverse WCA).
nav_127.detailed: Return course = TC ± 180°. TH(return) = TH(270) + 180 + WCA reversal = 90 + 10 = 100°?Actually: outbound TH = TC + WCA. Return TC = outbound TC + 180. Return TH = return TC + (-WCA).

nav_128.brief: Wind angle (WA) is the angle between TC and the wind direction.
nav_128.detailed: WA is measured clockwise from TC to the wind direction. Headwind: 0° ≤ WA ≤ 90° or 270° ≤ WA ≤ 360°. Crosswind: WA ≤ 90°.

nav_129.brief: Relative wind angle (RWA) is the angle between the wind direction and the heading.
nav_129.detailed: RWA determines the wind component relative to the aircraft's heading. 0° = headwind, 90° = crosswind from right, 180° = tailwind, 270° = crosswind from left.

nav_130.brief: Dead reckoning calculates position from speed, direction, time, and wind.
nav_130.detailed: Dead reckoning uses the last known position, then applies course, speed, time, and wind to estimate current position. It is the foundation of all navigation.

nav_132.brief: Heading 070, track 061, TAS 120, GS 118. Wind = 130/19 kt.
nav_132.detailed: Drift = 9° left. Calculated from wind triangle.

nav_134.brief: GS ≠ TAS even with only crosswind (crosswind causes drift but also changes GS).
nav_134.detailed: Any crosswind component means the TAS vector is not aligned with the track, so GS differs from TAS even without a headwind/tailwind component.

nav_135.brief: Drift angle (DA) is the angle between the longitudinal axis (heading) and the track.
nav_135.detailed: DA = TH - TC (or track - heading). Positive DA = drift to the right.

nav_136.brief: VFR pilots use visual navigation, dead reckoning, and radio navigation.
nav_136.detailed: VFR navigation: pilotage (visual landmarks), dead reckoning (DR), and radio navigation aids (VOR, NDB, GPS) as supporting tools.

nav_137.brief: Interception lines are used as guidance upon loss of orientation.
nav_137.detailed: Interception lines are prominent features (roads, rivers, coastlines) that can be flown to until a known navigation point is reached.

nav_138.brief: TAS 100 kt, 60 NM in 36 min = GS 100 kt. TAS = GS, so there is no wind component.
nav_138.detailed: GS = 60 NM / 0.6 h = 100 kt. TAS = 100 kt. GS = TAS = no wind.

nav_139.brief: Crosswind limit 16 kt, wind 22 kt: max angle = sin¯¹(16/22) = 46.7° ≈ 55°.
nav_139.detailed: The crosswind component = wind speed × sin(angle). For a 22 kt wind to have only 16 kt crosswind, the angle must be ≤ sin¯¹(16/22) ≈ 47°.

nav_140.brief: 22 NM in 12 min at TAS 110 kt: GS = 110 kt, so there is tailwind.
nav_140.detailed: GS = 22 NM / 0.2 h = 110 kt. TAS = 110 kt. GS = TAS means no wind, but if GS > TAS, there is tailwind. Here GS = TAS = 110, so no wind.

nav_141.brief: 84 NM route, 35 NM to checkpoint, TAS 90 kt, GS with wind... time = 45 min.
nav_141.detailed: Time = distance / GS. Given the data, the flight time from A to B is 45 minutes.

nav_142.brief: Safety height = highest obstacle + 500 ft within 5 NM of track, rounded up to 100 ft.
nav_142.detailed: The safety altitude is calculated by adding 500 ft to the highest obstacle within 5 NM each side of track, then rounding up to the next 100 ft.

nav_143.brief: The number of oscillations per second of an electromagnetic wave is called frequency.
nav_143.detailed: Frequency (f) is measured in Hertz (Hz). 1 Hz = 1 cycle per second. The wavelength λ = c/f where c = speed of light.

nav_144.brief: QTE is the true bearing from the station to the aircraft.
nav_144.detailed: QTE is used for position fixing. The ground station measures the true bearing from the station to the aircraft, or the pilot calculates it.

nav_145.brief: Ionospheric refraction of radio waves depends on solar radiation (ionisation).
nav_145.detailed: The ionosphere is created by solar UV radiation. At night, the D layer disappears, allowing sky wave propagation of MF/HF signals over long distances.

nav_146.brief: ADF reception range is 200 kHz to 526.5 kHz (LF/MF band).
nav_146.detailed: The ADF receiver covers the non-directional beacon (NDB) band from 190-1750 kHz, but the standard aviation NDB band is 200-526.5 kHz.

nav_147.brief: QDM getting larger while approaching VDF station: the wind is from the left.
nav_147.detailed: If the QDM increases, the aircraft is drifting right (wind from left), so the heading must be adjusted left to maintain the track to the station.

nav_148.brief: QDM 040: aircraft is northwest of the station.
nav_148.detailed: QDM 040 means the aircraft is on a bearing 040 from the station, which is northeast. Check: QDM = magnetic heading to station. If QDM = 040, the station is NE of the aircraft.

nav_149.brief: VDF accuracy can be affected by propagation errors and site errors.
nav_149.detailed: Propagation errors include coastal refraction and terrain effects. Site errors include nearby buildings, power lines, or other VHF transmitters.

nav_150.brief: With the ADF selector in ANT position, the ADF loop is used for signal reception only (no bearing indication).
nav_150.detailed: In ANT mode, the ADF acts as a simple AM receiver (listen to NDB ident). The bearing needle is parked at 90° or 180°. Switch to ADF for bearing.

nav_151.brief: The Radio Magnetic Indicator (RMI) directly indicates QUJ (true bearing to the station).
nav_151.detailed: The RMI combines a magnetic compass card with one or two bearing pointers. When tuned to a VOR or NDB, it shows the magnetic bearing to the station.

nav_152.brief: Locator beacons and en-route NDBs differ in coverage (range).
nav_152.detailed: Locator beacons have lower power and range (< 50 NM) than en-route NDBs (100+ NM). They are used for approach procedures.

nav_153.brief: Non-directional beacons (NDB) generally have a coverage above 120 NM.
nav_153.detailed: Standard NDBs have a range of 100-200 NM depending on power and frequency. Locator NDBs have lower range (< 50 NM).

nav_154.brief: LF/MF radio propagation is subject to mountain and coastal effects.
nav_154.detailed: LF/MF waves can be reflected, refracted, or shadowed by mountains. The coastline effect bends waves at land/sea interfaces.

nav_155.brief: ADF can be influenced by atmospheric effects, topographical effects, and acceleration forces.
nav_155.detailed: Atmospheric: thunderstorms generate static. Topographical: mountains and coastline. Acceleration: errors during turns due to loop antenna design.

nav_156.brief: VOR coverage is unlimited at higher altitudes, limited by line-of-sight (quasi-optical propagation).
nav_156.detailed: VOR operates at VHF (108-117.95 MHz). Range is line-of-sight. At typical GA altitudes, range is 40-100 NM. Higher altitude = greater range. There is also a slant range limit.

nav_160.brief: VOR coverage is unlimited at higher altitudes, limited by line-of-sight (quasi-optical propagation).
nav_160.detailed: VOR operates at VHF (108-117.95 MHz). Range is line-of-sight. At typical GA altitudes, range is 40-100 NM. Higher altitude = greater range. There is also a slant range limit.

nav_161.brief: To keep the transponder ready but not replying, the switch should be in STBY (standby).
nav_161.detailed: STBY mode powers the transponder but does not respond to interrogations. This is used on the ground before receiving ATC instructions to squawk a code.

nav_162.brief: 'Squawk ident' means the IDENT button should be pressed once.
nav_162.detailed: IDENT (identify) causes the aircraft's transponder return to 'blip' on ATC radar. The button should be pressed once briefly when instructed.

nav_163.brief: 'Squawk standby' means the operating mode STBY should be selected.
nav_163.detailed: STBY means the transponder is on but not replying. This is used when instructed by ATC or when the reply is not required.

nav_164.brief: Altitude enquiry via transponder (Mode C) reports pressure altitude.
nav_164.detailed: Mode C reports pressure altitude based on 1013.25 hPa setting. The pilot must set the correct local QNH for the ATC system to display corrected altitude.

nav_165.brief: A GPS navigation database is valid for 28 days.
nav_165.detailed: The aviation GPS database (Jeppesen, Garmin) is updated every 28 days to reflect changes in navigation data (waypoints, frequencies, airspace).

nav_166.brief: GPS accuracy can be monitored by a fifth satellite whose position is known.
nav_166.detailed: RAIM (Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring) uses a 5th satellite (or more) to check the consistency of navigation solutions and detect faults.

nav_168.brief: The Lambert conformal projection is an almost equidistant, area-accurate, orthomorphic (conformal) projection.
nav_168.detailed: The Lambert projection preserves shape (conformal) over small areas, has minimal area distortion, and is used for the ICAO 1:500,000 chart.

nav_169.brief: Quasi-optical waves travel through the air directly from the transmitter to the receiver (line-of-sight).
nav_169.detailed: VHF and UHF waves propagate quasi-optically: they travel in straight lines and are limited by the radio horizon.

nav_170.detailed: Service abbreviation HJ indicates operation during daylight hours only (from French 'heures du jour').

nav_171.brief: Terrestrial navigation is orientation by ground features during visual flight.
nav_171.detailed: Terrestrial navigation (pilotage) uses landmarks, roads, rivers, towns, and coastlines visible from the cockpit to navigate.

nav_172.brief: Descending from 9000 ft to 1500 ft at 1200 ft/min = 7500/1200 = 6.25 min.
nav_172.detailed: Altitude to lose = 9000 - 1500 = 7500 ft. Time = 7500 / 1200 = 6.25 min.
